topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Comparing fractions
topic.description: Compare and order unit fractions, and fractions with the same denominator
evidence: Order 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 from largest to smallest
Explain that a larger denominator means smaller unit fractions
Compare 2/5 and 4/5 and explain that 4/5 is larger because it has more fifths
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has eaten 3/8 of a cake and a friend has eaten 5/8 of the same cake, can they tell you who has eaten more — and put those fractions in order from smallest to biggest?

pedagogy.summary: Comparing and ordering unit fractions (1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5) and same-denominator fractions (2/5, 4/5) is the procedure that operationalises fraction magnitude. Two rules that FEEL contradictory must be held together: for unit fractions a larger denominator means a SMALLER fraction (more equal parts, each smaller), while for same-denominator fractions a larger numerator means a LARGER fraction (more of the same-sized part). Teach both with bars/number lines so the direction of each rule is grounded in piece size, and so children don't over-generalise a blanket 'bigger bottom = smaller'.
bestPractices: Order unit fractions against a common whole using aligned bars so 1/5 is visibly the smallest and 1/2 the largest
Use a 'cut into more pieces' action so children feel each piece shrink as the denominator grows
Order same-denominator fractions by counting how many of the SAME piece, keeping the piece size fixed
Place fractions on a shared number line so both comparisons are read as position
Make explicit WHY the denominator direction flips between the two cases (piece size vs how many pieces)
keyRepresentations: Aligned equal-length bars for unit fractions (a fraction wall column)
Number line locating the fractions being compared
Same-denominator strip where only the count of shaded parts changes
'Cut into more' animation shrinking each unit fraction
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias — orders unit fractions 1/5, 1/4, 1/3, 1/2 (bigger denominator judged bigger)
Over-correction — after learning 'bigger bottom = smaller', reverses same-denominator fractions too (1/5 > 2/5 > 3/5)
Compares numerators and denominators independently rather than as one quantity
Cannot place the fractions consistently on a number line to check the order
Ignores that the whole must be the same when comparing

learn.summary: Year 3 learners (age 7-8) compare and order unit fractions (1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5) and same-denominator fractions (1/5...4/5). Two directions that feel contradictory must be held together: for unit fractions a LARGER denominator means a SMALLER fraction (the whole is cut into more, smaller pieces), while for same-denominator fractions a LARGER numerator means a LARGER fraction (more of the same-sized piece). These are not one rule reversing; they compare different varying quantities. Ground both in piece size using aligned bars and a shared number line so children do not over-generalise a blanket 'bigger bottom = smaller'.

activities.title: Order unit fractions under one shared whole
feedback: If a learner puts 1/5 first and 1/2 last (whole-number bias), lay the unit fractions as aligned bars against ONE whole so 1/5 is visibly the shortest; ask them to point to which piece is largest.
Probe: 'You put 1/2 first. Show me on the bars (for example, equal pizzas cut into halves and fifths) WHY one half is bigger than one fifth.'
If pieces are not aligned to a common whole, redraw them under the same '1 whole' rule before comparing, and remind that the represented whole must be the same to compare the portions.
activities.rationale: Grounding fraction magnitude in part size against a common whole targets whole-number bias when ordering unit fractions.
sourceClaims: Students frequently show whole-number bias when ordering fractions, viewing those with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3); this can be diagnosed by having them label and compare fractions, and remedied by grounding magnitude in the number line and part size.
Year 3 pupils compare and order unit fractions, and fractions with the same denominators.
learnerActions: Take fraction cards 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 and arrange them from largest to smallest.

Represent each card as a bar the same length as a single common '1 whole' bar, split into that many equal parts with one part shaded, and line the bars up beneath that '1 whole' so the shaded pieces can be compared by length.
State and check the order: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 from largest to smallest, confirming 1/5 is the shortest and 1/2 the longest.
Explain out loud why 1/2 is bigger than 1/5 by pointing at the piece lengths against the same whole.
activities.intendedInsight: When the whole is the same, a unit fraction with a larger denominator is smaller because the whole is split into more, smaller pieces.

activities.title: Cut into more pieces and feel each one shrink
feedback: Probe: 'Which is bigger, 1/3 or 1/4? If I cut a cake into more and more pieces, what happens to the size of each piece?'
If a learner still judges more pieces as bigger, slow the cutting down and compare one piece before and after an extra cut on the same whole.
An optional 'cut into more' action or animation that adds a slice and visibly shrinks every piece makes the shrinking concrete; this is one way to show it, not the only way.
activities.rationale: An enacted partitioning action ties the abstract denominator rule to a felt change in piece size, reinforcing more-parts-means-smaller.
sourceClaims: Students frequently show whole-number bias when ordering fractions, viewing those with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3); this can be diagnosed by having them label and compare fractions, and remedied by grounding magnitude in the number line and part size.
learnerActions: Start with one whole and partition it into 2, then 3, then 4, then 5 equal pieces, each time comparing the size of a single piece to the previous one.
Describe what happens to the size of each piece as more cuts are added.
Connect the action back to the cards: more pieces (bigger denominator) means each piece, and so each unit fraction, is smaller.
activities.intendedInsight: Cutting a fixed whole into more equal parts makes each part smaller, so more pieces means a smaller unit fraction.

activities.title: Order same-denominator fractions by counting the same-sized piece
feedback: If a learner reverses the fifths (1/5 > 2/5 > 3/5 > 4/5) after learning 'bigger bottom = smaller' (over-correction), fix the piece size at one fifth and count how many are shaded; show 4/5 covers more of the bar than 2/5.

Probe: 'Why does "more fifths" mean MORE, but a bigger bottom number mean LESS?' Separate 'how big each piece is' from 'how many pieces there are' — the unit-fraction case varies the piece size, this case varies the count.
Reinforce that here the piece size does NOT change; only the count of shaded pieces does.
activities.rationale: Holding the piece fixed while varying the count isolates the numerator's meaning and guards against over-generalising the denominator rule to same-denominator sets.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils compare and order unit fractions, and fractions with the same denominators.
learnerActions: Take fifths fractions 1/5, 2/5, 3/5, 4/5 and order them from largest to smallest, keeping the piece size (one fifth) fixed.
Represent each as a bar where only the number of shaded fifths changes, and check that 4/5 covers more of the bar than 2/5.
State the order 4/5, 3/5, 2/5, 1/5 and explain that more fifths means more because each piece is the same size.
activities.intendedInsight: When the denominator is fixed, the numerator counts how many of the same-sized piece, so a larger numerator means a larger fraction.

activities.title: Place and read the fractions on a shared number line
feedback: Probe: 'Where would 3/5 sit compared to 1/2 on the line, bigger or smaller? How could the number line help you decide?'
If a learner compares numerators and denominators independently (component comparison), insist on one quantity per card and order by position on the line.
If 1/5 is placed furthest right, revisit the unit-fraction bars before returning to the line.
activities.rationale: A shared number line represents each fraction as a single quantity, countering component comparison and letting learners self-check both orderings against position.
sourceClaims: Students frequently show whole-number bias when ordering fractions, viewing those with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3); this can be diagnosed by having them label and compare fractions, and remedied by grounding magnitude in the number line and part size.
learnerActions: Place each fraction from both sets onto one shared number line between 0 and 1, consistent with its order.
Decide where 3/5 sits compared with 1/2 and judge whether it is bigger or smaller.
Use position on the line to check that the unit-fraction order and the fifths order agree with where each fraction lands.

Try a mixed set (e.g. 1/5, 1/2, 3/5) and use positions on the number line, together with the two rules, to order it; note that neither rule on its own can compare fractions such as 3/5 and 1/2, where both the numerator and the denominator differ.
activities.intendedInsight: Both comparisons can be read as position on one number line, which unifies the unit-fraction and same-denominator cases into a single idea of magnitude.

activities.title: Practise and check the orderings
feedback: For 2/5 vs 4/5, confirm 4/5 is larger because it has more fifths; if a learner instead picks 2/5 (over-applying 'bigger bottom = smaller' where the denominators are equal), return to the fixed-piece bar and count the shaded fifths.

Checking whether the order is correct is useful, but build the underlying magnitude sense first with bars and the number line, since simply recognising the right answer does not by itself elicit the reasoning.
Ask the learner to justify each answer so correct ordering is backed by the piece-size explanation, not a memorised rule.
activities.rationale: Targeted practice can consolidate ordering and reveal whole-number bias or over-correction. Ask for a piece-size or number-line explanation alongside the selected or ordered answer.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils compare and order unit fractions, and fractions with the same denominators.
learnerActions: Order 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 from largest to smallest as an ordering task.

Compare 2/5 and 4/5 and choose the larger, explaining the choice; be alert to the tempting wrong answer of picking 2/5 by over-applying 'bigger bottom = smaller' to a comparison where only the numerator differs.
Place a given fraction at the right spot on a number line as a final check.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent, correct ordering of both fraction types, with the reasoning articulated, confirms the magnitude idea has taken hold.

constraints: When comparing fractions with bars or area representations, the represented whole must be the same; aligned bars and number-line placements only work when they share one unit. As numbers, fractions still have comparable magnitudes (e.g. by position on a shared number line).
A static fraction wall or reference image lets children read off comparisons but does not let them enact the ordering, so use it as a reference scaffold alongside, not instead of, hands-on ordering.
Recognition or multiple-choice practice checks whether the order is correct but does not by itself require the learner to construct and justify the ordering; pair it with explanation.

Keep the two cases explicitly connected: unit-fraction comparison varies the denominator (numerator fixed at 1), while same-denominator comparison varies the numerator (denominator fixed) — explain that they compare different quantities, which is why 'bigger bottom = smaller' must not be over-generalised to same-denominator sets. This is not a single rule flipping.
Fraction comparison here uses lengths of bars and positions on a number line (or areas of equal wholes); for this objective a third spatial dimension adds no comparative information.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row claimed a static image 'can't let them ACT the ordering' and that dialogue is poor for this procedure; these have been softened to scoped limits (a static reference supports reading-off but not enacting) rather than universal laws, since the sources do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity.

Optional interaction examples (drag-to-unfurl bars, a 'cut into more' action, fifths bars growing, placement on a line) are retained as concrete ways to make the mechanism visible; they are illustrative, not mandatory.

The original pedagogy and quiz task described the denominator rule as 'flipping' between the two cases and referenced a 'larger-denominator distractor' for 2/5 vs 4/5; both are incoherent (the cases vary different quantities; 2/5 and 4/5 share denominator 5) and have been corrected rather than reproduced.

Self-audit of the arithmetic and ordering logic found the source orderings correct: unit fractions largest-to-smallest 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5; fifths largest-to-smallest 4/5, 3/5, 2/5, 1/5; 4/5 > 2/5. No conceptual errors were introduced into learner-facing actions.

probeDeeper: You put 1/2 first. Show me on the pizzas WHY one half is bigger than one fifth.
Which is bigger, 1/3 or 1/4? If I cut a cake into more and more pieces, what happens to the size of each piece?
You ordered the fifths 1/5, 2/5, 3/5, 4/5. Why does 'more fifths' mean MORE, but a bigger bottom number mean LESS?
Where would 3/5 sit compared to 1/2 on the line — bigger or smaller? How could the number line help you decide?
assess.correctAnswer: Unit fractions largest→smallest: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 (larger denominator = smaller piece). Same-denominator fractions largest→smallest: 4/5, 3/5, 2/5, 1/5 (more fifths = more). Each card placed consistently on the number line matching its order.

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias on unit fractions — orders 1/5 > 1/4 > 1/3 > 1/2, treating the larger denominator as the larger fraction
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lay the unit fractions as aligned bars against one whole so 1/5 is visibly smallest; cut a whole into more pieces to feel each shrink; reteach more-parts-means-smaller
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Puts 1/5 first and 1/2 last, or places 1/5 furthest right on the number line

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-correction — having learned 'bigger bottom = smaller', reverses the same-denominator set too (1/5 > 2/5 > 3/5 > 4/5)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fix the piece size (a fifth) and count how many are shaded; show 4/5 covers more of the bar than 2/5; separate 'how big each piece' from 'how many pieces'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders the fifths backwards, treating a bigger numerator as smaller

errorPatterns.pattern: Component comparison — compares numerators and denominators independently instead of as one quantity, muddling any set that mixes denominators
errorPatterns.nextMove: Represent each fraction as a length on a common number line and order by position; insist on one quantity per card
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders a mixed set by looking only at the top numbers (or only the bottom), ignoring the relationship

responseLevels.gap: Orders unit fractions by denominator size (1/5 largest), or reverses the same-denominator set — whole-number bias runs throughout.
responseLevels.full: Orders both sets correctly and fluently, places them consistently on a number line, and articulates the unifying idea — the denominator sets the piece size (more pieces → smaller each), the numerator counts how many of that piece — transferring to a novel comparison.
responseLevels.partial: Orders unit fractions correctly (1/2…1/5) and same-denominator fractions correctly when each set is done separately, but treats them as two unconnected rules — cannot explain why the denominator direction flips, or falters when sets are mixed or placed on one line.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are four fraction cards: 1/2, 1/5, 1/3, 1/4. Put them in order from LARGEST to smallest. Now here are four more: 3/5, 1/5, 4/5, 2/5 — put these in order from largest to smallest too. As you go, place each fraction on this number line. [Watch how the child orders each set and where they place the cards.]
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Whole-number bias makes a child order the unit fractions 1/5, 1/4, 1/3, 1/2 — the exact reverse of correct — so watching the direction on the unit set exposes it instantly. The same-denominator set is the control: it is ordered by numerator (bigger IS more), so a child who has merely memorised 'bigger bottom = smaller' and reverses everything is caught, distinguishing genuine magnitude reasoning from a reversed rote rule.

sources.claim: Students frequently show whole-number bias when ordering fractions, viewing those with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3); this can be diagnosed by having them label and compare fractions, and remedied by grounding magnitude in the number line and part size.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide 'Developing Effective Fractions Instruction K-8' (Siegler et al. 2010, NCEE 2010-4039), Recommendations 2 and 5

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Comparing fractions (age 7+)
topic.description: Solve problems involving counting in tenths, fractions of quantities, equivalence, fraction addition/subtraction, and fraction comparison
evidence: Solve a word problem requiring finding a fraction of a quantity
Solve a problem that requires comparing or ordering fractions
Choose and apply appropriate fraction knowledge to a multi-step problem
topic.assessmentPrompt: If a bag of 20 sweets is shared equally among 5 friends, can {{name}} work out what fraction each person gets — and how many sweets that is?

pedagogy.summary: This is the strategic, problem-solving capstone of early fractions: given a word problem, the child must recognise WHICH fraction idea it calls for (finding a fraction of a quantity, comparing/ordering, equivalence, or adding/subtracting), choose an appropriate method, carry it out, and judge whether the answer is reasonable. As a META topic the object of learning is not a single procedure but the disposition and habits of a strategic problem-solver — sense-making before calculating, monitoring progress, and checking plausibility. It is best developed through rich, varied, non-routine problems, worked examples that model strategy SELECTION (not just execution), and talk that makes children's reasoning and planning audible.
bestPractices: Teach strategy selection explicitly: present mixed problem sets where children must first decide 'is this a fraction-of, a compare, an equivalence, or an add/subtract problem?' before doing any arithmetic — the recognition step is the skill.

Use worked and partially-worked examples that model the PLANNING and monitoring, not just the answer (Polya / Schoenfeld): understand the problem, choose a strategy, carry it out, look back and check.
Insist on a plausibility / looking-back check every time ('a fraction of 20 can't be more than 20'; 'the larger share should have the answer we expect') to build self-monitoring.
Keep contexts and surface features varied so children generalise the underlying structure rather than pattern-matching key words ('altogether' → add is a trap).
Make reasoning audible: use talk moves (revoicing, 'why did you choose that?', 'does that answer make sense?') so strategic thinking is surfaced, discussed, and named rather than assumed.
Include problems with no single stated operation and multi-step problems, so children practise imposing structure themselves.
keyRepresentations: Bar / strip models to represent the quantities and relationships in a word problem before choosing an operation
A visible problem-solving frame (understand → plan → do → check) the child fills in
Double number line for fraction-of and comparison problems
Recording that separates the CHOICE of strategy from its execution (e.g. 'this is a fraction-of problem because...')
commonMisconceptions: Key-word matching: latches onto a surface word ('altogether', 'left') and applies the associated operation regardless of the problem's meaning
Applies the most recently taught procedure to every problem regardless of what it asks
Calculates without a plan and never checks whether the answer is plausible
Cannot start a problem unless the operation is explicitly stated ('but it doesn't tell me to divide')

learn.summary: Capstone for early fractions (ages 7-8): given a word problem, the child must recognise WHICH fraction idea it calls for (finding a fraction of a quantity, comparing/ordering, equivalence, or adding/subtracting), choose a method, carry it out, and judge whether the answer is reasonable. The object of learning is the disposition of a strategic problem-solver — sense-making before calculating, monitoring progress, and checking plausibility — developed through rich, varied, non-routine problems, worked examples that model strategy SELECTION (not just execution), and talk that makes reasoning audible. Recognition-before-calculation is the core skill; key-word matching ('altogether' → add) is the central trap to dismantle.

activities.title: Solve it WITH a mentor who never gives the method
feedback: When a child names an operation by quoting a surface word, don't just mark it wrong — offer a counter-problem where that word points the wrong way and let them discover the mismatch ('you said add because it says altogether — what if the problem is about finding 1/4 of the sweets? Would altogether still mean add?').
Revoice the child's plan back to them and push gently: 'are you sure this is an adding problem?'
If an answer is implausible, prompt the looking-back move rather than supplying the answer: 'could a fraction smaller than one whole, like 3/4, of 12 be more than 12?'
Keep problems mixed across the four fraction ideas so the child cannot pattern-match and must genuinely choose.
activities.rationale: Strategy selection and self-monitoring are dialogic, metacognitive skills that live in articulated reasoning, not a computed answer. A responsive partner can pose varied problems, probe the plan before the arithmetic, and prompt the plausibility check — the moves that build a strategic problem-solver. This is proposed as a strong fit for the metacognitive objective; a scripted or static resource cannot respond to a child's particular reasoning in the moment, though it may still teach other aspects. Efficacy of this specific activity is untested.
sourceClaims: Assisting students to MONITOR AND REFLECT on the problem-solving process is Recommendation 2, rated STRONG evidence (nine qualifying studies, positive effects on word-problem solving, persisting 4+ months); exposing students to MULTIPLE strategies so they select appropriately is Recommendation 4 (MODERATE); the guide warns 'too often students become wedded to just one approach and then flounder', and frames problem solving as reasoning about structure, not 'using key words'.
Mathematical problem solving depends on strategy selection, planning and looking-back/self-monitoring, not just execution; these metacognitive phases should be made explicit in instruction.
learnerActions: Work through a mixed bag of fraction word problems with a partner or in-role mentor (a teacher, another child, or a Socratic tutor character) who reads each problem aloud.
Before doing any arithmetic, say out loud what KIND of problem this is — find-a-fraction-of, compare/order, equivalence, or add/subtract — and HOW you can tell from the situation.
Talk through a plan (what will you do first, and why) before calculating.

When the mentor deliberately offers a tempting key word ('it says altogether, so we add?'), decide whether that word really fits the situation or whether the problem is actually about something else (e.g. finding 1/4 of a set).
After getting an answer, check it makes sense ('could 3/4 of 12 be more than 12?') every single time.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising what a problem is really asking — and checking whether an answer is plausible — is the skill, not the arithmetic. The habit becomes owned when the child hears themselves catch a key-word trap and reason from the situation's structure instead.

activities.title: Sort-then-model workspace: tag the problem, build a model, then answer
feedback: Target feedback at the CHOICE of type and the plausibility of the result, not only at final correctness.
If the type tag is wrong, prompt the child to re-read and describe what is happening before re-tagging.
A plausibility gate before submission ('is this answer bigger than it could possibly be?') makes looking-back routine.
activities.rationale: A sorting-and-modelling workspace can make the recognition step mandatory and let the child externalise the plan with immediate feedback. Dragging to build a bar model or a double number line and a 'does this make sense?' gate are concrete interaction examples that make the plan-then-do mechanism visible; they are offered as options, not required mechanics. This develops recognition and modelling but, being more structured, supports the open monitoring disposition less than live dialogue. Efficacy of this specific activity is untested.
sourceClaims: Assisting students to MONITOR AND REFLECT on the problem-solving process is Recommendation 2, rated STRONG evidence (nine qualifying studies, positive effects on word-problem solving, persisting 4+ months); exposing students to MULTIPLE strategies so they select appropriately is Recommendation 4 (MODERATE); the guide warns 'too often students become wedded to just one approach and then flounder', and frames problem solving as reasoning about structure, not 'using key words'.
learnerActions: For each word problem, first TAG it by type: fraction-of, compare, equivalence, or add/subtract.
Build a bar/strip model — or a double number line for fraction-of and comparison problems — of the situation to show the quantities and relationships BEFORE choosing an operation.
Use the model structure to decide what to do, then calculate.
Pass a 'does this make sense?' check before submitting your answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Externalising the plan-then-do structure — tag, model, then calculate — forces the recognition step and makes the situation's structure (not a key word) the basis for choosing an operation.

activities.title: Mixed problem set that discourages key-word matching
feedback: When a key-word-based option is chosen, return to the situation and ask what is actually happening before re-selecting.

Because a scored set checks the OUTCOME of strategy selection, follow up every item with a short 'how did you know?' so the monitoring and looking-back disposition is still exercised, not just measured.
Design some items so a tempting option matches a surface key word ('altogether' → add) or the most recently practised procedure, so pattern-matching is surfaced rather than rewarded.
activities.rationale: A scored set can efficiently test whether children pick the right strategy across varied problems, with tempting options encoding the two main misconceptions. On its own it assesses the outcome of strategy selection rather than building the monitoring disposition, which needs open reasoning — so it is best paired with discussion. Efficacy of this specific activity is untested.
sourceClaims: Assisting students to MONITOR AND REFLECT on the problem-solving process is Recommendation 2, rated STRONG evidence (nine qualifying studies, positive effects on word-problem solving, persisting 4+ months); exposing students to MULTIPLE strategies so they select appropriately is Recommendation 4 (MODERATE); the guide warns 'too often students become wedded to just one approach and then flounder', and frames problem solving as reasoning about structure, not 'using key words'.
learnerActions: Work a mixed set of varied fraction word problems, first categorising each by type.
For problems presented as multiple choice, pick the answer, then check whether your choice came from the situation's structure or from a surface word.
Where possible, write or say why the chosen type fits the situation, not just which answer you picked.
activities.intendedInsight: Across varied surface features, the underlying structure determines the method; options that reward key-word matching or last-procedure-applied reveal when a child is pattern-matching instead of reasoning.

activities.title: Model the planning, not just the answer (worked and partial examples)
feedback: Prompt for the 'look back and check' phase whenever a child stops at the answer.

When a child cannot begin because no operation is stated, do not supply the operation — ask them to draw what's happening with a bar model; the structure of the drawing can help them work out the operation.
Use talk moves — revoicing, 'why did you choose that?', 'does that answer make sense?' — to surface and name strategic thinking.
activities.rationale: Worked and partially-worked examples that model planning and monitoring (not just the answer) and a visible solving frame make the metacognitive phases explicit, which the sources describe as the aim of instruction. Multi-step and no-stated-operation problems require the child to impose structure, intended to build transfer. Efficacy of this specific activity is untested.
sourceClaims: Mathematical problem solving depends on strategy selection, planning and looking-back/self-monitoring, not just execution; these metacognitive phases should be made explicit in instruction.

Assisting students to MONITOR AND REFLECT on the problem-solving process is Recommendation 2, rated STRONG evidence (nine qualifying studies, positive effects on word-problem solving, persisting 4+ months); exposing students to MULTIPLE strategies so they select appropriately is Recommendation 4 (MODERATE); the guide warns 'too often students become wedded to just one approach and then flounder', and frames problem solving as reasoning about structure, not 'using key words'.
learnerActions: Study worked and partially-worked examples that show understand → plan → do → check, with the CHOICE of strategy made visible ('this is a fraction-of problem because...').
Fill in a visible problem-solving frame (understand → plan → do → check) for new problems, completing missing steps in partially-worked examples.
Include at least some problems with no stated operation and some multi-step problems, so you practise imposing structure yourself.
activities.intendedInsight: Expert problem-solving has explicit phases — planning and looking-back are as important as execution. Separating the choice of strategy from its execution makes the strategic step learnable rather than assumed.

constraints: This is a META objective: the goal is the disposition and habits of a strategic problem-solver (sense-making, monitoring, plausibility-checking), not mastery of a single procedure. Children must already be able to find a fraction of a set, compare/order fractions, work with equivalence, and add/subtract fractions; if a child cannot find a fraction of a set at all, revisit that prerequisite before this work.
Keep problems MIXED across the four fraction ideas and vary surface features; a single-type set lets children pattern-match and defeats the recognition objective.
Deliberately include key words that point the wrong way ('altogether' in a fraction-of problem) so key-word matching can be surfaced and challenged rather than rewarded.

Insist on a plausibility / looking-back check every time (for a proper fraction of a positive quantity the answer is smaller than the whole, e.g. 'a fraction less than one whole, such as 3/4, of 20 can't be more than 20').

Recognition-only or multiple-choice responses measure the OUTCOME of strategy selection but do not by themselves elicit the independent planning, justification, and self-monitoring that the objective targets; pair them with open 'how did you know?' reasoning.

Scaffolds such as a fixed solving frame or a sort-tag-model workspace structure the thinking but constrain openness; fade them so the child eventually imposes structure unprompted on novel, multi-step problems.
When a child cannot begin because no operation is stated, scaffold sense-making (draw the situation) rather than supplying the operation.

Static tap-to-reveal pictures and 3D manipulation were judged poor fits for THIS metacognitive objective because strategic problem-solving is generative and dialogic and has no spatial content to manipulate; this is a scope judgement for this objective, not a universal claim that such media cannot teach.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed PROPOSALS, not validated interventions, and no claim of empirical testing of these specific activities is made.

One cited source (Polya/Schoenfeld) is marked unverified in the original row; the IES/WWC Practice Guide claim is marked verified. Evidence strength has not been re-checked and should not be upgraded.

The original framed the dialogic tutor as 'ideal' and static-image/3D artefacts as 'poor'. These were catalog fit rankings; they have been softened to scoped suitability judgements with stated affordances/limits rather than universal pedagogical laws. A fixed worked example cannot be manipulated but can still teach; a multiple-choice format can be used during teaching, not only to assess.

Plausibility example '3/4 of 12 cannot be more than 12' verified: 3/4 of 12 = 9 < 12. The shorthand 'a fraction of 20 can't be more than 20' is strictly true for proper fractions (less than 1); this is appropriate for the age 7–8 examples but is not a universal statement about all fractions and should be stated with that scope.

The double number line representation (original keyRepresentation) was missing from all activities in an earlier candidate; it is present in the sort-then-model workspace for fraction-of and comparison problems, matching the preservation claim.

Activity 3 asks the child to check whether a chosen option came from structure or a surface word; this is metacognitive priming appropriate to a learning (not purely diagnostic) context and does not pre-label specific options for the child.

No arithmetic, force/motion, or geometric idealisation errors were identified in the source to correct; the main risk flagged was the key-word trap, which is handled deliberately. Independent re-audit found no new critical learner-facing errors.

probeDeeper: 'How did you know this was a comparing problem and not an adding one?' — pushes the recognition into an explicit justification.

'You said add because it says altogether — what if I told you the problem was about finding 1/4 of the sweets? Would altogether still mean add?' — a counterexample that tests whether key-word matching survives challenge.
'Once you have an answer, how would you check it's sensible?' — surfaces whether a monitoring/looking-back strategy exists.
'If you got stuck, what would you try?' — reveals whether the child has any strategic repertoire (draw it, try a simpler case) or only waits to be told.
assess.correctAnswer: There is no single right answer to score — the aim is to surface HOW the child decides what a problem is asking and how they judge an answer. A strong response recognises each problem's underlying structure (this is a find-a-fraction-of problem; this is a compare/order problem), states a sensible first step and why, and offers a plausibility check ('the answer should be smaller than the whole').

errorPatterns.pattern: Key-word matching: 'it says altogether so I add' / 'it says left so I take away' — follows a surface word instead of the problem's meaning
errorPatterns.nextMove: Surface it for discussion — offer a counter-problem where the key word points the wrong way and let the child discover the mismatch; build the habit of describing the situation before naming an operation. Do not simply mark it wrong.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child names the operation by quoting a word from the problem rather than describing the situation; picks 'add' for a fraction-of problem that happens to contain 'altogether'

errorPatterns.pattern: Applies the most recently taught procedure to every problem regardless of what it asks
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss what is DIFFERENT about the three problems; make the recognition step explicit ('these aren't all the same kind — how are they different?'). A disposition to build, not an error to reteach.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child treats all three varied problems as the same type (e.g. adds fractions in all of them) because that was the last thing practised

errorPatterns.pattern: No plausibility check: accepts an answer larger than the whole for a fraction-of problem, or a smaller fraction 'winning' a comparison, without noticing
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the looking-back move rather than reteaching the calculation: 'could a fraction of 12 be more than 12?' Make plausibility-checking a routine final step.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives an unreasonable answer and, when asked 'does that make sense?', has no way to judge — the checking habit is absent, not the arithmetic

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot begin unless the operation is stated: 'but it doesn't tell me what to do'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not supply the operation — scaffold sense-making of the situation with a bar model ('draw what's happening'); the structure will suggest the operation. If the child also cannot find a fraction of a set at all, revisit that prerequisite.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child stalls on a problem with no explicit operation word, waiting to be told to divide or add

responseLevels.gap: Chooses operations by key words or applies one procedure to everything; cannot say why a problem is a particular type; has no way to judge whether an answer is reasonable and stalls when no operation is stated.
responseLevels.full: Reads a novel or multi-step problem, justifies which fraction idea it needs from the situation's structure, plans and carries out an appropriate method, and routinely checks the answer is plausible — transferring the recognise-plan-do-check habit to unfamiliar contexts and resisting key-word traps.
responseLevels.partial: Can name the type and method for familiar, single-step problems and often gets them right, but selection is fragile — lists what to do without explaining why it fits the situation, is misled by surface wording, or omits the plausibility check unless prompted (the multistructural level: knows the pieces, doesn't coordinate recognise→plan→check).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I'm going to give you three different fraction problems, one at a time. Before you work any of them out, just tell me: what kind of problem is this, and what would you do first? Then we'll talk about how you'd know if your answer makes sense.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking the child to name the TYPE and first step BEFORE calculating separates strategic reasoners from key-word matchers and last-procedure appliers: a strategic child reads the situation and justifies the choice; a non-strategic child either grabs a surface word ('altogether means add'), applies whatever was taught most recently to all three, or freezes because no operation is stated. Because it is surfaced for discussion and not scored, it reveals the child's problem-solving disposition rather than their arithmetic.

sources.claim: Assisting students to MONITOR AND REFLECT on the problem-solving process is Recommendation 2, rated STRONG evidence (nine qualifying studies, positive effects on word-problem solving, persisting 4+ months); exposing students to MULTIPLE strategies so they select appropriately is Recommendation 4 (MODERATE); the guide warns 'too often students become wedded to just one approach and then flounder', and frames problem solving as reasoning about structure, not 'using key words'.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide, Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through 8 (NCEE 2012-4055)

sources.claim: Mathematical problem solving depends on strategy selection, planning and looking-back/self-monitoring, not just execution; these metacognitive phases should be made explicit in instruction.
sources.source: Polya, How to Solve It; Schoenfeld, Mathematical Problem Solving

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Comparing fractions (age 8+)
topic.description: Compare two fractions with the same numerator or the same denominator by reasoning about size; record comparisons with >, =, or < symbols
evidence: Compare 3/8 and 3/4: same numerator, larger denominator means smaller pieces so 3/8 < 3/4
Compare 5/6 and 2/6: same denominator so 5/6 > 2/6
Justify a comparison using a visual model and explain why both fractions must refer to the same whole
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees 3/5 and 3/8, can they tell you which is bigger just by thinking about the size of each piece — without needing to draw it out?

pedagogy.summary: Comparing two fractions that share a numerator or a denominator, by reasoning about the SIZE of the parts rather than the size of the digits. Same denominator: the parts are the same size, so more of them is more (5/6 > 2/6). Same numerator: the same COUNT of parts, but a larger denominator makes each part smaller, so the fraction is smaller (3/8 < 3/4). Both fractions must refer to the same whole. Comparisons are recorded with >, =, <.
bestPractices: Anchor same-numerator reasoning in sharing: the more people share, the smaller each share — 1/3 of an object is greater than 1/4 (IES Rec 1).
Reason about part SIZE and count, never the digits alone: 'the same number of parts, but each eighth is smaller than each fourth'.
Insist both fractions refer to the SAME whole before comparing.
Use fraction strips/bars aligned to one whole and a single number line.
Confront whole-number bias with contrasting cases (3/8 vs 3/4, where the bigger denominator gives the smaller fraction).
Read the >/</= symbol as opening toward the larger amount.
keyRepresentations: Aligned fraction strips / bars on one whole
Single 0–1 number line
Same-whole area models
Equal-sharing scenario (more sharers = smaller share)
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias — a larger denominator means a larger fraction (1/8 > 1/3 because 8 > 3; 3/8 > 3/4 by comparing denominators) (IES)
Comparing across different wholes (3/4 of a small bar vs 1/2 of a large bar)
Treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers
Over-applying 'bigger bottom = smaller' so blindly it mis-fires on same-denominator pairs

learn.summary: Compare two fractions that share a numerator or a denominator by reasoning about the SIZE and COUNT of the parts, not the size of the digits. Same denominator: parts are equal-sized, so more of them is more (5/6 > 2/6). Same numerator: the same count of parts, but a larger denominator makes each part smaller, so the fraction is smaller (3/8 < 3/4). When comparing by shaded models, both fractions must be drawn on the SAME whole for the picture to be fair; comparisons are recorded with >, =, <.

activities.title: Lock the numerator, grow the denominator: watch the parts shrink
feedback: If a learner writes 3/8 > 3/4 because 8 > 4, point back to the shaded bars on the same whole: 'You have three pieces on each bar. Which single piece is bigger, an eighth or a fourth? So which set of three covers more?'
If correct, extend: 'If you cut into sixteenths instead, would one piece be bigger or smaller than an eighth? What does that tell you about 3/16 versus 3/8?'
If a learner compares bars of different lengths, stop and insist both fractions be drawn on identical wholes before deciding.
activities.rationale: Same-numerator reasoning follows from sharing: the more sharers, the smaller each share (1/3 > 1/4). Making the fixed count of parts visibly shrink as the denominator grows directly confronts whole-number bias, a documented misconception addressed by contrasting cases.
sourceClaims: Same-numerator comparison follows from sharing (more sharers = smaller share; 1/3 > 1/4); whole-number bias (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3 because 8 > 3, or 3/8 > 3/5 by comparing denominators) is a documented misconception addressed by contrasting cases; children must grasp that a part's size decreases as the denominator increases.
learnerActions: Set up two bars (strips, drawn area models, or an interactive tool) pinned to the SAME whole.
Set both bars to 3/4 to start (numerator 3 and denominator 4 on each), so the two shaded amounts are identical.
On the first bar, raise the denominator from 4 to 8 so it shows 3/8; keep the second at 3/4.
Describe what happens to each part as the bottom number grows from 4 to 8, then state which shaded amount is larger.
Write the correct symbol between them (3/8 __ 3/4) with the sign opening toward the larger amount.
Say aloud: 'Same number of parts (3), but each eighth is smaller than each fourth, so 3/8 is less than 3/4.'
activities.intendedInsight: When the numerator is held fixed, a larger denominator cuts the whole into more, smaller parts, so the fraction gets SMALLER, not bigger. The digits '8 > 4' do not mean '3/8 > 3/4'.

activities.title: Same denominator: count the equal parts
feedback: If a learner reverses this (says 2/6 > 5/6) by over-applying a 'bigger number means smaller' idea carried over from same-numerator pairs, clarify when each rule applies: 'The bottoms are the same here — sixths are sixths. So just count: is five pieces more or less than two?'
If correct, ask them to read the symbol aloud and confirm it opens toward the larger amount.
activities.rationale: Learners who memorise 'bigger denominator means smaller' can blanket-apply it and mis-fire on same-denominator pairs. Pairing this case with the same-numerator case forces attention to WHEN each line of reasoning is valid, rather than to the digits alone.
learnerActions: On one whole, shade 5/6 and 2/6 on aligned bars or on a single 0–1 number line.
State that the sixths are all the same size on both.
Decide which is larger by counting how many equal parts are shaded, then write 5/6 __ 2/6.
Explain: 'Same-size sixths, and five of them is more than two, so 5/6 > 2/6.'
activities.intendedInsight: When the denominator is shared, the parts are identical in size, so the fraction with more parts (larger numerator) is larger. This is a DIFFERENT comparison from the same-numerator case and must not be solved by 'bigger bottom = smaller'.

activities.title: Does 3/4 always beat 3/8? The same-whole rule
feedback: If a learner concludes 3/8 > 3/4 from mismatched drawings, ask: 'Were both bars the same size to begin with? Redraw them the same length and look again.'
If correct, challenge: 'Can you make two fractions where the one with the bigger bottom number is actually the smaller fraction, and show why on equal wholes?'
activities.rationale: Comparing the shaded regions of fractions drawn on different wholes is a distinct misconception from whole-number bias and needs its own explicit confrontation; drawing on a shared whole keeps the picture fair, a precondition stressed in the pedagogy.
learnerActions: Draw 3/4 on a short bar and 3/8 on a long bar, deliberately mismatched.
Compare the shaded regions by eye and notice the drawing can be misleading.
Redraw both fractions on identical wholes and compare again.
State in your own words why, when you compare by shaded pictures, both fractions must be drawn on the same whole for the comparison to be fair.
activities.intendedInsight: When you judge which fraction is larger by looking at shaded regions, both must be drawn on the same whole for the picture to be fair; 3/4 of a small bar can look smaller than 3/8 of a large bar, even though, as numbers, 3/4 > 3/8.

activities.title: Practise and sort comparisons
feedback: Accept an answer only when the learner can justify it by part size or count; a right symbol with a digit-only reason ('8 is bigger') should prompt 'bigger what — bigger number, or bigger piece?'
Mix same-numerator and same-denominator items so learners must select the right reasoning each time, not run one rule blindly.
activities.rationale: Practice and ordering consolidate comparison once part-size reasoning is built; interleaving the two pair types guards against mechanically applying a single rule. Recognition/selection tasks consolidate and check classification but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction and justification that the modelling activities require.
learnerActions: Decide the correct sign for same-numerator pairs (e.g. 3/8 vs 3/4) and same-denominator pairs (e.g. 5/6 vs 2/6).
Order short sets of same-numerator fractions and, separately, same-denominator fractions from smallest to largest.
Sort pairs into >, =, and < groups and, where used, match a fraction pair to its symbol.
For each answer, state the reason in part-size/count language rather than quoting digits.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency in applying the two lines of reasoning across varied pairs, with the correct rule chosen for the structure of each pair.

activities.title: Reference fraction wall (support)
feedback: Use this to jog memory, then ask the learner to reconstruct the comparison on their own same-whole model and explain it.
activities.rationale: A fixed fraction wall supports recall of relative sizes but does not let the learner vary a denominator or test a new comparison, so it is a reference scaffold rather than the main investigation.
learnerActions: Line up two rows of a fraction wall, e.g. place 3/8 under 3/4 on the same whole, to see relative sizes.
Use a lift-the-flap or note to recall 'eighths are smaller, so 3/8 is less than 3/4'.
Return to the drawing/building activities to test and justify an actual comparison.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction wall helps recall relative sizes of common fractions as a reference aid.

constraints: When comparing by shaded models/pictures, both fractions must be drawn on the same whole; a picture drawn on a different-sized whole can mislead. (As numbers, fractions such as 3/4 and 3/8 remain comparable regardless of any drawing.)
Reason about the SIZE and COUNT of parts, never the digits alone (e.g. 'the same number of parts, but each eighth is smaller than each fourth').
Read > and < as opening toward the larger amount; = means the two amounts are equal.

The same-numerator and same-denominator cases are DIFFERENT comparisons: with a shared denominator compare numerators (more same-size parts is more); with a shared numerator compare part sizes (larger denominator = smaller parts). Do not let a learner apply 'bigger bottom = smaller' to a same-denominator pair.
The fraction wall is a recall aid only; it cannot let the learner vary the denominator or test a comparison, so it should not replace the modelling/building activities.
Recognition and sorting tasks consolidate and check classification but do not on their own elicit independent construction of a model and a justification.
This microtopic targets same-numerator and same-denominator comparisons for age 8–9; general comparison of fractions with different numerators AND denominators is beyond this scope.

Physical fraction strips and card models have slight real thickness and are approximations of ideal equal parts; treat any paper or on-screen model as a model of the same-whole comparison, not the ideal figure itself.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The IES/WWC claim is marked verified in the source row; the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked unverified (verified:false) and is not cited in any activity's sourceClaims.

Interactive examples (two bars pinned to one whole, locking numerators, dragging the denominator, auto-drawn comparison symbol, mismatched-whole warning, tapping fraction-wall rows, lift-the-flap) are preserved as OPTIONAL ways to make the mechanism concrete; equivalent results can be reached with paper strips, drawn area models, or a single number line.

Original source rated a third dimension and an in-role conversation as poor-fit for this planar comparison task; these are retained as observations about this task's nature, not as universal claims that such media can never teach fraction comparison.

The original row states the common-whole requirement without qualification; it has been scoped here to comparing represented (shaded) portions, since fractions as numbers remain comparable irrespective of the drawn whole.

The source's whole-number-bias illustration '3/8 > 3/5 because 8 > 5' is retained only inside the cited misconception claim; it is a wrong belief to confront (correctly 3/8 < 3/5), never offered as a valid comparison in a learner task.

probeDeeper: You said 3/8 is smaller. If I cut the whole into even more parts — sixteenths — would one part be bigger or smaller than an eighth?
Which is bigger, 3/4 of this bar or 3/4 of that longer bar? Does 3/4 always beat 3/8?
Write the correct sign between 5/6 and 2/6 — which way does it point, and why?
Make up two fractions where the one with the bigger bottom number is actually the smaller fraction.
assess.correctAnswer: 3/8 < 3/4 (same number of parts, but eighths are smaller than fourths, so three eighths is less than three fourths); 5/6 > 2/6 (same-size sixths, and five of them is more than two). Both drawn on the same whole.

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias — '3/8 is bigger than 3/4 because 8 is bigger than 4'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Align both bars on the same whole; show each eighth is smaller than each fourth; use contrasting cases so the bigger denominator gives the smaller fraction
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders the same-numerator pair by denominator size

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-corrected rule — 'bigger bottom always means smaller', mis-fired so 2/6 beats 5/6
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach the concept; clarify WHEN each rule applies — same denominator means compare the numerators (more same-size parts is more)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reverses or freezes on the same-denominator control set

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares across different wholes — draws 3/4 on a small bar and the other on a large bar and compares the shaded regions directly
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist both fractions be drawn on identical wholes before any comparison
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses mismatched-size wholes for the two fractions

responseLevels.gap: Orders by comparing digits (denominator or numerator alone); says 3/8 > 3/4; may reverse the same-denominator pair.
responseLevels.full: Writes 3/8 < 3/4 and 5/6 > 2/6, justifies each on a same-whole model by reasoning about part size and count, and recognises the whole must be the same for a fair comparison.
responseLevels.partial: Gets the same-denominator comparison right but falters on the same-numerator pair (whole-number bias), or gets both by a rule without a same-whole model or part-size reasoning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Task: using bars drawn on the same whole (or a number line), show which is larger and write >, <, or = — first for 3/8 and 3/4, then for 5/6 and 2/6. I'll watch how you build and decide each one.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The same-numerator pair (3/8 vs 3/4) triggers whole-number bias — a child ordering by denominator writes 3/8 > 3/4. The same-denominator control (5/6 vs 2/6) catches a child who has memorised 'bigger bottom = smaller' and blanket-reverses, wrongly making 2/6 > 5/6. Only part-size reasoning gets both right.

sources.claim: Same-numerator comparison follows from sharing (more sharers = smaller share; 1/3 > 1/4); whole-number bias (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3 because 8 > 3, or 3/8 > 3/5 by comparing denominators) is a documented misconception addressed by contrasting cases; children must grasp that a part's size decreases as the denominator increases.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide, Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for K-8 (Siegler et al., 2010, NCEE 2010-4039)

sources.claim: Pupils compare and order unit fractions and fractions with the same denominators in Year 3 (age 7–8); fraction comparison develops across KS2.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS1-2)

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Comparing fractions (age 9+)
topic.description: Compare and order fractions with different numerators and denominators by creating common denominators/numerators or comparing to a benchmark such as 1/2; justify conclusions with visual models
evidence: Compare 3/8 and 5/12 by finding a common denominator of 24
Order 2/3, 3/5, and 7/10 from smallest to largest
Use the benchmark 1/2 to decide that 5/8 > 3/7
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has eaten 2/3 of their lunch and a friend has eaten 3/4 of theirs, can they work out who's eaten more — by finding a common way to compare the fractions?

pedagogy.summary: Comparing and ordering fractions with different numerators AND denominators, using either a common denominator (rename both with equivalent fractions, then compare numerators) or benchmark reasoning (is each fraction less than, equal to, or more than 1/2 — or near 0 or 1?). Benchmarks are fast and build number sense; common denominators are general. Conclusions are justified with visual models. This is a known hard skill — on the 2004 NAEP, 50% of 8th-graders could not order three fractions from least to greatest.
bestPractices: Teach benchmark reasoning with 0, 1/2 and 1: decide which side of 1/2 each fraction sits on (5/8 > 1/2 because 5 is more than half of 8; 3/7 < 1/2) (IES Rec 3).
Teach the common-denominator method as renaming both fractions with equivalents, then comparing numerators.
Use minimally-labelled number lines (0, 1/2, 1) for landmark placement, and dual-labelled lines (one unit sequence above, another below) for different denominators (IES Rec 2).
Choose the strategy to fit the numbers — benchmarks when they straddle 1/2, common denominator when they are close.
Keep the same-numerator shortcut available (2/3 > 2/5).
Justify with a model and guard against whole-number bias.
keyRepresentations: Common denominator via equivalent-fraction renaming
Number line marked 0, 1/2, 1 (benchmark lane)
Dual-labelled number line for different denominators
Ratio table / times-tables for the common multiple
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias — ordering by numerator or denominator alone (3/8 vs 5/12 → '5 > 3 so 5/12 is bigger', or '12 > 8 so smaller') (IES)
Comparing without a common denominator (cross-adding, or comparing tops and bottoms separately)
Renaming only one fraction, or using a non-common multiple
Benchmark misapplied — e.g. judging 3/7 > 1/2

learn.summary: Learners compare and order fractions with different numerators and denominators using two complementary strategies: (1) renaming both fractions to a common denominator and comparing numerators, and (2) benchmark reasoning with 0, 1/2, and 1 (deciding which side of 1/2 each fraction sits on, or whether it is near 0 or 1). Benchmarks are quick and build number sense; common denominators are general-purpose. Conclusions are justified with visual models (partitioned bars, number lines). The core misconception to guard against is whole-number bias — ordering by numerator or denominator alone. This is a known hard skill: on the 2004 NAEP, 50% of 8th-graders could not order three fractions from least to greatest.

activities.title: Strategy workbench: common denominator OR benchmark
feedback: If a learner compares numerators and denominators separately or cross-adds, show that only a shared denominator licenses comparing the top numbers — re-partition both bars to the same grid and compare again.

If a learner renames only one fraction or uses a denominator that is not a common multiple of both, point out both fractions must reach the SAME denominator; verify each rename with the ×n/n equivalence.
If a learner misplaces a fraction relative to 1/2 (e.g. calls 3/7 more than 1/2), have them compare the numerator to half the denominator: half of 7 is 3.5, and 3 is less than 3.5, so 3/7 < 1/2.
Confirm correct reasoning by asking them to justify with the visual model, not just the final symbols.
activities.rationale: The IES/WWC guide recommends benchmarks 0, 1/2, 1 as reference points and number lines (minimally-labelled for landmarks; dual-labelled for different denominators) to support comparison, and names whole-number bias as the core misconception. Offering both renaming and benchmark strategies lets learners pick the efficient method and build general competence.
sourceClaims: Comparing/ordering fractions is a key indicator of understanding and is hard (2004 NAEP: 50% of 8th-graders could not order three fractions least-to-greatest); benchmarks 0, 1/2, 1 are recommended reference points, dual-labelled and minimally-labelled number lines support comparison of different denominators, and whole-number bias is the core misconception.
learnerActions: Take a pair such as 3/8 versus 5/12. Choose the common-denominator path: re-partition both bars (on paper or with a model) to the same fine grid — twenty-fourths — so 3/8 becomes 9/24 and 5/12 becomes 10/24, then compare the numerators 9 versus 10.

Take a pair such as 5/8 versus 3/7. Choose the benchmark path: place each on a number line marked 0, 1/2, 1. Decide which side of 1/2 each sits on (5/8 is more than 1/2 because 5 is more than half of 8; 3/7 is less than 1/2 because 3 is less than half of 7).
Switch into an ordering task: drag or write three or more fractions (e.g. 2/3, 3/5, 7/10) onto a line or into order, choosing whichever strategy fits the numbers.
State, for each comparison, which strategy you chose and why it suited those particular numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: Renaming two fractions to the same denominator makes them directly comparable (the comparison collapses to comparing numerators), and the 1/2 benchmark settles many comparisons at a glance without full computation. Choosing the strategy to fit the numbers is part of the skill.

activities.title: Dual-labelled and benchmark number lines
feedback: If a learner places a fraction on the wrong side of 1/2, return to comparing the numerator with half the denominator.
If a learner is unsure whether a fraction is near 0 or near 1, check how close the numerator is to 0 or to the denominator (e.g. 1/5 is near 0, 4/5 is near 1).
If a learner struggles to compare across the two denominators, align the two labelled sequences and read off which mark lies further right.
activities.rationale: IES/WWC recommends minimally-labelled number lines for landmark placement and dual-labelled lines for comparing different denominators. A reference line aids recall and placement; note it does not by itself carry out a full ordering or re-partition, so pair it with the active strategies above.
sourceClaims: Comparing/ordering fractions is a key indicator of understanding and is hard (2004 NAEP: 50% of 8th-graders could not order three fractions least-to-greatest); benchmarks 0, 1/2, 1 are recommended reference points, dual-labelled and minimally-labelled number lines support comparison of different denominators, and whole-number bias is the core misconception.
learnerActions: Use a number line marked only 0, 1/2, 1 and place common fractions where they belong relative to those landmarks; for each, say whether it is more than, equal to, or less than one half.
Decide whether 4/9 is more or less than a half by comparing 4 with half of 9 (4.5): 4 is less than 4.5, so 4/9 < 1/2 — no common denominator needed.
Order 1/5, 4/5, 5/9 using only benchmarks: 1/5 sits just above 0, 5/9 is just over 1/2 (5 is more than 4.5), and 4/5 is near 1, giving 1/5 < 5/9 < 4/5.
For two different denominators, use a dual-labelled line (one unit sequence of marks above the line, the other below) to see where each fraction falls and which is larger.
Explain how the landmarks 0, 1/2 and 1 let you decide a comparison without finding a common denominator.
activities.intendedInsight: A number line anchored to 0, 1/2 and 1 gives fractions a magnitude and a 'side of 1/2' (and a sense of nearness to 0 or 1), so many comparisons can be read off directly; dual labelling lets two different denominators be compared on one line.

activities.title: Check and consolidate ordering and benchmark decisions
feedback: If a learner orders by single digits ('7/10 is smallest because 10 is biggest'), rename all three to a common denominator or place them on a 0/½/1 line and compare magnitudes.
If a learner grinds a full common-denominator computation for 5/8 vs 3/7, prompt the quicker 1/2 benchmark.
Reward correct answers that also carry a model-based justification.
activities.rationale: Recognition and fill-in tasks efficiently check whether learners can apply each strategy and avoid whole-number bias, and surface whether a learner works in only one register (benchmark or common denominator). These checks confirm application but do not, on their own, elicit the independent construction that the workbench tasks require.
learnerActions: Order a set such as 2/3, 3/5, 7/10 from smallest to largest and show working (e.g. common denominator 30: 3/5 = 18/30, 2/3 = 20/30, 7/10 = 21/30, giving 3/5 < 2/3 < 7/10).
Answer a quick benchmark question: 'Is 5/8 more or less than 1/2?' and justify.
Rename both fractions of a pair to a shared common denominator before comparing, and check the order you get.
Sort a set of fractions into 'less than 1/2' and 'more than 1/2'.
Keep the same-numerator shortcut in play: with equal numerators, the larger denominator gives the smaller fraction (2/3 > 2/5).
Check that a different common denominator does not change the order (e.g. using 60 instead of 30 gives the same ordering).
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent comparison means ordering correctly, choosing an efficient strategy, and justifying with a model — not just getting a final symbol right. Any valid common denominator yields the same order.

constraints: Learners must reach fractions with DIFFERENT numerators and denominators; same-denominator or same-numerator pairs alone are stepping stones, not the full objective.
Both strategies should be available: benchmark reasoning when fractions straddle 1/2 or sit near 0 or 1, and common denominators when fractions are close together or benchmarks do not separate them.

A benchmark/reference number line with fractions pre-placed is a recall and placement scaffold; it does not re-partition fractions or carry out an ordering, so it must be combined with active renaming and ordering work.

Recognition-only responses (multiple choice, sorting, fill-in) check application but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a full ordering with justification; include a task where the learner produces the ordering and its reasoning.
Always require justification with a visual model and explicitly guard against whole-number bias (ordering by numerator or denominator alone).
Verify each rename with the ×n/n equivalence and ensure both fractions reach the same common multiple.

Comparing a fixed numerator (as in same-numerator pairs) with a fixed denominator varies different quantities; there is no 'denominator rule that flips', so explain each comparison by magnitude rather than a sign-flip rule.

Live re-partitioning of bars to a shared grid and drag-to-order on a line are example interaction mechanisms that make the strategies concrete; they are illustrative, not required mechanisms — the same work can be done with drawn bars and written orderings.

Interpret this content for approximately ages 9–10; in the England curriculum Year 5 pupils compare and order fractions whose denominators are all multiples of the same number, and Year 6 extends this to comparing and ordering fractions more generally, including fractions greater than 1 (source marked unverified).

probeDeeper: Why does giving both fractions the same denominator let you just compare the top numbers?
Is 4/9 more or less than a half? How can you tell without a common denominator?
You used 30 as the common denominator — could a different common denominator work? Would the order change?
Order these using only benchmarks, no calculation: 1/5, 4/5, 5/9.
assess.correctAnswer: 3/5 < 2/3 < 7/10 (common denominator 30: 3/5 = 18/30, 2/3 = 20/30, 7/10 = 21/30). And 5/8 > 3/7, because 5/8 is more than 1/2 (5 is more than half of 8) while 3/7 is less than 1/2 (3 is less than half of 7).

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias — orders by numerator or denominator alone ('7/10 is smallest because 10 is biggest')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rename all three to a common denominator, or place them on a 0/½/1 line, and compare magnitudes
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders without renaming, using single digits

errorPatterns.pattern: Renames only one fraction or uses a non-common denominator
errorPatterns.nextMove: Both fractions must be renamed to the SAME denominator; verify each rename with the ×n/n equivalence
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Converts one fraction but not the other, or compares over different denominators

errorPatterns.pattern: Benchmark misapplied — 'judges 3/7 to be more than 1/2'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare the numerator to half the denominator (half of 7 is 3.5, so 3/7 < 1/2)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Puts 3/7 on the wrong side of 1/2

responseLevels.gap: Orders by single digits (numerator or denominator); benchmark reasoning absent or wrong.
responseLevels.full: Orders correctly via common denominators (or sound benchmark reasoning) and settles 5/8 vs 3/7 with 1/2 without full computation, justifying both and selecting the efficient strategy for the numbers.
responseLevels.partial: Uses a common denominator correctly for the ordering but cannot apply the 1/2 benchmark efficiently (grinds or errs), or benchmarks but cannot carry out a general common-denominator comparison — works in only one register.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Task: order these three fractions from smallest to largest and show your working — 2/3, 3/5, 7/10. Then use the benchmark 1/2 to decide quickly which is larger: 5/8 or 3/7. I'll watch which methods you use.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who renames to a common denominator (or reasons by benchmarks) orders correctly and settles 5/8 vs 3/7 with 1/2, without full computation. A whole-number-bias child orders by numerators or denominators alone; a child lacking benchmark sense grinds a common denominator for 5/8 vs 3/7 or misjudges which side of 1/2 they fall.

sources.claim: Comparing/ordering fractions is a key indicator of understanding and is hard (2004 NAEP: 50% of 8th-graders could not order three fractions least-to-greatest); benchmarks 0, 1/2, 1 are recommended reference points, dual-labelled and minimally-labelled number lines support comparison of different denominators, and whole-number bias is the core misconception.
