topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Comparing fractions (age 10+)
topic.description: Compare and order fractions including fractions greater than 1, by converting to common denominators or using benchmarks
evidence: Order 3/4, 7/8, 5/6, and 11/12 from smallest to largest
Compare 7/5 and 4/3 using common denominators
Place improper fractions and mixed numbers on a number line in correct order
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to sort 5/3, 7/4, and 2/1 in order from smallest to biggest, can they convert them to a common denominator and order them correctly?

pedagogy.summary: Comparing and ordering fractions — including those greater than 1 — uses common denominators (always reliable), benchmarks (1/2, 1), or 'distance from a landmark'. For a set clustered just below 1, such as 3/4, 7/8, 5/6, 11/12, the elegant method is complement-to-1: the gaps to a whole are 1/4, 1/6, 1/8, 1/12, so the smallest gap is the largest fraction (11/12 largest, 3/4 smallest). For fractions above 1, compare via common denominators (7/5 = 21/15 vs 4/3 = 20/15) or convert to mixed numbers and place on a number line.
bestPractices: Choose a strategy that fits the numbers: common denominators always work; benchmark to 1/2 or 1; complement-to-1 for sets clustered near a whole
Recognise a fraction greater than 1 sits past 1 on the number line, and convert improper↔mixed to place and order it
Justify the ordering (why one is bigger), not just rank the symbols
Use a common denominator to make numerators directly comparable, rather than comparing tops and bottoms separately
Simplify or find common multiples to reach a shared denominator efficiently
keyRepresentations: Number line spanning past 1 (place 7/5, 4/3 and mixed numbers)
Common-denominator fraction strips
Benchmark markers at 1/2 and 1
Complement-to-1 gap diagram for near-whole sets
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias: bigger numerator and/or denominator means a bigger fraction (may land the right order for the wrong reason)
Compares numerators and denominators separately ('7 > 4 and 5 > 3 so 7/5 > 4/3')
Same-numerator lock reversed — with equal numerators, picks the bigger denominator as bigger (2/5 > 2/3)
Treats a fraction greater than 1 as if it were less than 1, or places it wrongly on the line
Compares without finding a common denominator

learn.summary: Help learners (age 10–11) compare and order fractions, including fractions greater than 1, by reasoning about value rather than digit size. Core strategies: common denominators (always reliable), benchmarking to 1/2 and 1, and complement-to-1 for sets clustered just below a whole (e.g. 3/4, 7/8, 5/6, 11/12, where the gaps to 1 are 3/4 → 1/4, 7/8 → 1/8, 5/6 → 1/6, 11/12 → 1/12, so the smallest gap means the largest fraction). For fractions above 1, convert to a common denominator (7/5 = 21/15 vs 4/3 = 20/15) or to mixed numbers and place on a number line. Throughout, the discriminating goal is a justified ordering, since whole-number bias can produce a correct rank for the wrong reason on favourable sets.

activities.title: Place and order fractions on a number line, measuring each gap to 1
feedback: If a learner ranks by digit size, note that this particular set happens to come out right by digits — press them to justify by value or gaps to 1, then try 2/3 vs 2/5 where digits mislead.

For 2/3 vs 2/5: both count two pieces, but fifths are smaller pieces than thirds, so two thirds exceed two fifths and 2/3 > 2/5 — a larger denominator makes each piece smaller, not the fraction larger.
If 7/5 is placed between 0 and 1, point back to the line: 7/5 is five fifths (one whole) plus two more fifths, so it must sit past 1 at 1 2/5.
Confirm 7/5 > 4/3 by the common denominator: over fifteenths, 21/15 > 20/15, so the single numerator comparison settles it.
activities.rationale: A number line makes relative size and 'distance to a landmark' visible, which can target the whole-number-bias error that treats numerator and denominator as independent, and supports correct placement of fractions greater than 1. Common denominators are presented as the always-reliable fallback.
sourceClaims: Fractions are compared by value using equivalent fractions/common denominators or benchmarks; the dominant error is whole-number bias (judging by numerator/denominator digit size and comparing numerators and denominators separately), which reflects treating the two parts as independent whole numbers rather than one quantity.
learnerActions: Place the set 3/4, 7/8, 5/6, 11/12 onto a number line running from 0 past 2.
For each fraction, mark or measure the distance from the fraction to the '1' mark (its gap to a whole): 3/4 → 1/4, 7/8 → 1/8, 5/6 → 1/6, 11/12 → 1/12.
State the order smallest to largest (3/4 < 5/6 < 7/8 < 11/12) and explain the link: the BIGGEST gap to 1 means the SMALLEST fraction, so 3/4 is smallest and 11/12 (hugging 1) is largest.
Place 7/5 and 4/3 on the same line and notice both land PAST 1; convert each to a mixed number (7/5 = 1 2/5) to confirm position.
Rewrite 7/5 and 4/3 over a common denominator (21/15 vs 20/15) and compare the numerators to decide which is larger.
Compare the counter-pair 2/3 and 2/5: which is larger, and why does the same number of larger-denominator pieces come to less?
activities.intendedInsight: Fraction size is one quantity located on the number line, not two independent whole numbers. For a near-whole set the fraction closest to 1 is largest; fractions greater than 1 sit past 1; and a common denominator turns any comparison into a single numerator comparison.

activities.title: Justify the ordering, not just the rank
feedback: Reward an explanation tied to value, size of pieces, or distance to a landmark over one tied to digit size.
For 5/6 vs 7/9, show the common denominator (45/54 vs 42/54), so 5/6 > 7/9 even though both of its digits are smaller — exactly the case the separate-comparison method gets wrong.
Encourage efficiency: for a set clustered near a whole, complement-to-1 is quicker than finding a full common denominator, but the common denominator always works.
activities.rationale: Because whole-number bias can yield a correct rank for the wrong reason on favourable sets, eliciting justification is how understanding is distinguished from a lucky rank; a pair where digit size and value diverge forces the reasoning. Offering multiple strategies supports flexible, number-sensitive choice.
sourceClaims: Fractions are compared by value using equivalent fractions/common denominators or benchmarks; the dominant error is whole-number bias (judging by numerator/denominator digit size and comparing numerators and denominators separately), which reflects treating the two parts as independent whole numbers rather than one quantity.
learnerActions: Order a fresh near-whole set (e.g. 2/3, 5/6, 9/10, 7/8) using the complement-to-1 method, writing each gap to 1 and explaining your reasoning.

Then tackle a pair where digit size and value DISAGREE — for example 5/6 vs 7/9, where '7 > 5 and 9 > 6' wrongly suggests 7/9 is larger — and settle it by writing both over a common denominator and comparing the deciding numerators.
Explain in words why comparing numerators and denominators separately is not a valid method, using the pair above as the case where it breaks down.
State for each answer the strategy you chose (common denominator, benchmark, or complement-to-1) and why it fitted those numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: A correct ranking is not the same as a correct method; the justification is what shows genuine understanding, and the chosen strategy should fit the numbers.

activities.title: Short comparison and placement checks
feedback: For 7/5 vs 4/3, a response of 'equal' or '4/3 because 4 and 3 are bigger' signals whole-number bias; revisit the common denominator 21/15 vs 20/15.
For 2/3 vs 2/5, choosing 2/5 is the bigger-denominator distractor; return to same-numerator reasoning about piece size.
Pair any quick check with a request to explain the choice, since selecting the right answer does not by itself show the learner can construct the reasoning.
activities.rationale: Brief targeted checks can surface specific misconceptions through purpose-built distractors. They assess application but, on their own, do not elicit independent construction of a justification, so they should accompany the explanation work above.
sourceClaims: Fractions are compared by value using equivalent fractions/common denominators or benchmarks; the dominant error is whole-number bias (judging by numerator/denominator digit size and comparing numerators and denominators separately), which reflects treating the two parts as independent whole numbers rather than one quantity.
learnerActions: Order 3/4, 7/8, 5/6, 11/12 smallest to largest.
Decide which is larger, 7/5 or 4/3, and show the common-denominator working.
Decide which is larger, 2/3 or 2/5, and explain the role of the denominator.
Place 7/5 on a 0–2 number line.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can apply comparison strategies quickly and avoid common distractors (choosing 'equal', choosing 4/3 'because 4 and 3 are bigger', or choosing 2/5 because its denominator is larger).

activities.title: Reference fraction wall (support tool)
feedback: Treat the wall as a check or reference, not as the reasoning itself — after confirming, ask the learner to restate which is larger and why in terms of value.
activities.rationale: A prepared length reference supports comparison and can reinforce the magnitude idea. As a fixed scaffold it does not require the learner to place a new set or measure gaps themselves, so it should support, not replace, the active ordering and justification tasks.
learnerActions: Use a fraction wall extended past 1 to reveal which of two bars is longer and by how much.
Use it to check an ordering you have already reasoned out, or to settle a disputed pair.
activities.intendedInsight: A length model reinforces that fractions represent magnitudes that can be directly compared, including beyond one whole.

constraints: Target age is roughly 10–11; the content assumes prior work on equivalent fractions and common denominators.
Recognition/selection checks (choosing which is larger, placing a given fraction) assess application but do not by themselves elicit an independent justification; pair them with explanation tasks.
A pre-built fraction wall is a reference/support: it does not require the learner to order a new set or measure gaps to a landmark independently, so it should not be the only activity.
Complement-to-1 is efficient specifically for sets clustered just below a whole; present common denominators as the always-reliable general method so learners do not over-apply the shortcut.
Keep the goal on justified value comparison: a correct rank produced by digit-size reasoning should not count as mastery, so include at least one set where digit size and value diverge.
Explain same-numerator comparisons by piece size (more same-size pieces is more; a larger denominator makes each piece smaller) rather than any claim that a denominator rule 'reverses' or 'flips'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Critical-editor pass performed without new source verification: arithmetic and logic checked — complement-to-1 gaps for 3/4, 7/8, 5/6, 11/12 are 1/4, 1/8, 1/6, 1/12; ordered smallest-to-largest 3/4 < 5/6 < 7/8 < 11/12 (gaps 1/4 > 1/6 > 1/8 > 1/12); 7/5 = 21/15 > 20/15 = 4/3; 7/5 = 1 2/5 sits past 1; 2/3 > 2/5; 5/6 vs 7/9 = 45/54 vs 42/54 so 5/6 > 7/9. No arithmetic errors found.

The original row's fresh practice set (2/3, 5/6, 9/10, 7/8) is a case where digit size coincidentally matches value; a divergent pair (5/6 vs 7/9) is included in Activity 2 so the justification requirement genuinely bites.
The summary's gap list was relabelled per fraction (3/4 → 1/4, etc.) to match the activity text, since the unlabelled set-order list could be misread as already size-ordered.

The source material's claims that the number line is the single 'best'/'killer' way to see the insight, that depth/3D 'adds nothing', and that in-role dialogue cannot teach this are catalog-fit judgements not established by the cited WWC evidence; they have been softened to affordance-based framing (number line may make magnitude visible) rather than stated as universal pedagogical laws.

probeDeeper: Which of 2/3 and 2/5 is bigger? Explain why the one with the bigger denominator is the smaller fraction.
How far is each of 3/4, 7/8, 5/6 and 11/12 from one whole? What does that tell you about which is biggest?
Is 7/5 bigger or smaller than 1? Where does it sit on a number line?
You said 7/5 > 4/3 — show me using a common denominator.
assess.correctAnswer: Smallest to largest: 3/4 < 5/6 < 7/8 < 11/12 (gaps to 1 are 1/4 > 1/6 > 1/8 > 1/12, so 3/4 is furthest below 1 and 11/12 closest). 7/5 > 4/3 (common denominator /15: 21/15 > 20/15).

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias — 'bigger numbers make a bigger fraction', ranking by digit size ('11/12 is biggest because 11 and 12 are the biggest numbers')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a common denominator or same-size-pieces reasoning: more parts of the same size is more, but bigger denominators make smaller pieces. Order by value, not digits.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Justifies the order by the size of the digits rather than the value; gets 2/3 vs 2/5 wrong (picks 2/5) when probed

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares numerators and denominators separately — '7 > 4 and 5 > 3, so 7/5 > 4/3'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rewrite both over a common denominator (21/15 vs 20/15) so a single numerator comparison decides it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats top and bottom as two independent comparisons; the method fails on pairs where the two comparisons disagree

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot handle fractions greater than 1 — treats 7/5 as if less than 1, or cannot reach a common denominator to compare
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show 7/5 sits past 1 on the number line (7/5 = 1 2/5); find a common denominator via the LCM of 5 and 3.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places 7/5 between 0 and 1, or leaves the pair uncompared for want of a common denominator

responseLevels.gap: Ranks by digit size (whole-number bias) and cannot justify; cannot find common denominators; treats fractions greater than 1 as less than 1.
responseLevels.full: Orders using common denominators or complement-to-1 with justification, compares fractions greater than 1 correctly (7/5 > 4/3 via /15), places improper and mixed numbers on a number line, and handles the 2/3-vs-2/5 counter-case; transfers to a new set.
responseLevels.partial: Orders correctly using common denominators for some pairs but relies on surface cues for others, or gets the near-1 set right without a secure method (cannot explain complement-to-1), or hesitates with fractions greater than 1.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Order 3/4, 7/8, 5/6 and 11/12 from smallest to largest, and tell me how you decided. Then compare 7/5 and 4/3 — which is larger?' Watch the strategy and listen to the justification.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands uses common denominators or complement-to-1 and can justify each step. A child running whole-number bias may still rank THIS set correctly, because bigger digits happen to align with bigger value here — so the justification, not the ranking, is what discriminates. The follow-up 2/3-vs-2/5 probe (bigger denominator, smaller fraction) catches the biased child, and 7/5 vs 4/3 checks they compare fractions above 1 by size rather than by 'which has bigger numbers'.

sources.claim: Fractions are compared by value using equivalent fractions/common denominators or benchmarks; the dominant error is whole-number bias (judging by numerator/denominator digit size and comparing numerators and denominators separately), which reflects treating the two parts as independent whole numbers rather than one quantity.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Equivalent fractions (age 8+)
topic.description: Generate simple equivalent fractions and explain why they are equivalent using visual fraction models
evidence: Given 1/3, generate 2/6 as equivalent and show with area model
Simplify 4/8 to 1/2 and justify with a fraction strip
Complete equivalence chains: 1/4 = ?/8 = ?/12
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is shown a fraction bar split into 3 parts with 1 shaded (= 1/3), can they draw an equivalent bar with 6 parts that shows exactly the same amount shaded?

pedagogy.summary: The procedure of generating equivalent fractions — multiplying (or, to simplify, dividing) the numerator and denominator by the same number — grounded in visual models where the same area or length is re-partitioned into more or fewer equal parts. Includes simplifying by dividing both by a common factor and completing equivalence chains (1/4 = 2/8 = 3/12). The explanation must travel with the procedure so it does not harden into a rote rule.
bestPractices: Derive the ×n rule from re-partitioning a model: split each part into n → n times as many parts, each 1/n the size, the amount unchanged.
Work both directions — build up (1/3 → 2/6) and simplify (4/8 → 1/2) — so equivalence is reversible.
Complete equivalence chains (1/4 = 2/8 = 3/12) to expose the multiplicative pattern.
Always pair the move with 'why is it the same amount?' shown on a diagram, to head off the additive error.
Connect to times-tables / multiplicative reasoning and to ratio tables.
keyRepresentations: Area model re-partitioned (each part split into n)
Fraction strips
Stacked number lines
Equivalence chain / ratio table
Times-table pattern of numerators and denominators
commonMisconceptions: Additive equivalence — add the same number to top and bottom (1/3 → 2/4) — whole-number thinking (IES)
Changing only one part — doubling the numerator but not the denominator
Simplifying by subtracting a common number rather than dividing
Counting parts mechanically without checking the amount is unchanged

learn.summary: Teach generating equivalent fractions as a procedure grounded in re-partitioning the same quantity: splitting each part of a model into n gives n times as many parts, each 1/n the size, so the amount is unchanged — mirrored numerically as multiplying numerator and denominator by n. Work both directions (build up and simplify by dividing out a common factor), complete equivalence chains, and always pair the numeric move with 'why is it the same amount?' on a diagram to head off the additive error (adding the same number to top and bottom).

activities.title: Re-partition a bar to build equivalent fractions
feedback: If the learner adds a constant to each number, place 1/3 and the new fraction on the same strip or number line so the differing lengths are visible; contrast +1 (shifts the amount) with ×2 (re-partitions the same amount).
If the learner changes only one number (e.g. 1/3 → 2/3), show that splitting each part changes BOTH the count of shaded parts and the total together, so both numbers must move.
When a learner simplifies by subtracting (e.g. 4/8 → 3/7), group the parts on the model and divide both counts into equal groups, then verify the shaded amount matches the original.
When the learner gets 2/6 with the length unchanged, name the move: 'you split each part into 2, so 1 shaded part became 2 and 3 total became 6 — the amount didn't change.'
activities.rationale: The IES/WWC guide describes equivalent fractions as re-partitioning the same quantity and attributes the additive error to whole-number thinking; deriving the ×n rule from a visible re-partition is intended to keep the explanation travelling with the procedure so it is less likely to harden into a rote rule.
sourceClaims: Equivalent fractions are generated by re-partitioning the same quantity (e.g. sharing four pizzas among eight children yields 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2); a fraction can be written in infinitely many equivalent ways. The additive 'add numerators and denominators / add the same number to top and bottom' error stems from whole-number thinking.
learnerActions: Start with a bar showing 1/3: one of three equal parts shaded.
Split each part into 2 and recount: the bar now shows 2/6, but the shaded LENGTH is unchanged.
Write the numeric move alongside the picture: ×2 on the top and ×2 on the bottom, 1/3 = 2/6.
Repeat splitting each part into 3 and into 4 to generate 3/9 and 4/12, each time checking the shaded length stays the same.
Deliberately test 'add 1 to each' (1/3 → 2/4): redraw 2/4 and compare its shaded length to 1/3 — it is longer, so the amount changed.
Build a simplify version: group the parts of 4/8 into equal groups and divide both counts by the common factor to reach 1/2, checking the shaded amount is unchanged.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying both numerator and denominator by the same whole number greater than 1, or dividing both by a common factor greater than 1, re-partitions the SAME amount into more (or fewer) equal parts, so the value is preserved; adding the same non-zero number to both changes the amount (except for a fraction equal to one whole, such as 2/2 → 3/3).

activities.title: Complete equivalence chains and simplify both directions
feedback: If a chain cell is filled by adding rather than multiplying, return to the strip for that step and show the shaded length.
If the learner reaches different simplest forms by different divisors, check each division: dividing 4/8 by 2 gives 2/4, then by 2 again gives 1/2 — the same simplest form as dividing by 4 once.
For the number pattern, point out that each numerator and denominator is the previous one scaled by the same factor, linking to times-tables.
activities.rationale: Fill-in chains, matching, and simplify-both-ways tasks practise the reversible multiplicative pattern and let the learner expose the additive answer as wrong; the IES/WWC guide establishes that a fraction has infinitely many equivalent names via re-partitioning, and the national curriculum places recognising/generating equivalents and beginning to simplify in this age range. These are practice items and do not by themselves supply the re-partition justification, which the first activity provides.
sourceClaims: Equivalent fractions are generated by re-partitioning the same quantity (e.g. sharing four pizzas among eight children yields 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2); a fraction can be written in infinitely many equivalent ways. The additive 'add numerators and denominators / add the same number to top and bottom' error stems from whole-number thinking.
Pupils recognise and generate equivalent fractions and begin to simplify in KS2 (Years 3–5).
learnerActions: Fill in the blanks in a chain: 1/4 = ?/8 = ?/12, stating the multiplier used from 1/4 to reach each fraction (×2 for eighths, ×3 for twelfths).
Complete 2/5 = ?/10 = ?/20 and describe the pattern in the numerators and denominators.
Simplify 4/8 to its simplest form; then try dividing by 2 first and compare — do you reach the same simplest form?
Sort or match a set of fractions into 'equivalent to 1/3' and 'not equivalent', explaining each decision.
Answer 'which is 1/3 written in sixths?' and explain why an additive answer like 2/4 is wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalence is reversible and multiplicative: the same quantity has infinitely many equivalent names, and building up (×n) and simplifying (÷ common factor) are the same relationship run in opposite directions.

activities.title: Explain and defend the rule
feedback: Accept a justification only when it links the numeric move to the unchanged shaded amount on the model.
If the learner states 'do the same to both' without the diagram justification, ask them to show the same amount before and after on the strip.
activities.rationale: Requiring the learner to construct and voice the justification is intended to keep the move from hardening into a rote rule and can surface whether the additive error has really been corrected.
sourceClaims: Equivalent fractions are generated by re-partitioning the same quantity (e.g. sharing four pizzas among eight children yields 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2); a fraction can be written in infinitely many equivalent ways. The additive 'add numerators and denominators / add the same number to top and bottom' error stems from whole-number thinking.
learnerActions: After making 1/3 into 2/6 by ×2, explain on the strip WHY that keeps the value the same.
Judge a claim: 'Jo made 1/3 into 2/4 by adding one to each' — is Jo right? Show why or why not on a model.
State the rule you used in your own words and test it on one new example of your choice.
activities.intendedInsight: A correct equivalence method can be justified on a diagram and distinguished from the additive error through reasoning, not just by recalling 'do the same to both'.

constraints: Target age roughly 8–9 (KS2 Years 3–5): recognise and generate simple equivalents and begin to simplify.
Always pair each numeric move (×n or ÷ common factor) with a visible model showing the amount is unchanged; do not teach the rule in isolation.
Work both directions — build up and simplify — so equivalence is reversible.

A worked reference display (tap a fraction to reveal its equivalents with the ×n annotation) aids recall but is a recall aid only: it does not let the learner carry out and check the procedure, so it cannot replace the re-partitioning activity.

Practice formats (fill-in chains, matching, and selecting the correct equivalent) practise and assess the procedure but do not on their own build the re-partition justification; include at least one task where the learner explains why the amount is unchanged.

Optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete (a bar that redraws as 2/6 with unchanged shaded length when each part is split; a numeric panel mirroring ×2 top and bottom; dragging a '+1' card and seeing the shaded length change colour; a chain builder; a merge-parts simplify mode) are illustrations, not required implementations — any medium, including paper strips and number lines, that shows the unchanged amount works.

One listed source (national curriculum programmes of study) is marked verified:false in the row; the IES/WWC guide is marked verified:true. Evidence strength is carried over unchanged and not independently re-checked.

The original 'turns red / flashes red' and 'directly exposed in the child's hands' framing was softened: a colour-change on an incorrect move is a useful feedback illustration, not evidence that one medium uniquely teaches the concept. Comparative-efficacy and 'only this teaches' style claims from the original fit rankings were removed.
Rationale wording was shifted to intended/aims-to phrasing where efficacy is a design expectation rather than an established result.

Arithmetic self-check: 1/3 split each part into 2 → 2/6; into 3 → 3/9; into 4 → 4/12. 4/8 ÷4 = 1/2, and ÷2 twice (4/8→2/4→1/2) reaches the same simplest form. Chain 1/4 = 2/8 = 3/12 and 2/5 = 4/10 = 8/20 check out. The additive example 1/3 'add 1 to each' giving 2/4 is retained only as a deliberately-wrong case to contrast, never as a valid method.

probeDeeper: You multiplied top and bottom by 2. Why does that keep the value the same — show me on the strip.
Jo made 1/3 into 2/4 by adding one to each. Is Jo right? Show why or why not.
To simplify 4/8 you divided by 4. Could you have divided by 2 first? Would you reach the same simplest form?
Complete 2/5 = ?/10 = ?/20 — what is the pattern in the numbers?
assess.correctAnswer: Generates e.g. 2/6, 3/9, 4/12 by splitting each third into equal parts / multiplying top and bottom by the same number, each shown as the same shaded amount; simplifies 4/8 → 1/2 by dividing both by 4; completes 1/4 = 2/8 = 3/12.

errorPatterns.pattern: Additive equivalence — makes '2/4' from 1/3 by adding 1 to top and bottom
errorPatterns.nextMove: Place both on the strip/line to show the lengths differ; contrast +1 (shifts the amount) with ×2 (re-partitions the same amount)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 2/4, 3/5 … adding a constant; the shown strip no longer matches 1/3

errorPatterns.pattern: Changes only one part — doubles the numerator (1/3 → 2/3) and calls it equivalent
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model that splitting each part changes the count of shaded parts AND the total together; both numbers move
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Alters numerator or denominator alone while generating

errorPatterns.pattern: Simplifies by subtracting — '4/8 → 3/7 or 2/6' by taking a common number off, or cannot check the amount is unchanged
errorPatterns.nextMove: Group the parts on the model and divide both counts into equal groups; verify the shaded amount is the same
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Subtracts rather than divides both by a common factor when simplifying

responseLevels.gap: Uses additive or single-part moves; simplifies by subtracting; cannot show the amount is preserved.
responseLevels.full: Fluently generates and simplifies equivalents by multiplying/dividing both parts by the same factor, justifies with a re-partition model, completes the chain, and rejects the additive method with reasoning.
responseLevels.partial: Correctly multiplies both parts to build up equivalents but cannot reliably simplify, or states the rule ('do the same to both') without the re-partition justification; completes some chain cells.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is 1/3 shown on an area model and a fraction strip. Task: make three different fractions that are equal to 1/3, showing each on the model, and tell me the rule you used. Then simplify 4/8 to its simplest form, and complete this chain: 1/4 = ?/8 = ?/12. I'll watch how you work.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the method reveals whether the child multiplies BOTH parts by the same factor and checks the amount is unchanged, versus adding a constant to each, changing only one part, or subtracting to simplify. The build-up task, the simplify task and the chain together catch errors in both directions; a right method looks different in the hand from a wrong one.

sources.claim: Equivalent fractions are generated by re-partitioning the same quantity (e.g. sharing four pizzas among eight children yields 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2); a fraction can be written in infinitely many equivalent ways. The additive 'add numerators and denominators / add the same number to top and bottom' error stems from whole-number thinking.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide, Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for K-8 (Siegler et al., 2010, NCEE 2010-4039)

sources.claim: Pupils recognise and generate equivalent fractions and begin to simplify in KS2 (Years 3–5).
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS1-2)

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Equivalent fractions (age 9+)
topic.description: Explain why a fraction a/b is equivalent to (n×a)/(n×b) using visual models; use this principle to recognise and generate equivalent fractions, including tenths and hundredths
evidence: Use a fraction strip to show 2/3 = 4/6 = 6/9
Explain that multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number gives an equivalent fraction because the size of the whole is unchanged
Generate three fractions equivalent to 3/5 and verify with diagrams
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to make 2/3 look different without changing its value, can they multiply the top and bottom by the same number and explain why the fraction stays the same?

pedagogy.summary: The general principle that multiplying the numerator and denominator by the same number n gives an equivalent fraction, and WHY: splitting each of the b parts into n equal pieces makes n×b pieces in the whole and n×a shaded, so the same amount is renamed with a finer counting-unit — the whole and the shaded magnitude are unchanged. This extends to tenths and hundredths (3/10 = 30/100) and is the same as multiplying the fraction by n/n, a name for 1.
bestPractices: Justify with re-partition: each part becomes n parts, so both counts grow ×n while the magnitude is fixed — the point does not move.
Generalise from many worked cases to the statement a/b = (n×a)/(n×b) (IES: any fraction can be written infinitely many equivalent ways).
Frame the move as multiplying by n/n = 1, so the value cannot change.
Apply directly to tenths and hundredths (3/10 = 30/100) as a bridge to decimals.
Confront the additive error head-on — multiplying is repeated re-partitioning; adding a constant is not.
keyRepresentations: Area model re-partitioned (each part → n parts)
Stacked / dual-labelled number lines
Multiplying by n/n (a name for 1)
Ratio table of numerators and denominators
Tenths ↔ hundredths grid
commonMisconceptions: Additive equivalence — adding the same number to top and bottom keeps it equal (IES whole-number thinking)
Whole-number bias — (n×a)/(n×b) 'must be bigger' because the numbers are bigger (4/6 > 2/3)
Multiplying only one part
Believing the value must change because 'you did something to it'

learn.summary: Learners understand WHY multiplying numerator and denominator by the same whole number n (n ≥ 1) gives an equivalent fraction: splitting each of the b parts into n equal pieces makes n×b pieces in the whole and n×a shaded, so the SAME magnitude is renamed with a finer counting-unit. This is the same as multiplying by n/n, a name for 1, so the value cannot change. It extends to tenths and hundredths (3/10 = 30/100). The central contrast is with the additive error: adding a constant to top and bottom is not re-partitioning and in general changes the amount (the only exception is a fraction equal to 1, such as 2/2 → 3/3); for example, adding 1 to the numerator and 1 to the denominator turns 2/3 into 3/4, which is larger, not equal.

activities.title: Rename the same amount: fix the shaded length, change the labels
feedback: If both counts grew but the shaded length stayed put, you have renamed the same amount — that is why 2/3 = 4/6.
If you changed only one part (just the top or just the bottom), re-cut EVERY part instead: splitting each piece changes both the shaded count and the total count together.
If the additive bar (3/4) visibly reached past the 2/3 strip, you have shown that adding 1 to each part is not equivalence — it moves you to a bigger amount.
To check the value is unchanged, ask: did I split each part into equal pieces (keeps the amount), or did I add extra amount (changes it)?
activities.rationale: Equivalence is produced by re-partitioning the same quantity into finer equal parts, so any fraction has infinitely many equivalent names; holding a fixed magnitude while the labels change makes the invariance concrete and directly confronts the additive whole-number error. Paper strips are approximations of ideal flat regions, so the teaching point is the preserved shaded magnitude, not the paper itself.
sourceClaims: Equivalence is produced by re-partitioning the same quantity into finer equal parts (four pizzas among eight children: 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2), so any fraction has infinitely many equivalent names; the additive 'add the same number to top and bottom' error is whole-number thinking, and treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers underlies errors like 3/8 > 3/5.
learnerActions: Shade 2/3 of a bar (or mark 2/3 as a point on a number line) and keep that shaded length physically fixed — e.g. with a strip of coloured paper laid over the bar.
Subdivide every third into 2 equal pieces, then 3, then 4, and each time count the total pieces and the shaded pieces.
Record the sequence of names for the SAME shaded length: 2/3 → 4/6 → 6/9 → 8/12, and alongside each write the equation ×2, ×3, ×4 applied to both numerator and denominator.
State in your own words why the shaded amount never moved: each part was re-cut into more, smaller pieces, so both counts grew together while the whole and the shaded magnitude stayed the same.

Now test the additive move: change 2/3 by adding 1 to the numerator and 1 to the denominator to get 3/4. Shade 3/4 on an identical bar and lay it against the 2/3 strip. Observe that 3/4 reaches further — it is a different, larger amount.
Explain the difference out loud: multiplying re-cuts the same whole; adding a constant to each part does not re-cut anything, so here (and for any fraction not equal to 1) it lands on a new amount.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying numerator and denominator by a whole number n (n ≥ 1) re-partitions the same whole into finer equal parts, renaming a fixed magnitude; adding the same number to each is not re-partitioning and changes the amount (unless the fraction equals 1). Multiplying by n/n is multiplying by 1.

activities.title: Overlay check: is 4/6 bigger than 2/3?
feedback: If the two marks land on the same point, you have shown 4/6 = 2/3 despite the larger numbers.
If you expected 4/6 to be bigger, count the piece size: sixths are half the size of thirds, so 4 of them equal 2 thirds.
2/2 = 1, and multiplying any amount by 1 leaves it unchanged — that is the whole reason the rule works.
activities.rationale: Directly addresses whole-number bias (that scaled-up numbers 'must be bigger') by making the equal point/length visible on a common whole and tying it to multiplication by 1.
sourceClaims: Equivalence is produced by re-partitioning the same quantity into finer equal parts (four pizzas among eight children: 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2), so any fraction has infinitely many equivalent names; the additive 'add the same number to top and bottom' error is whole-number thinking, and treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers underlies errors like 3/8 > 3/5.
learnerActions: Place 2/3 and 4/6 on a shared number line (or overlay two identical strips, one cut into thirds with 2 shaded, one cut into sixths with 4 shaded).
Decide whether 4/6 lands on the same point as 2/3 or further along.
Explain why 4/6 is NOT bigger even though 4>2 and 6>3: there are more pieces, but each is smaller, so the total shaded amount is the same.
Connect this to multiplying by 2/2: state what 2/2 equals and why multiplying by it cannot change the value.
activities.intendedInsight: A larger numerator and denominator do not imply a bigger amount when both were scaled by the same factor — the pieces are correspondingly smaller, so the magnitude is unchanged.

activities.title: Generalise and bridge to tenths and hundredths
feedback: If each generated fraction matches 3/5 on your diagram, you have produced genuine equivalents, not just applied a step.
For 3/10 = 30/100, each tenth was cut into 10 hundredths: 10× as many pieces, each a tenth the size, same amount.
If you can say the factor (here 10/10 = 1) and why it preserves value, you understand the rule rather than just the procedure.
activities.rationale: Year 5 pupils identify, name and write equivalent fractions including tenths and hundredths; generalising from several verified cases to the symbolic statement supports durable understanding and the decimal bridge.
sourceClaims: In Year 5 (age 9–10) pupils identify, name and write equivalent fractions of a given fraction, represented visually, including tenths and hundredths.
learnerActions: Generate three fractions equivalent to 3/5 and verify each with a strip or number-line diagram.
State the general rule in words and symbols: a/b = (n×a)/(n×b) for any whole number n ≥ 1, and explain why it holds (re-partition each part into n).
Write 3/10 as hundredths: 3/10 = 30/100. State what you multiplied by (10/10) and why the value does not change.
Explain how this renaming into hundredths helps when working with decimals.
activities.intendedInsight: The equivalence rule generalises to any whole-number factor n ≥ 1 and to the tenths↔hundredths renaming that underpins decimals; the justification (re-partition = multiply by n/n = 1) is the same every time.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: Jo vs Sam
feedback: Jo is right: 2/3 = 4/6. Multiplying both by 2 splits each third into two sixths — twice as many parts, each half the size — so the shaded amount and the whole are unchanged; it is the same point renamed, and ×2/2 is multiplying by 1.
Sam is wrong: adding 1 to the numerator and 1 to the denominator turns 2/3 into 3/4, a different, larger amount, because he is not re-partitioning the same whole.
If you endorsed Sam, place 2/3 and 3/4 on one line: they are different points. Adding shifts the amount; splitting each part keeps it.
If you said 4/6 > 2/3 because the numbers are bigger, overlay them: same point. More pieces, each smaller — same total.
If you only said 'do the same to both' without mentioning re-partitioning or the fixed amount, add the reason: each part is cut into more equal pieces, so the magnitude is preserved.
activities.rationale: A two-tier predict-explain task is proposed to discriminate genuine magnitude-preserving understanding from procedural recall and from the additive and whole-number-bias misconceptions; requiring the reason before observation is the intended diagnostic element. The cited claim supports the misconception content, not the format's efficacy.
sourceClaims: Equivalence is produced by re-partitioning the same quantity into finer equal parts (four pizzas among eight children: 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2), so any fraction has infinitely many equivalent names; the additive 'add the same number to top and bottom' error is whole-number thinking, and treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers underlies errors like 3/8 > 3/5.
learnerActions: Read the claim: Jo says 2/3 = 4/6 (she multiplied top and bottom by 2); Sam says 2/3 = 3/4 (he added 1 to the numerator and 1 to the denominator). Before drawing, PREDICT with a reason whether 2/3 and 3/4 land on the same point.
Place 2/3, 4/6 and 3/4 on one shared number line (or overlay identical strips) and observe where each falls.
Decide who is right and justify: explain why multiplying keeps the amount but adding does not.

Answer the probes: Why does multiplying both the numerator and the denominator by 2 give twice as many parts but the same amount of chocolate? When you write 2/3 as 4/6, are you multiplying by 2 or by 2/2 — and what is 2/2? Is 3/4 bigger, smaller or equal to 2/3 — prove it on a line?
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalence is renaming a fixed magnitude by re-partitioning (multiplying by a form of 1); adding 1 to each part of 2/3 lands on a different, larger amount (3/4). Stating the reason before checking exposes whether the understanding is genuine.

constraints: A reference display of ×n families (tap 2/3 → 4/6, 6/9, 8/12 with ×n annotations) aids recall but does not let the learner enact the magnitude-preserving re-partition; use it as a support, not the main teaching move.

Recognition/selection tasks (choose which fraction equals 3/5; match ×n pairs; fill in 3/10 = ?/100) are useful for testing the rule and surfacing the additive distractor, but do not by themselves elicit the learner's own re-partition explanation — pair them with a construction or spoken justification.

When using paper strips or cutouts, treat them as approximations of ideal flat regions (real paper has slight thickness); the point is the preserved shaded magnitude, so keep the shaded length physically fixed when comparing names.
Correct the 'multiply only one part' error at the model: both numerator and denominator must change together because every part is re-cut; changing one alone is not equivalence.

A live, draggable subdivision slider with a linked ×n equation and a colour change on the additive move is one way to make the mechanism visible; it is an optional interaction example, not a requirement — the same insight can be reached with paper strips and a number line. Comparative efficacy between these media is not established by the sources.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source diagnostic states Sam adds 1 to the numerator and 1 to the denominator to get 2/3 = 3/4; the audited arithmetic is correct (2/3 ≈ 0.667 < 3/4 = 0.75, so Sam is wrong; 2/3 = 4/6 exactly). No arithmetic error found in the migrated examples.

The source IES claim quotes 'errors like 3/8 > 3/5' as a stated misconception (the true relation is 3/8 < 3/5); it is retained verbatim and framed correctly as an error, never presented to learners as true.
The National Curriculum source is marked unverified in the original; the tenths/hundredths age framing is retained as cited but not independently re-checked here.

The original 'directly defeats'/'cannot animate'/'best grasped not by dialogue' style claims about formats have been softened to scoped affordances; comparative efficacy of any single interaction format is not established by the sources.

The keyRepresentations 'ratio table' is not a standalone activity; the ×n sequence recording in activity 1 captures the same numerator/denominator tabular pattern. A dedicated ratio table could be added if a distinct representation is wanted.

assess.poeTask: Before drawing: Sam claims adding 1 to the top and bottom keeps a fraction the same, so 2/3 = 3/4. Ask the child to PREDICT, with a reason, whether 2/3 and 3/4 land on the same point on a number line. The reason stated before observing is the diagnostic part. Then place both on a shared line (or overlay strips): 3/4 sits to the right of 2/3, refuting the additive rule — while 2/3 and 4/6 coincide exactly.
probeDeeper: Why does multiplying top and bottom by 2 give twice as many parts but the same amount of chocolate?
When you write 2/3 as 4/6, what are you really multiplying 2/3 by — is it 2, or is it 2/2? What is 2/2?
Sam's method turned 2/3 into 3/4. Is 3/4 bigger, smaller, or equal to 2/3? Prove it on a line.
Write 3/10 as hundredths. What did you multiply by, and why doesn't the value change?
assess.correctAnswer: Jo is right: 2/3 = 4/6. Multiplying both by 2 splits each third into two sixths — twice as many parts, each half the size — so the shaded AMOUNT and the whole are unchanged; it is the same point renamed (and ×2/2 is multiplying by 1). Sam is wrong: adding 1 to each turns 2/3 into 3/4, a different, larger amount, because he is not re-partitioning the same whole.

errorPatterns.pattern: Additive equivalence — 'you can add the same number to top and bottom and it stays equal, so 2/3 = 3/4'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Place 2/3 and 3/4 on one number line to show different points; contrast splitting each part (×) with shifting the amount (+)
errorPatterns.distractor: Sam is right too — adding 1 to the top and 1 to the bottom keeps the fraction the same
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Endorses Sam, or says both methods are fine

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias — 'Jo changed it: 4/6 is bigger than 2/3 because 4>2 and 6>3'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay 2/3 and 4/6 on strips / a shared line — same length, same point; multiplying by 2/2 is multiplying by 1
errorPatterns.distractor: Jo changed the fraction — 4/6 is bigger than 2/3 because the numbers are bigger
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the value grew after multiplying both parts

errorPatterns.pattern: Multiplying only one part — thinks doubling just the top (or just the bottom) gives an equivalent
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show on the model that splitting each part changes the count of shaded parts AND the total — both numbers must move together
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked to check or generate another case, changes one part only

responseLevels.gap: Endorses the additive method, or says multiplying changes the value (bigger numbers = bigger amount); offers no magnitude-preserving reasoning.
responseLevels.full: Explains ×n as re-partitioning each part into n — both counts grow while the whole and shaded magnitude stay fixed (same point renamed) — shows adding moves the point, and transfers the reasoning to tenths → hundredths.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the ×n rule and picks Jo, but justifies only procedurally ('you do the same to both') without the re-partition / same-magnitude explanation, or cannot say why adding fails — listing the steps without relating parts to the whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Jo says 2/3 = 4/6 because she multiplied the top and the bottom by 2. Sam says 2/3 = 3/4 because he added 1 to the top and 1 to the bottom. Who is right? Explain, using a picture or a number line, WHY that method keeps the fraction the same and the other one doesn't.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The correct child links ×n to re-partitioning that preserves magnitude and explains why adding fails. A child with the additive misconception endorses Sam or treats both methods as equally valid; a whole-number-bias child says 4/6 > 2/3 because the numbers are bigger. It is hard to give the magnitude-preserving reason without genuine understanding, and hard to endorse Sam if you hold it.
