topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Simplifying Fractions
topic.description: Use common factors to simplify fractions to their simplest form; use common multiples to express fractions with a common denominator
evidence: Simplify 18/24 to 3/4 by identifying the HCF of 18 and 24
Express 2/3 and 5/8 with a common denominator of 24
Explain why dividing numerator and denominator by a common factor produces an equivalent fraction
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has the fraction 12/16, can they simplify it to its lowest terms — and explain what they divided the top and bottom by?

pedagogy.summary: Simplifying is the equivalence principle run in reverse: instead of multiplying numerator and denominator by n, you DIVIDE both by a common factor, which regroups the same quantity into fewer, larger pieces without changing its value. Simplest form is reached when numerator and denominator share no common factor but 1 (i.e. you have divided by the HCF). The same machinery — finding a common multiple — lets you rewrite two fractions over a shared denominator. Both skills rest on one idea from Year 5: a/b = (n×a)/(n×b), so a/b = (a÷n)/(b÷n). Teach simplification as 'un-grouping' back to the coarsest partition, not as a memorised rule.
bestPractices: Anchor the procedure to the equivalence principle already learned: show that dividing top and bottom by the same number is the inverse of multiplying by the same number, so the value is unchanged — use a fraction wall or area model where 6/8 and 3/4 occupy identical length.

Connect directly to common factors/multiples work: to simplify, divide by a common factor (fastest via the HCF); to find a common denominator, use a common multiple (efficiently the LCM). Make the number theory visible, not incidental.

Distinguish 'an equivalent, simpler fraction' from 'simplest form' explicitly — a child who writes 6/8 = 3/4 has simplified; a child who writes 6/8 = ... but stops at a form still sharing a factor has not finished. Ask 'can you go further?' every time.
Use dividing-by-HCF as the efficient route but accept repeated division by any common factor (÷2 then ÷2) as valid — the concept, not the shortcut, is the target.
Contrast simplifying with the illegal move of adding or subtracting the same number from top and bottom, which does change the value; have children test 6/8 vs (6-2)/(8-2)=4/6 against the wall.
keyRepresentations: Fraction wall / bar model where equivalent fractions align to identical length (6/8 sits exactly over 3/4)
Area model / grid that can be re-partitioned by merging small cells into larger groups (24 cells shaded 18, re-grouped into 4 columns of which 3 are shaded → 3/4)
Factor pairs and HCF listing beside the fraction (18 = 2×3×3, 24 = 2×2×2×3, common = 2×3 = 6)
Number line showing 18/24 and 3/4 landing on the identical point
Common-multiple ladder for the common-denominator task (thirds and eighths both re-cut into 24ths)
commonMisconceptions: Simplifying by SUBTRACTING a common amount from numerator and denominator (6/8 → 4/6 by taking 2 from each) instead of dividing — treats the fraction additively.
Stopping before simplest form: dividing 18/24 by 2 to get 9/12 and calling it done, not checking for a remaining common factor.
Operating on only one part — dividing the numerator but not the denominator (or renaming only the denominator when finding a common denominator).
Believing simplifying changes the fraction's value ('3/4 is bigger than 6/8 because 4 is fewer pieces') rather than renaming the same quantity.
When finding a common denominator, changing the denominators to match but forgetting to scale the numerators correspondingly.

learn.summary: Teach simplifying as the equivalence principle run in reverse: dividing numerator and denominator by a common factor regroups the same quantity into fewer, larger pieces without changing its value, just as multiplying both by n does. Simplest form is reached when numerator and denominator share no common factor but 1 (you have divided by the HCF). The same number-theory machinery — finding a common multiple — lets two fractions be rewritten over a shared denominator. Anchor to the Year 5 fact a/b = (n×a)/(n×b), so a/b = (a÷n)/(b÷n), and treat simplification as 'un-grouping' back to the coarsest partition, not a memorised rule.

activities.title: Un-grouping a bar: 18/24 back to simplest form
feedback: If the bar length stays fixed while the label changes, the value is unchanged — that non-movement IS the point: same quantity, fewer pieces.
If a chosen divisor leaves leftover cells that won't tile evenly, it is not a common factor of both numbers — that felt 'doesn't fit' is what 'common factor' means.
If you stop at 9/12, ask 'can you go further? do 9 and 12 still share a factor?' — 9/12 is correct but not finished.
Dividing by the HCF (6) reaches simplest form in one step; for 18/24, ÷2 then ÷3 is equally valid and reaches the same place — the concept, not the shortcut, is the target.
activities.rationale: A re-partitionable area/bar model lets the learner perform the regrouping and see the fixed length, making 'same value, fewer pieces' and 'common factor' felt rather than merely told. An optional divisor-snap mechanism (groups form only when the divisor divides both numbers, otherwise leftovers appear) may make the failure of a non-common factor concrete; a 'simplest form' indicator that stays dark until no factor above 1 remains may discourage stopping early. These interaction examples are illustrative proposals, not required and not empirically validated.
sourceClaims: Understanding equivalent fractions — that a fraction can be renamed by multiplying or dividing numerator and denominator by the same number without changing its value — is foundational, and instruction should build simplifying on this principle using visual number-line and area models rather than rote rules.
Pupils should use common factors to simplify fractions and use common multiples to express fractions in the same denomination (Year 6 statutory content).
learnerActions: Start with a bar partitioned into 24 cells with 18 shaded, labelled 18/24.
Choose a number to 'group by' (a divisor) and merge the cells into equal groups of that size, watching the fraction label recompute (e.g. grouping in sixes gives 4 fat groups with 3 shaded → 3/4).

Observe that for each valid grouping of the original 24-cell bar the shaded LENGTH does not move while the label takes an equivalent form (grouping by 2 → 9/12, by 3 → 6/8, by 6 → 3/4) — the quantity is unchanged, only the cut is coarser.
Deliberately try a divisor that is NOT a common factor (e.g. 5): notice the cells will not group evenly and leftovers remain, so that divisor is rejected.
Keep going until no grouping beyond 1 is possible, then state the simplest form and name the HCF (6) that would have reached it in one step.
Also try the valid repeated route (÷2 then ÷3) and confirm it lands on the same 3/4.
activities.intendedInsight: Dividing both parts by a common factor regroups the same quantity into fewer, larger equal pieces, leaving the value (length) unchanged; simplest form is reached only when no common factor above 1 remains.

activities.title: Common denominator by re-cutting to a shared multiple
feedback: If you changed only the denominators (2/24, 5/24) the fractions now mean far less than before — re-cutting the whole into more parts means you must count correspondingly more shaded parts.
Both 24 and 48 are common multiples of 3 and 8, so both give a valid shared denominator; 24 is the smallest (the LCM).
Match the scaling factor: 3→24 is ×8, so 2→16; 8→24 is ×3, so 5→15.
activities.rationale: Re-cutting two bars to a shared grid makes a common multiple visible as a partition both fractions can sit on, and re-shading exposes the classic error of changing denominators without scaling numerators. A ladder of common multiples may make the LCM choice explicit. These are proposed scaffolds, not validated interventions.
sourceClaims: Pupils should use common factors to simplify fractions and use common multiples to express fractions in the same denomination (Year 6 statutory content).
learnerActions: Place bars for 2/3 and 5/8 (or thirds and eighths) side by side.
Find a common multiple of 3 and 8 to use as the shared denominator (24 works; 48 also works — find the smallest, the LCM).
Re-cut BOTH bars into 24ths and rewrite each fraction: 2/3 = 16/24 and 5/8 = 15/24, scaling each numerator by the same factor used on its denominator.
Check: 2/3 becomes 16/24 because both parts were multiplied by 8; 5/8 becomes 15/24 because both were multiplied by 3 — the numerator must scale with the denominator.
Compare using 24 versus 48 and explain why 24 is the smallest denominator that works.
activities.intendedInsight: Expressing fractions over a common denominator uses a common multiple (efficiently the LCM); when you change a denominator you must scale its numerator by the same factor, or you change the quantity.

activities.title: Divide versus subtract: testing the illegal move
feedback: If 4/6 and 6/8 land at different lengths on the wall, the value changed — subtracting from both parts is not simplifying.
If 3/4 and 6/8 land at the same length, dividing both parts preserved the value — that is the legal move.
activities.rationale: Directly testing the additive misconception against a length model lets the learner see the value shift, addressing the common belief that any identical change to both parts is harmless. The wall comparison is the diagnostic surface.
sourceClaims: Understanding equivalent fractions — that a fraction can be renamed by multiplying or dividing numerator and denominator by the same number without changing its value — is foundational, and instruction should build simplifying on this principle using visual number-line and area models rather than rote rules.
learnerActions: Take 6/8 and perform the illegal move of subtracting the same amount from both parts: (6−2)/(8−2) = 4/6.
Lay 6/8 and 4/6 on the same fraction wall or bar and compare their lengths.
Observe that the lengths differ, so subtracting the same number from top and bottom DID change the value.
Contrast with dividing both parts by 2: 6/8 → 3/4, whose length matches 6/8 exactly.
State what the test showed: multiplying or dividing both parts by the same non-zero number keeps the value, but subtracting the same amount from both parts generally changes it (as 6/8 → 4/6 did).
activities.intendedInsight: Simplifying is division of both parts by a common factor, not subtraction of a common amount; the additive move generally changes the value (it keeps it only in special cases such as fractions equal to 1), so it is not a valid equivalence method.

activities.title: Check and explain (assessment of output)
feedback: Only 3/4 among 9/12, 6/8, 3/4, 12/16 is fully simplified; the others still share a factor with their denominator.
9/12 is not wrong, just not finished — 9 and 12 still share a factor of 3, so simplify again to 3/4.

For 18/24, answers like 16/22 or 12/18 (from subtracting a common amount from both parts) or 3/24 (dividing only the numerator) reveal the wrong operation, not just a stopping error — revisit the bar model.
activities.rationale: Short checkable items with distractors built from the subtract-instead-of-divide and stop-early errors make this a diagnostic assessment of the output. Recognition and short-answer items check the result; by themselves they do not elicit the regrouping insight, so this complements rather than replaces the manipulative work.
learnerActions: Write 18/24 in its simplest form and show the working (via HCF 6, or ÷2 then ÷3).
Rewrite 2/3 and 5/8 so they share the same denominator.
Identify which of 9/12, 6/8, 3/4, 12/16 is fully simplified and explain why the others are not.
Explain why dividing both parts by the same non-zero number does not change the value, while subtracting the same amount from both parts generally does.
Answer: your friend simplified 18/24 to 9/12 and stopped — is 9/12 wrong, or just not finished? How do you know?
activities.intendedInsight: Simplest form and common-denominator rewriting can be stated and justified, distinguishing a correct-but-unfinished answer from a wrong operation.

constraints: Build simplifying on the equivalence principle learners met in Year 5 (a/b = (n×a)/(n×b)); do not teach it as an isolated rule.
Make the number theory explicit: divide by a common factor (efficiently the HCF) to simplify; use a common multiple (efficiently the LCM) for a common denominator.
Always ask 'can you go further?' — distinguish 'an equivalent simpler fraction' from 'simplest form'. Stopping at 9/12 is unfinished, not wrong.
Accept repeated division by any common factor (e.g. ÷2 then ÷2 where both divide evenly, or ÷2 then ÷3 for 18/24) as valid; the concept, not the HCF shortcut, is the target.
Simplifying compares and regroups the SAME fraction; no denominator rule 'flips' — dividing both parts by a shared factor is a single consistent operation.

A static tap-to-reveal worked example (e.g. tap to show factor pairs of 18 and 24, highlight the HCF, reveal ÷6 on both parts) can serve as a reference card but does not let the learner try divisors or feel the regrouping; use it alongside, not instead of, hands-on work.
Recognition/short-answer items assess the output (simplest form, common denominator) but do not by themselves elicit the regrouping insight; pair them with construction on a model.
Scale BOTH parts by the same factor: dividing only the numerator, or changing denominators without scaling numerators, changes the quantity.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One listed source (DfE National Curriculum, Year 6 Fractions) is marked verified:false in the source row; treat its claim as unconfirmed.

Arithmetic self-audit: 18/24 ÷ 6 = 3/4 (correct); HCF(18,24)=6 via 18=2×3×3, 24=2×2×2×3, common 2×3=6 (correct). For a shared denominator of 24, 2/3 = 16/24 (×8) and 5/8 = 15/24 (×3) are correct equivalent rewrites, not a sum. 6/8 with the subtract move gives (6−2)/(8−2)=4/6 (a correct depiction of the misconception).

Clarification on the source assessment's additive-misconception examples: subtracting a common amount from 18/24 can correctly yield 12/18 (subtract 6 from each) or 16/22 (subtract 2 from each) — both are legitimate depictions of the subtract-instead-of-divide error, differing only in the amount removed. The source is NOT internally inconsistent here; the divide-vs-subtract activity simply uses the single, cleaner 6/8 → 4/6 example to keep one consistent base fraction.

The source's catalog fit ratings assert that 3D and in-role dialogue add no conceptual value here. These are medium-fit opinions, not established facts; a conversation could still coach and a spatial model could still illustrate. Guidance retains only the narrow observable point (execution and felt regrouping are what the manipulative directly supports) without asserting that other media are impossible.

The 'the concept lives only in the manipulation' and 'a quiz only assesses' framings from the source are softened to narrow affordances: the checking activity is a complementary assessment of output, and recognition alone does not elicit production of the regrouping.

probeDeeper: You wrote 18/24 = 3/4. How do you know 3/4 is as simple as it gets — could you simplify it further? Why not?
Why does dividing the top and bottom by the same number NOT change the fraction's value, when subtracting the same number from both DOES change it?
Your friend simplified 18/24 to 9/12 and stopped. Is 9/12 wrong, or just not finished? How would you know?
To add 2/3 and 5/8 you first put them over 24. Why 24 — would 48 also work? What is the smallest denominator that works, and how did you find it?
assess.correctAnswer: 18/24 = 3/4 (divide both by the HCF 6, or ÷2 then ÷3). Common denominator 24: 2/3 = 16/24 and 5/8 = 15/24.

errorPatterns.pattern: Simplifies by subtracting the same amount from top and bottom ('take 6 off each: 18/24 becomes 12/18') instead of dividing — treats the fraction additively.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put 18/24 and their subtracted answer on the same bar/wall — the lengths differ, so the value changed. Re-establish that only ×n/n or ÷n/n leaves the quantity unchanged; reteach the equivalence principle.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer like 12/18 or 4/6 for 6/8; when asked to show working, the child subtracts rather than divides.

errorPatterns.pattern: Stops before simplest form ('18/24 = 9/12, done') — divides by a common factor once but does not check whether the result still shares a factor.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach — the operation is sound. Prompt 'can you go further? do 9 and 12 still share a factor?' Build the habit of checking for remaining common factors; suggest dividing by the HCF in one step.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Produces a correct-but-not-final equivalent (9/12 or 6/8) and treats the task as complete.

errorPatterns.pattern: Operates on only one part — divides the numerator but leaves the denominator (or, in the common-denominator task, changes denominators to 24 but leaves the numerators unchanged: 2/24 and 5/24).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the bar: changing the number of parts you count without re-cutting the whole (or vice versa) makes a different quantity. Reteach that equivalence scales BOTH parts by the same factor.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers such as 3/24 for simplifying, or 2/24 and 5/24 for the common-denominator half.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reach an equivalent simpler fraction, or subtracts from both parts; changes denominators without scaling numerators. Does not connect the action to keeping the value the same.
responseLevels.full: Simplifies to 3/4 by dividing both parts by a common factor (ideally the HCF), verifies no common factor remains, and explains that dividing both parts by the same number regroups the same quantity so the value is unchanged. Rewrites 2/3 and 5/8 as 16/24 and 15/24, scaling numerators with denominators, and can justify the choice of 24 as a common multiple. Transfers the reasoning to a new fraction on request.
responseLevels.partial: Divides both parts correctly to produce an equivalent fraction and can find a common denominator, but stops before simplest form, or can execute the steps without explaining why the value is unchanged — lists the procedure without the relational reason.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is 18/24. Write it in its simplest form, and show how you got there. Then rewrite 2/3 and 5/8 so they share the same denominator.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the child work separates the child who DIVIDES both parts (correct) from the child who subtracts a common amount, who divides only one part, or who stops before simplest form. A child reasoning correctly divides top and bottom by a shared factor and checks nothing divides further; a child with the additive misconception produces 16/22 or 4/6-type answers that look plausible but reveal the wrong operation. The common-denominator half exposes whether they scale numerators when they change denominators — the classic partial-credit trap.

sources.claim: Understanding equivalent fractions — that a fraction can be renamed by multiplying or dividing numerator and denominator by the same number without changing its value — is foundational, and instruction should build simplifying on this principle using visual number-line and area models rather than rote rules.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide: Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for Kindergarten Through 8th Grade (Siegler et al., 2010; NCEE 2010-4039), Recommendation 2

sources.claim: Pupils should use common factors to simplify fractions and use common multiples to express fractions in the same denomination (Year 6 statutory content).
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics Programmes of Study, Year 6 Fractions

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Reasoning with Equivalences
topic.description: Recognise and use repeated reasoning to generalise: extend patterns in equivalent fractions and percentage conversions, derive unknown facts from known facts, describe general rules for sequences and predict terms
evidence: Notice that multiplying any number by 25 can be done by multiplying by 100 then dividing by 4, and explain why
Describe the general rule for a sequence and predict the 20th term
Generalise: to find 10% divide by 10, to find 5% halve 10%, and use this to find 35% of any number
topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} sees a sequence of equivalent fractions — like 1/2, 2/4, 3/6… — can they describe the rule and use it to find the next few terms, or to quickly convert between fractions and percentages?

pedagogy.summary: At 9-10, repeated reasoning is used to build general METHODS and predict beyond the drawn cases: seeing that ×25 can be done as ×100 then ÷4 and explaining why, building 35% from 10% (÷10) and 5% (half of 10%) as a reusable percentage toolkit, and describing a sequence's general rule to predict the 20th term without listing all twenty. The pivotal MP8 shift here is from a term-to-term (recursive) view to a position-to-term (functional) rule that lets you jump straight to any term. Teaching should force the 'jump' — ask for the 20th or 100th term — so the recursive habit becomes insufficient and a general rule is needed.
bestPractices: Derive percentage facts from 10% (÷10) and build others by halving/scaling, naming it as a general method for any percentage
Ask for a FAR term (20th, 100th) so listing becomes impractical and a position-to-term rule is needed
Justify equivalent methods (×25 = ×100 ÷4) by why they work, not as isolated tricks
Have the child state the general rule and verify it against a known term before trusting it
keyRepresentations: Percentage bar / double number line (100% → 10% → 5% → 35%)
Sequence tables pairing position (n) with term to expose the position-to-term rule
Equivalent-fraction and factor models for ×25 = ×100 ÷4
Ratio tables for scaling methods
commonMisconceptions: Predicts the 20th term by extending term-by-term (or drawing all terms) instead of a position-to-term rule
Uses only a term-to-term rule ('add 4') and cannot jump to a far term efficiently
Treats each percentage as a separate conversion rather than building from 10% and 5%
States a general rule from a few cases without verifying it on a known term

learn.summary: Help 9-10 year-olds shift from term-to-term (recursive) reasoning to position-to-term (functional) rules so they can jump straight to any term, and build a reusable percentage toolkit from 10% and 5%. The core move is forcing the 'jump' — asking for a far term (20th, 100th) so listing becomes impractical and a general rule is needed — then insisting the rule be verified against a known term. Equivalent calculation methods (×25 = ×100 then ÷4) should be justified by why they work, not memorised as tricks.

activities.title: Sequence machine: force the jump to a far term
feedback: If the child writes 21, 25, 29… or says 'just keep adding 4', note that this term-to-term habit works but won't reach the 100th term efficiently — tabulate position against term so the relationship (4×position + 1) is visible, then ask for the 100th term.

If the child scales a known term by the position ratio (e.g. says the 20th term = 4×the 5th term), test that shortcut against a known term: does 4×(the 1st term) give the 4th term correctly? (4×5 = 20, but the 4th term is 17.) Use the position table to show that scaling multiplies the constant start-offset too, so the result is too big.
If the child announces a rule but won't check it, ask 'does your rule give the 3rd term correctly? check it' so verification becomes a habit rather than an afterthought.
activities.rationale: Asking for a far term rather than the next one is what forces the distinction between recursive and functional thinking; a position table reveals the structure (difference × position + offset) and makes the general method efficient. An optional interactive form — a position slider that tempts listing alongside a 'rule' box that leaps straight to the chosen term and checks against the listed value — can make the contrast concrete, but the learning works on paper with a table too.
sourceClaims: MP8: by attending to repeated calculations students abstract general rules (e.g. abstracting a formula) and look for general methods and shortcuts, checking reasonableness
Pupils should recognise and use structure to find efficient general methods and choose efficient strategies; representations should reveal the relationship
learnerActions: Look at a sequence such as 5, 9, 13, 17, … and notice the constant difference of 4.
Try to reach the 20th term by extending term-by-term and feel how slow and error-prone this gets.
Make a table pairing position (n) with term so the relationship becomes visible.
State a position-to-term rule (e.g. term = 4×position + 1) and use it to jump straight to the 20th term (81).
Check the rule against a known early term (does it give the 3rd term correctly?) before trusting it.
Then be asked for the 100th term, where listing is clearly impractical, so the general rule proves its worth.
activities.intendedInsight: A position-to-term rule lets you reach any term in one step, which counting-on cannot do efficiently; a rule is only trustworthy once checked against a known term.

activities.title: Build a percentage toolkit from 10% and 5%
feedback: If the child treats each percentage as a separate calculation, prompt them to start from 10% (÷10) and 5% (half of 10%) and ask which combination of those parts makes the target.
If the child assembles 35% correctly, ask whether the same approach gives 65% so they generalise the method rather than memorising one case.
An optional 'builder' where 10% and 5% tiles snap together to make 35% can make the part-whole structure tangible, but a drawn percentage bar or a ratio table serves the same purpose.
activities.rationale: Deriving unknown facts from known facts and naming the reusable method embodies the repeated-reasoning target; a percentage bar, double number line or ratio table reveals the part-whole and scaling relationship.
sourceClaims: MP8: by attending to repeated calculations students abstract general rules (e.g. abstracting a formula) and look for general methods and shortcuts, checking reasonableness
Pupils should recognise and use structure to find efficient general methods and choose efficient strategies; representations should reveal the relationship
learnerActions: Find 10% of an amount by dividing by 10.
Find 5% by halving the 10% value.
Assemble 35% of an amount by combining three 10% parts and one 5% part (e.g. 35% of £80 = 24 + 4 = 28).
Explain that this is a general method: name which parts you'd combine to make a different percentage such as 65%.
Use a percentage bar or double number line (100% → 10% → 5% → 35%) to see how the parts make up the whole.
Use a ratio table to scale the 10% and 5% parts to a different total amount, showing the method generalises across amounts, not just one figure.
activities.intendedInsight: Any multiple of 5% can be built by combining derived facts (10% and 5%) rather than treated as a separate one-off conversion. Other percentages, such as 37%, need further derived facts like 1%. This gives a reusable method that scales to any amount.

activities.title: Justify an equivalent calculation method
feedback: If the child only states the shortcut, ask them to explain why ×100 then ÷4 equals ×25, using 25 = 100 ÷ 4.
If the child's explanation holds, ask them to check it against a direct calculation to confirm reasonableness.
activities.rationale: Justifying equivalent methods rather than memorising them is central to MP8 and to choosing efficient, structurally-grounded strategies.
sourceClaims: MP8: by attending to repeated calculations students abstract general rules (e.g. abstracting a formula) and look for general methods and shortcuts, checking reasonableness
Pupils should recognise and use structure to find efficient general methods and choose efficient strategies; representations should reveal the relationship
learnerActions: Work out why multiplying any number by 25 can be done by multiplying by 100 then dividing by 4.
Use a factor/equivalent-fraction model (25 = 100 ÷ 4) to explain the equivalence, not just assert it.
Try the method on a worked example and check the result matches the direct multiplication.
Explain in words why the two routes must give the same answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalent methods and shortcuts are reliable because of structure (25 = 100 ÷ 4), not because they are isolated tricks; understanding why lets you judge when a shortcut applies.

activities.title: Probe and discuss the generality of a rule
feedback: Listen for a position-to-term rule (term = 4×position + 1, so the 20th is 81) reached by linking the constant difference 4 to the position, plus a check against a known term — using the rule to jump rather than counting on is the target.

If the child uses a proportional shortcut (scaling a known term by the position ratio), have them test it on an early known term so the mishandled start-offset is exposed — e.g. 4×(the 5th term) gives 4×21 = 84, whereas the true 20th term is 81. The gap of 3 appears because scaling multiplies the +1 offset by 4 as well (4×1 = 4 instead of 1), so the answer is 3 too big.
There is no single scored answer here; the goal is reasoning that is general and self-checked.
activities.rationale: Open probing distinguishes genuine functional understanding from recursive habits and surfaces the proportional-reasoning trap of treating the sequence as proportional, which wrongly scales the constant offset. These prompts also require learners to construct and justify, not merely recognise.
sourceClaims: MP8: by attending to repeated calculations students abstract general rules (e.g. abstracting a formula) and look for general methods and shortcuts, checking reasonableness
learnerActions: Answer 'how would you find the 100th term — does your method still work?' to test whether a rule is genuinely general.
Evaluate a classmate's claim: 'the 20th term is 4×(the 5th term) — is that right? check it on the 2nd term' and explain the flaw.
Explain how to build 35% of £80 from 10% and 5%, and whether the same method gives 65%.
Explain why ×25 equals ×100 then ÷4.
activities.intendedInsight: Stating a rule is not enough; its generality must be tested against far cases and known terms, and proportional shortcuts that wrongly scale the constant offset along with the term fail these checks.

constraints: A static percentage bar or sequence table can display the relationship but cannot force the far-term jump or test a learner's stated rule; use it as a reference scaffold, not as the task that elicits independent generalisation.

Recognition-only formats (picking the correct method or the 20th term from options) can test the general method, but should be paired with a 'why/how' step so they elicit justification rather than guessing; on their own they do not require the learner to construct and verify a rule.
Include a term-by-term distractor (one that gives only the next term) when testing sequences, to catch recursive-only thinking.
Verification against a known term should be required, not optional: a rule stated from a few cases is not yet trusted.

Percentages and linear sequences are numeric relationships; manipulable numbers, tables, ratio tables or bars support the work. 3D representation is not needed here, though this is a judgement about this content, not a universal claim.

Open discussion without a concrete referent gives the learner nothing to manipulate or test; pair any discussion with an actual sequence, number or percentage to reason about (as the probing activity does).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the worked examples: sequence 5, 9, 13, 17 has first term 5 and common difference 4, giving term = 4n + 1; the 20th term is 4×20 + 1 = 81 (consistent with the source). 35% of £80 = (10% = 8)×3 + (5% = 4) = 24 + 4 = 28; the source's part-structure is correct. ×25 = ×100 ÷ 4 is valid since 25 = 100 ÷ 4. No arithmetic errors found in migrated examples.

The original 'force the jump / only this teaches why the rule beats counting on' framing is retained as a pedagogical rationale but softened: a static table, ratio table or paper task can also teach the position-to-term rule; the interactive contrast is one effective way, not the only way.
The claim that '3D adds no structure' was reframed as a scoped judgement about this numeric content rather than a universal law.

The proportional-shortcut misconception (20th term = 4×5th term = 4×21 = 84, rather than the correct 81) ignores the start-offset; retained as an error to probe and critique, never offered as a valid method or answer.

probeDeeper: Ask 'how would you find the 100th term — does your method still work?' to test whether the rule is genuinely general
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'a classmate says the 20th term is 4×(the 5th term) — is that right? check it on the 2nd term' to probe the proportional-reasoning trap
Ask 'to find 35% of £80, how do you build it from 10% and 5%? would the same method give 65%?' to test the general percentage method
Ask 'why does multiplying by 25 equal multiplying by 100 then dividing by 4?' to surface justification of an equivalent method
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a position-to-term rule (term = 4×position + 1, so the 20th is 81) reached by linking the constant difference 4 to the position, and a check against a known term. Using the rule to jump, not counting on, is the target.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses only a term-to-term rule ('add 4') and extends term-by-term, unable to jump to the 20th efficiently
errorPatterns.nextMove: Tabulate position against term so the relationship (4×position + 1) is visible; ask for the 100th term to make listing clearly impractical
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child starts writing 21, 25, 29… or says 'keep adding 4' with no position rule

errorPatterns.pattern: Builds a position rule but uses a proportional shortcut wrongly (e.g. 20th = 4×(5th term)), ignoring the constant offset
errorPatterns.nextMove: Test their shortcut against a known term (does it give the 4th term correctly?); expose the offset with the position table
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child scales a known term by the position ratio rather than using term = difference×position + start-offset

errorPatterns.pattern: States a general rule from a few cases without verifying it on a known term
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT just accept or correct; ask 'does your rule give the 3rd term correctly? check it' so verification becomes habitual
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child announces a rule and won't check; is surprised if it fails an early term

responseLevels.gap: Extends term-by-term, cannot reach a far term without listing, and treats each percentage as a separate conversion
responseLevels.full: Derives a position-to-term rule and jumps to the 20th/100th term, verifies it on a known term, and builds any percentage from 10%/5% — stating and checking general methods unprompted
responseLevels.partial: Finds a far term or builds a percentage when prompted, but relies on term-to-term steps or an unverified rule and doesn't justify the general method

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A sequence starts 5, 9, 13, 17, … What is the 20th term? Don't write out all twenty — tell me the general rule you'd use and how you found it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Counting on 'add 4' sixteen more times can also reach 81, but shows a recursive, not general, grasp. A child with repeated-reasoning insight builds a position-to-term rule and jumps; a child without it extends term-by-term or cannot handle '20th' without listing. Asking for the 20th (not the 5th) is what forces the distinction.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Tenths
topic.description: Count up and down in tenths; recognise that tenths arise from dividing an object into 10 equal parts and from dividing one-digit numbers or quantities by 10
evidence: Count: one tenth, two tenths, three tenths … up to ten tenths (one whole)
Show that dividing a shape into 10 equal parts gives tenths
Explain that 3 ÷ 10 = 3/10
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} splits a chocolate bar with 10 equal pieces, can they tell you each piece is one tenth — and count up from 1/10 to 10/10 in order?

pedagogy.summary: Tenths are the first structured step into fractions born from dividing ONE whole into ten equal parts — the bridge from fractions to decimal place value. The load-bearing ideas: ten equal tenths recompose exactly one whole (10/10 = 1), each tenth is small (it takes ten to rebuild the whole), and 3/10 is the same as 3÷10 (three wholes shared among ten). Teach with strips, tens-frames-as-lengths and number lines so counting in tenths lands cleanly at one whole rather than becoming 'ten'.
bestPractices: Count up and down in tenths on a number line and a strip, stopping deliberately at 10/10 = one whole to break the 'ten-tenths is ten' bias
Insist on ten EQUAL parts of one whole (not any ten pieces) using a partitioned strip
Connect 3/10 to 3÷10 by sharing three whole strips across ten places
Compare a tenth with a half (5/10 = 1/2) so children feel a tenth is far smaller than a half
Keep the whole visible and constant so a tenth of a bigger whole is seen to be a bigger piece with the same name
keyRepresentations: Whole strip partitioned into ten equal tenths (recomposes to one whole)
0-to-1 number line marked in tenths
Sharing model: three wholes shared among ten to show 3/10 = 3÷10
Overlay of tenths against a half (5/10 = 1/2)
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias — reads ten-tenths as 'ten', or thinks a tenth is big 'because 10 is a big number'
Larger denominator = larger part (a tenth 'bigger than a half because 10 > 2')
Accepts any ten pieces as tenths, ignoring that the parts must be equal
Sees no connection between 3/10 and 3÷10 ('3 ÷ 10 can't be done, 3 is smaller than 10')
Thinks a tenth of a large whole and a tenth of a small whole are the same size

learn.summary: Tenths build on earlier work with fractions such as halves and quarters: dividing ONE whole into ten equal parts, and the bridge toward decimal place value. The load-bearing ideas are that ten equal tenths recompose exactly one whole (10/10 = 1), that each tenth is small because it takes ten of them to rebuild the whole, and that 3/10 is the same as 3÷10 (three wholes shared among ten). Partitioned strips, length-based number lines, and sharing models let counting in tenths land cleanly at one whole rather than drifting into 'ten'.

activities.title: Collect the tenths back into one whole
feedback: If the learner says ten-tenths is 'ten', physically recompose the ten tenths against the original whole: the row is the same length as one whole, not longer.
If the learner says a tenth is bigger than a half 'because 10 is more than 2', overlay five tenths onto one half so they see it takes five tenths just to make one half.
Reinforce that the denominator names how many equal parts make ONE whole, so with the same whole more parts means each part is smaller.
activities.rationale: A counting-and-recomposing sequence that deliberately stops at 10/10 = one whole is intended to address whole-number bias (reading fractions by their digits) and to build the magnitude sense Year 3 pupils are expected to develop when counting up and down in tenths; its effectiveness here is proposed rather than tested.
sourceClaims: Students commonly show whole-number bias, viewing fractions with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3), and must be helped to see fractions as single numbers with magnitude; equal-partitioning (parts must be equal) is a documented roadblock.
Year 3 pupils count up and down in tenths, recognise that tenths arise from dividing an object into ten equal parts, and connect tenths to dividing one-digit numbers or quantities by 10.
learnerActions: Start with a single whole bar or strip and partition it into ten equal segments.
Collect the segments one at a time while counting aloud: one-tenth, two-tenths, three-tenths … up to ten-tenths.
At the tenth count, reassemble the ten segments end-to-end against the original whole and check that they match exactly, labelling the result '10/10 = 1 whole'.
Lay a piece covering exactly five tenths over one half of the whole and confirm that 5/10 = 1/2, so a single tenth is plainly far smaller than a half.
activities.intendedInsight: Ten equal tenths put back together remake exactly one whole, so 10/10 = 1 (not 'ten'), and each tenth is small because it takes ten of them to rebuild the whole — far smaller than a half.

activities.title: Share three wholes among ten to see 3/10 = 3÷10
feedback: If the learner says '3 ÷ 10 can't be done because 3 is smaller than 10', carry out the sharing concretely so they watch each place receive three tenths.
Name the completed share out loud: 'three shared among ten gives three tenths each, so 3 ÷ 10 = 3/10.'
If they write 10/3, re-link the notation: three of the ten equal pieces of one whole is 3/10.
activities.rationale: Connecting the fraction notation to an equal-sharing division is intended to address the misconception that 3/10 and 3÷10 are unrelated and matches the Year 3 expectation to connect tenths with dividing quantities by 10.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils count up and down in tenths, recognise that tenths arise from dividing an object into ten equal parts, and connect tenths to dividing one-digit numbers or quantities by 10.
learnerActions: Set out three identical whole bars and ten plates (or ten places) to share them among.
Partition each whole into tenths and deal the tenths out equally, one at a time, until each of the ten places has received the same amount.
State how much each place received (three tenths) and write the sharing as 3 ÷ 10 = 3/10.
Discuss why this works even though 3 is smaller than 10: you share the three wholes into smaller pieces rather than giving whole bars each.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction such as 3/10 is the result of sharing three wholes equally among ten, so 3/10 = 3÷10; dividing by a number larger than the dividend is possible and gives a fraction less than one.

activities.title: Equal parts only, and the same whole
feedback: If the learner accepts unequal pieces as tenths, contrast the equal and unequal splits and ask which one is made of ten pieces that are all the same size.
If the learner thinks a tenth is always the same absolute size, place the two different-sized wholes side by side so the two tenths can be compared directly.
Emphasise that the name 'tenth' tells you the number of equal parts in its whole, not a fixed length.
activities.rationale: Equal-partitioning is a documented roadblock, and the relative nature of a fraction (the piece that is a tenth of a bigger whole is bigger when both wholes are visible) is a known source of confusion; contrasting cases and keeping the whole visible make the condition explicit.
sourceClaims: Students commonly show whole-number bias, viewing fractions with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3), and must be helped to see fractions as single numbers with magnitude; equal-partitioning (parts must be equal) is a documented roadblock.
learnerActions: Compare a whole split into ten EQUAL pieces with a whole split into ten UNEQUAL pieces.
Decide which one shows tenths and explain why (the ten parts must be the same size).
Check by trying to recompose each set back into the whole and noticing which one tiles the whole with matching equal pieces.

Then compare a tenth of a small whole bar with a tenth of a larger whole bar, keeping both wholes visible, and describe how the two tenths differ in physical size even though both are called 'a tenth'.
activities.intendedInsight: Only ten EQUAL parts of one whole count as tenths; and because a tenth is defined relative to its whole, the physical piece that is a tenth of a larger whole is larger than a tenth of a smaller whole when both wholes are shown, though both pieces share the name 'a tenth' and name the same fraction of their own whole.

activities.title: Place and name tenths on a number line
feedback: If a learner places 5/10 anywhere other than halfway, relate the point to the half-overlay from the first activity.
If they answer 'ten' for 10/10, point to where the tenth tenth lands — exactly at 1, the end of the whole.
Encourage reading each mark as a quantity, not just as a count of ticks.
activities.rationale: Positioning tenths on a line as single numbers with magnitude reinforces the magnitude understanding that counters whole-number bias; placing and naming on a line checks and consolidates this understanding rather than building the recompose-to-one-whole insight, and recognising a correct position does not by itself confirm the learner can produce the reasoning, so use it after the hands-on work.
sourceClaims: Students commonly show whole-number bias, viewing fractions with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3), and must be helped to see fractions as single numbers with magnitude; equal-partitioning (parts must be equal) is a documented roadblock.
learnerActions: Use a 0-to-1 number line marked in tenths.
Count up and down the line in tenths, naming each mark.
Place given tenths (for example 3/10) at the correct point and identify which point equals one half (5/10).
Fill in missing values such as 'ten-tenths = __' and justify with the recomposition idea rather than by counting ticks.
activities.intendedInsight: Tenths are single numbers with a fixed position and magnitude between 0 and 1, with 10/10 sitting exactly at one and 5/10 exactly at one half.

constraints: Keep the whole visible throughout, and keep it the same size except when deliberately comparing tenths of different-sized wholes, so that a tenth is always understood relative to its own whole.
Insist on ten EQUAL parts of one whole; any ten pieces are not tenths unless they are the same size.
Deliberately pause counting at 10/10 and reassemble to one whole, rather than letting the count slide into 'ten'.

Placing, naming, matching, and fill-in tasks (e.g. on a number line) check and consolidate understanding but do not by themselves build the recompose-to-one-whole insight; use them after the hands-on partitioning and sharing work.

A static labelled tenths strip can show the facts (this is 3/10; these ten make one whole; 5/10 = one half) but cannot itself enact the moment ten tenths fuse back into one whole; pair it with a recomposition the learner performs.

Partitioning and recomposing a visible whole provides the concrete experience of ten tenths reforming one whole; spoken discussion can support the reasoning about why a tenth is small but does not itself supply that partitioning and recomposition, so include the hands-on work rather than relying on discussion to provide it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and their efficacy is untested.

Self-audit of the magnitude claims: 10/10 = 1, 5/10 = 1/2, and 3÷10 = 3/10 are correct; a tenth is correctly described as far smaller than a half (five tenths make one half). No arithmetic errors found.
The original assessment correctly reads the denominator as the number of equal parts in one whole; this was preserved, and no conceptual corrections to the source were required.

As a number, one-tenth is always the same fraction; the 'bigger/smaller piece' point concerns the physical portion of a particular whole and holds only when both wholes are shown together, so it is retained with the explicit 'keep both wholes visible' condition.
The original's stronger comparative wording about dialogue adding little and 3D being decorative was softened to scoped affordances; comparative efficacy of media is untested and not asserted.

assess.poeTask: Show the child a whole strip. Ask: 'If I cut this into ten equal pieces and then lay all ten back end-to-end in a row, will the row be shorter than, the same length as, or LONGER than the whole strip? Predict, and say why.' A whole-number-biased child predicts 'longer, because now there are ten of them.' Then lay the ten tenths against the original whole — they match exactly. The pre-observation reason ('ten pieces so more') is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: How many tenths make one whole? And how many tenths is one half?
I have a bigger bar, also cut into ten equal pieces. Is one piece of that bar also called a tenth? Is it the same size as a tenth of the small bar?
Which is more, 3 tenths or 3 halves? Why?
Why do we write 3/10 and not 10/3 for three of the ten pieces?
assess.correctAnswer: Ten-tenths equals 1 (one whole), because ten equal tenths put back together make the whole bar again. Each tenth is much smaller than a half, because it takes ten tenths to make a whole but only two halves — so a tenth is far smaller (five tenths make one half).

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias — ten-tenths read as 'ten', and a tenth judged bigger than a half 'because 10 is more than 2'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Recompose ten tenths into one whole in front of the child; overlay five tenths on one half; reteach the denominator as parts-of-one-whole
errorPatterns.distractor: Ten-tenths is 10, because I counted ten pieces.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'ten' for 10/10, or says a single tenth is bigger than a half

errorPatterns.pattern: Equal-parts ignored — thinks 'tenths' just means ten pieces, regardless of whether they are the same size
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast an equal ten-split with an unequal one; only equal parts can be called tenths; check by recomposing to one whole
errorPatterns.distractor: Any bar broken into ten pieces shows tenths, even if the pieces are different sizes.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts a bar broken into ten UNEQUAL pieces as showing tenths

errorPatterns.pattern: Fraction disconnected from division — does not see 3/10 as 3÷10 ('you can't do 3 ÷ 10, three is smaller than ten')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Share three whole strips across ten places so each place gets 3/10; name the share as 3÷10 = 3/10
errorPatterns.distractor: 3 ÷ 10 can't be done, because 3 is smaller than 10.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 3÷10 is impossible or 0, and treats 3/10 as unrelated to sharing three wholes among ten

responseLevels.gap: Says ten-tenths equals ten; judges a tenth bigger than a half because 10 > 2; accepts unequal pieces as tenths.
responseLevels.full: States ten-tenths = 1 and justifies by recomposition, orders a tenth as far smaller than a half by the ten-vs-two-parts argument, connects 3/10 with 3÷10, and transfers (a tenth of a different-sized whole is correspondingly bigger or smaller).
responseLevels.partial: Counts in tenths and states 10/10 makes one whole and that tenths are ten equal parts, but lists these facts without connecting them — cannot explain a tenth is small BECAUSE ten rebuild the whole, cannot link 3/10 to 3÷10, and stumbles on a tenth of a different-sized whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A chocolate bar is one whole. It is snapped into ten equal pieces. I eat the pieces one at a time and count: one-tenth, two-tenths, three-tenths… When I have eaten all of them, I have eaten ten-tenths. What number does ten-tenths equal, and why? And is each single piece bigger or smaller than a half — how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A whole-number-biased child says ten-tenths is 'ten' (treating 10/10 as the count) and/or says a tenth is big 'because 10 is a big number'. Correct reasoning requires reading the denominator as the number of equal parts in ONE whole, so 10/10 rebuilds one and each part is small — the reason (tier 2) exposes the bias even when a rehearsed child guesses 'one'.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Decimal place value (age 8+)
topic.description: Compare numbers with the same number of decimal places up to two decimal places
evidence: Order 0.45, 0.54, 0.39 from smallest to largest
Compare 3.72 and 3.27 using place-value reasoning
Place three two-decimal-place numbers on a number line in order
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is comparing two prices — £4.75 and £4.57 — can they tell you which is more expensive without using a calculator?

pedagogy.summary: Comparing decimals with the SAME number of decimal places uses exactly the same process as comparing whole numbers: work from the highest place value down, and decide at the first place where the digits differ. Because the numbers are the same length, there is no ragged-length trap, so this is the foundational easy case — the whole-number strategy and correct place-value reasoning happen to agree. The genuine misconceptions (longer-is-larger, shorter-is-larger) only surface with unequal-length decimals and belong to the next topic.
bestPractices: Compare the highest place value first (whole number, then tenths, then hundredths) and stop at the first place where they differ — for 3.72 vs 3.27 the wholes tie, so tenths (7 vs 2) decides
Align the decimal points vertically so equal places line up in columns
Read every digit by its place-value name ('4 tenths 5 hundredths'), never as a bare digit string
Use a number line and a length model (linear blocks, LAB) rather than area/volume blocks, because length shows relative size directly
Flag that reading the decimal part as a whole number ('72 beats 27') happens to work here but will fail on ragged decimals like 0.4 vs 0.15 — build the place-value habit now
keyRepresentations: Number line marked in hundredths (0–1, and 3–4 for the 3.72/3.27 pair)
Place-value columns aligned on the decimal point
LAB / linear arithmetic (length) blocks
10×10 hundredths grid for area backup
commonMisconceptions: Reads the decimal part as a whole number ('72 > 27') — lands the right answer here but is a fragile, non-place-value strategy
Compares from the right (last digit first) as if column-adding
Ignores or misreads the whole-number part when it is present

learn.summary: Comparing decimals that have the SAME number of decimal places (up to two) uses the same process as comparing whole numbers: work from the highest place value down and decide at the first place where digits differ. Because the numbers are equal length here, there is no ragged-length trap — correct place-value reasoning and an (incorrect) read-it-as-a-whole-number strategy happen to agree, so this is the foundational easy case. The genuine longer-is-larger / shorter-is-larger misconceptions only surface with unequal-length decimals (a later topic). The teaching aim is to build the place-value habit now, before it is tested by ragged decimals.

activities.title: Order decimals on a number line and a length bar
feedback: If a child reads '72 beats 27', accept the right answer but push the reasoning: rebuild each number as tenths and hundredths on the line and ask what the 7 and the 2 are actually worth.
If a child compares from the right (last digit first), use the number line to show the biggest place decides size; practise reading left-to-right and naming the highest place first.
Reinforce correct reasoning by having them re-voice it: '3.72 and 3.27 — the wholes are equal at 3, so the tenths decide, and 7 tenths is more than 2 tenths.'

Probe transfer: 'Would "fifteen beats four" still work for 0.4 vs 0.15? Why or why not?' to flag that the whole-number trick breaks on ragged decimals (here 0.4 > 0.15, so the 'fifteen beats four' trick fails).
activities.rationale: Ordering is a spatial act; placing cards on a line and seeing the winner settle furthest right, backed by a length-bar view, is intended to turn 'compare the highest place first' into something felt. A length model may show relative size more directly than an area or volume model, but the cited source does not establish this comparative efficacy — treat it as a design preference. The 3.72/3.27 pair adds the check that learners establish equal wholes before moving to tenths.
sourceClaims: Comparing decimals uses the same highest-place-value-first process as whole numbers; comparisons between EQUAL-LENGTH decimals are a weak diagnostic because a correct place-value strategy and an (incorrect) treat-as-whole-number strategy produce the same answer — the longer-is-larger and shorter-is-larger misconceptions require ragged-length decimals to reveal.
learnerActions: Take three cards — 0.45, 0.54, 0.39 — and place each on a number line ticked every 0.1 with minor ticks every 0.01, smallest to largest.
Say aloud why 0.54 lands furthest right and 0.39 nearest the start, naming the tenths: 'five tenths beats four tenths beats three tenths'.
View each number also as a growing length bar so the relative sizes are visually clear (0.54 is the longest bar).
Then place 3.72 and 3.27 on a 3–4 number line, first checking the whole-number parts tie at 3, then deciding on the tenths (7 vs 2).
State the order and justify by comparing the highest differing place first.
activities.intendedInsight: Decimal size can be read as position on a line: ordering is decided by the highest place at which the digits differ, read left to right, not by the raw digit string or the rightmost digit.

activities.title: Align place-value columns and read every digit by its name
feedback: If a learner says 0.60 is bigger than 0.6 'because it has more digits', align the columns and read the hundredths place: 0 hundredths adds nothing, so 0.60 = 0.6.
If they name digits as bare numbers ('sixty'), re-prompt for the place-value name ('six tenths').
Praise stopping at the first differing column rather than reading all the way to the end.
activities.rationale: Column alignment and place-value naming build the durable strategy that will survive ragged-length decimals later, where reading the decimal part as a whole number fails.
sourceClaims: Comparing decimals uses the same highest-place-value-first process as whole numbers; comparisons between EQUAL-LENGTH decimals are a weak diagnostic because a correct place-value strategy and an (incorrect) treat-as-whole-number strategy produce the same answer — the longer-is-larger and shorter-is-larger misconceptions require ragged-length decimals to reveal.
learnerActions: Write a pair such as 3.72 and 3.27 one above the other with the decimal points aligned vertically so equal places line up in columns.
Read each digit by its place-value name — 'three ones, seven tenths, two hundredths' — never as a bare digit string.
Scan from the highest place downward and circle the first column where the digits differ; declare that column the decider.
Compare 0.6 and 0.60: first write 0.6 as 0.60 by appending a trailing zero so both have two decimal places, then read the places (6 tenths and 0 hundredths in each) to show they are equal in value.
activities.intendedInsight: Aligning on the decimal point and naming each digit by its place makes the comparison a place-value decision, and shows a trailing zero can be appended (0.6 = 0.60) to equalize length without changing the value.

activities.title: Pairwise comparison and placement practice (scorable check)
feedback: Correct order: 0.39 < 0.45 < 0.54 (decided on the tenths: 3, 4, 5).
Correct comparison: 3.72 > 3.27 (wholes tie at 3, so tenths 7 > 2 decide).
A right answer with 'seventy-two beats twenty-seven' reasoning is fragile — follow up with the number-line rebuild and a ragged pair (e.g. 0.4 vs 0.15) to make place value explicit.
activities.rationale: Ordering and pairwise comparison map cleanly onto scorable items and give quick practice, but they confirm the answer more than the method. Because equal-length pairs are a weak diagnostic, pair every scored item with a request for the reasoning. Keep all items equal length to stay within this topic.
sourceClaims: Comparing decimals uses the same highest-place-value-first process as whole numbers; comparisons between EQUAL-LENGTH decimals are a weak diagnostic because a correct place-value strategy and an (incorrect) treat-as-whole-number strategy produce the same answer — the longer-is-larger and shorter-is-larger misconceptions require ragged-length decimals to reveal.
learnerActions: Order 0.45, 0.54, 0.39 from smallest to largest.
Choose which is larger: 3.72 or 3.27, and give the reason.
Place a given two-decimal-place value at the right spot on a 0–1 line.
For each item, say which digit you looked at first and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Equal-length comparisons can be done quickly and correctly by comparing the highest differing place, and the reasoning (not just the answer) should be stated.

constraints: Keep all practised and scored comparisons the same length (up to two decimal places) within this topic; teaching the ordering of unequal-length / ragged decimals, which reveal longer-is-larger and shorter-is-larger, belongs to the next topic. Two exceptions are allowed: appending a trailing zero to show equivalence (writing 0.6 as 0.60 so 0.6 = 0.60) as an equal-value demonstration, and a single brief, unscored verbal transfer probe (e.g. 0.4 vs 0.15) used only to show that the read-it-as-a-whole-number trick breaks.

Equal-length comparisons are a weak diagnostic on their own: a correct place-value strategy and a read-it-as-a-whole-number strategy give the same answer, so always elicit the reasoning, not just the ordering.
A static number line with tap-to-reveal place values is useful as a reference card, but ordering should remain an active decision the child makes, not a result they read off.

Prefer a number line and a length (linear) model for showing relative size; a 10×10 hundredths grid can serve as an area backup. Depth/volume models are not needed for this one-dimensional size idea (a design preference, not a proven ranking of media).
Watch for the specific error of comparing from the right (last digit first) as if column-adding, and for ignoring or misreading a present whole-number part.
Optional interaction examples (drag-and-snap cards, a colour-the-winner cue, a growing length bar, slider placement, tap-to-reveal place values) make the mechanism concrete but are not mandatory.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the single source was not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source supports that equal-length decimal comparisons are a weak diagnostic (place-value and whole-number strategies agree); it does not establish comparative efficacy of number-line vs other media, so claims that a length model 'shows relative size more directly' are presented as a design preference, not proven necessity.

The non-preferred 'static image / reference card' option is retained as a scaffold note and the 'conversation' option as an omission; the original rated the conversation format poor ('no persona or open inquiry'), which is a fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law.

Trailing-zero equivalence (0.6 = 0.60) appears in the assessment probes and response levels, so it is included here as a reading/naming equivalence check within scope, framed as appending a trailing zero to equalize length rather than as ragged ordering.

probeDeeper: Which digit did you look at first, and why that one?
In 3.72, what is the 7 worth? And what is the 2 worth in 3.27?
What about 0.6 and 0.60 — are those the same size or different? How do you know?
If I gave you 0.4 and 0.15, would 'fifteen beats four' still work? Why or why not?
assess.correctAnswer: 0.39 < 0.45 < 0.54 (decided on the tenths: 3, 4, 5), and 3.72 > 3.27 (wholes tie at 3, so the tenths 7 > 2 decide). Justifies by comparing the highest place first.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the decimal part as a whole number: 'point-seventy-two is bigger than point-twenty-seven because 72 beats 27'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Accept the answer but push the reasoning: rebuild each number as tenths and hundredths on the number line, then show a ragged pair (0.4 vs 0.15) where the whole-number trick fails — make the place-value habit explicit now.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Justifies by the digit string rather than place value; says 'seventy-two' not 'seven tenths'; lands the right answer here but for the wrong reason

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares from the right, starting at the last digit as if adding in columns
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the number line, show that the biggest place decides size; practise reading left-to-right and naming the highest place first.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Points to the hundredths digit first, or hesitates about which end to start from; mis-orders when the whole-number part carries the decision

responseLevels.gap: Orders by the raw digit string or from the right and cannot justify by place value; mis-orders when the whole part matters.
responseLevels.full: Compares the highest differing place first, articulates 0.54 = 5 tenths > 0.45 = 4 tenths, places numbers correctly on a line, recognises 0.6 = 0.60, and transfers cleanly to a new equal-length set.
responseLevels.partial: Gets equal-length comparisons right and can say 'more tenths wins', but relies on the numbers being the same length and cannot yet explain place value or handle a trailing-zero case like 0.6 vs 0.60.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child these cards: 0.45, 0.54, 0.39. Say: 'Put these in order, smallest to largest, and tell me how you decided.' Then hand them 3.72 and 3.27 and ask which is larger. Watch which digit they look at first and listen to the reason — do not prompt a method.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Because all three cards are the same length, a correct place-value strategy and a treat-it-as-a-whole-number strategy give the SAME order (per Steinle & Stacey, equal-length pairs are a weak diagnostic on their own). So this task is not trying to catch longer-is-larger — that lives in the ragged-decimal topic (mt_933BohS9BH). What it discriminates is HOW the child reasons: a secure child names tenths and compares from the highest place; a fragile child says 'seventy-two beats twenty-seven' or starts from the right — a right answer reached by a method that will break the moment lengths differ. The 3.72/3.27 pair adds the check that they establish the wholes are equal before moving to the tenths.

sources.claim: Comparing decimals uses the same highest-place-value-first process as whole numbers; comparisons between EQUAL-LENGTH decimals are a weak diagnostic because a correct place-value strategy and an (incorrect) treat-as-whole-number strategy produce the same answer — the longer-is-larger and shorter-is-larger misconceptions require ragged-length decimals to reveal.
