topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Converting tenths to hundredths
topic.description: Express a fraction with denominator 10 as an equivalent fraction with denominator 100 and use this to add fractions with denominators 10 and 100 (e.g. 3/10 + 4/100 = 34/100)
evidence: Rewrite 7/10 as 70/100
Explain why 5/10 = 50/100 using a hundredths grid
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to add 3/10 and 17/100, can they rewrite 3/10 as hundredths first — and then add the two fractions together?

pedagogy.summary: Converting tenths to hundredths applies the equivalent-fraction principle (×10/×10) so that tenths and hundredths share a common denominator and can be added. It rests on place value: one tenth IS ten hundredths, so 3/10 is 30 hundredths, and 3/10 + 4/100 becomes 30/100 + 4/100 = 34/100. The whole point is that you cannot combine the two until they are the same-sized pieces.
bestPractices: Anchor every conversion on a 10×10 hundredths grid: one full column of ten small squares is one tenth, making '1 tenth = 10 hundredths' visible rather than a rule
Convert BEFORE combining — shade the tenths as whole columns, then the extra hundredths as single squares, then count all the small squares
Connect to place-value columns (tenths | hundredths) and to money/metric (£0.30 = 30p, 3/10 m = 30 cm) so the ×10 relationship is felt in familiar units
Insist the answer is read back in hundredths and, when ready, as a decimal (34/100 = 0.34) to bridge to decimal notation
Contrast a correct conversion with the '7/110' error out loud so children can articulate why you never add the denominators
keyRepresentations: 10×10 hundredths grid (column = tenth, square = hundredth)
Place-value chart with tenths and hundredths columns
Number line 0–1 marked in hundredths
Base-ten flat/rod (rod = tenth of the flat, small cube = hundredth)
commonMisconceptions: Adds across both denominators: 3/10 + 4/100 = 7/110 (adds tops and bottoms)
Treats 3/10 as 3 hundredths, shading three single squares, and reports 7/100
Thinks the denominators can be added because 'they are close', ignoring that the pieces are different sizes

learn.summary: Converting tenths to hundredths rests on place value and the equivalent-fraction principle (×10/×10): one tenth is ten hundredths, so 3/10 = 30/100, and 3/10 + 4/100 becomes 30/100 + 4/100 = 34/100. Learners cannot combine tenths and hundredths until the pieces are the same size, so the conversion must happen before adding. A 10×10 hundredths grid (each column = one tenth = ten small squares) makes this relationship concrete; a base-ten flat/rod model, place-value columns, number lines, money (£0.30 = 30p) and metric (3/10 m = 30 cm) anchor it in familiar units, and the decimal form (34/100 = 0.34) bridges to decimal notation.

activities.title: Build 3/10 + 4/100 on a hundredths grid
feedback: If three columns are shaded, confirm: 'One column is ten small squares, so three columns is thirty hundredths — 3/10 = 30/100.'

If only three single squares are shaded for 3/10, lay a tenth-column (strip of ten) beside one single square and ask how many small squares fit in the column; rebuild the column-of-ten before returning to the sum.
When the total is reported, prompt the learner to read it back in hundredths (34/100) and, when ready, as the decimal 0.34.
activities.rationale: The concept is a transformation that becomes undeniable when seen: shading three tenths and watching them occupy thirty small squares makes '1 tenth = 10 hundredths' concrete rather than a memorised rule. An optional live tally that counts '30 hundredths' as the columns land, and shows 30/100 + 4/100 = 34/100 with the decimal 0.34, can make the recomputation visible; letting the learner first shade three lone squares turns the common error into a self-correcting moment. A base-ten flat/rod set offers the same ×10 structure in a different medium, and a static labelled grid (tap a column to reveal 'this column = 10 hundredths') works as a reference companion, though a fixed picture is not manipulable and so does not let the learner carry out the conversion themselves.
sourceClaims: Creating a common denominator via the equivalent-fraction principle (multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number) is the foundation for adding fractions with unlike denominators, and adding numerators AND denominators is a documented, high-frequency error.
learnerActions: Take a blank 10×10 hundredths grid where each full column of ten small squares represents one tenth.
Shade 3/10 by filling three whole columns, then count the small squares covered to confirm it is 30 hundredths.
Add 4/100 by shading four more single squares.
Count all the shaded small squares and report the total as hundredths (34/100), then, when ready, write it as a decimal (0.34).
Deliberately try shading just three lone single squares for 3/10 first, notice that this is only 3/100, then correct it to three full columns.

Optionally model the same amounts with base-ten blocks, where the flat is one whole, a rod is one tenth, and a small cube is one hundredth, to see the same ×10 relationship in a different manipulative.
activities.intendedInsight: Three tenths covers the same shaded area as thirty hundredths, so tenths must be converted to hundredths before they can be added to hundredths.

activities.title: Explain why 5/10 = 50/100 and challenge the 7/110 error
feedback: If the learner says 5/10 = 5/100, ask them to count the squares in five full columns on the grid to see it is 50.
If they write 7/110, return to the grid: one column is ten squares, so 3/10 covers thirty squares; you can only add once the pieces are the same size — rebuild 3/10 = 30/100 first.
Confirm correct reasoning: 'A tenth is ten hundredths, so you scale both the top and bottom by ten — the amount does not change, only the size of the pieces.'
activities.rationale: Articulating why the add-across-both-denominators error is wrong, and distinguishing which addends already share a denominator, strengthens the equivalence rather than the mechanical count. Checkable prompts (rewrite 7/10 = 70/100; choose between 34/100, 7/110 and 7/100 where the last two are distractors to reject; sort by whether conversion is needed) surface the add-across error directly. Response-selection formats like these can be used during teaching to prompt reasoning, though on their own they check recognition rather than eliciting independent construction.
sourceClaims: Creating a common denominator via the equivalent-fraction principle (multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number) is the foundation for adding fractions with unlike denominators, and adding numerators AND denominators is a documented, high-frequency error.
learnerActions: On a hundredths grid, show 5/10 and explain why it covers 50 small squares, not 5.
Rewrite 7/10 as an equivalent fraction over 100 (70/100).
Respond to a classmate who claims 3/10 + 4/100 = 7/110: explain out loud why you never add the denominators, using the idea that the pieces are different sizes until converted.
When offered answer choices such as 34/100, 7/110 and 7/100, pick 34/100 and say explicitly why each of the other two is wrong.
Sort several sums into 'already hundredths' versus 'convert a tenth first' before solving them.
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalent tenths-to-hundredths conversions come from multiplying numerator and denominator by ten; denominators are never added because they name the size of the pieces, which must match before combining.

activities.title: Connect to place value, money and metric, then to decimals
feedback: If a learner cannot yet convert on paper without the grid, that is partial mastery — return to the grid to re-anchor '1 tenth = 10 hundredths', then retry on paper.

If the method is sound but the square count slips (e.g. 33 or 35), scaffold the count ('ten, twenty, thirty… thirty-one, thirty-two, thirty-three, thirty-four') rather than reteaching the concept — the idea is held, the count slipped.
Confirm the money/metric link: '30p out of 100p is 30 hundredths of a pound, just like 30/100.'
activities.rationale: Anchoring the conversion in money, metric units and the place-value chart lets the ×10 relationship be felt in familiar quantities, and reading answers back as decimals builds the bridge to decimal notation. Transfer to a new pair without the grid distinguishes fluent understanding from grid-dependent success.
learnerActions: Place tenths and hundredths into a place-value chart with labelled tenths and hundredths columns and read the conversion from the columns.
Match each fraction to a familiar unit: 3/10 = £0.30 = 30p, and 3/10 m = 30 cm, noting the ×10 relationship.
Mark 0.34 on a 0–1 number line divided into hundredths and relate it to 34/100.
Write a converted answer such as 34/100 as the decimal 0.34 and say why they are the same quantity.
Transfer to a fresh pair, e.g. 6/10 + 7/100 (= 67/100), aiming to convert without needing the grid.
activities.intendedInsight: The tenth-to-hundredth ×10 relationship is the same structure seen in place value, money and metric measures, and it bridges directly to decimal notation.

constraints: Convert before combining: shade tenths as whole columns, then extra hundredths as single squares, then count all the small squares — do not add until the pieces are the same size.
Never add denominators; 3/10 + 4/100 is not 7/110, and 3/10 is not 3/100. These are the two priority errors to surface and correct, not merely caveat.
A static labelled grid or tap-to-reveal image is a reference scaffold: it can show 7/10 = 70/100 but is not manipulable, so it supports rather than replaces active grid or base-ten work.

Paper or card grid cutouts have slight thickness and can be handled; a drawn or on-screen grid is a flat model of the same quantity — in every case the question is about the fractional amount represented, not the physical object.
Response-selection and sorting tasks can prompt reasoning during teaching but, used alone, check recognition rather than eliciting independent construction of the conversion.

An optional live-tally/snap-counting grid makes the recomputation visible but is one way to realise the activity, not a required mechanism; the same learning works with a drawn grid, base-ten blocks, or spoken counting.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified, and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The single cited source supports the equivalent-fraction/common-denominator principle and the add-across error as high-frequency; it does not establish the comparative efficacy of the grid, the base-ten model, the live tally, or any specific response format.

An earlier version asserted that spatial depth 'adds nothing' and that dialogue 'adds no value'. These are unsupported categorical claims, not pedagogical laws, and have been softened to affordance statements; the flat grid is well-suited to this planar, quantitative concept but is not proven uniquely necessary.
The earlier claim that a static image 'cannot let the child do the conversion' is retained only as an objective scaffold limit (a fixed image is not manipulable), not as a claim that it cannot teach.
The base-ten flat/rod representation from the original was restored as an optional alternative manipulative; its comparative effectiveness is not independently established.

Arithmetic self-audit: 3/10 = 30/100; 30/100 + 4/100 = 34/100 = 0.34; 7/10 = 70/100; 5/10 = 50/100; 6/10 + 7/100 = 67/100 — all consistent. The erroneous values 7/110 and 7/100 appear only as misconceptions to be corrected or as distractors to reject, never as valid answers in learner-facing tasks.

probeDeeper: How many small squares are in one whole column? So how many hundredths is 3/10?
If a friend told you 3/10 + 4/100 = 7/110, what would you say to them?
What about 5/10 — how many hundredths is that? Show me on the grid why it is 50 and not 5.
Could you write your answer of 34/100 as a decimal as well?
assess.correctAnswer: Shades three full columns for 3/10 (recognising that is 30 small squares / 30 hundredths), adds four single squares for 4/100, and reports 34/100 (may also say 0.34).

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds across both denominators: 'three tenths plus four hundredths is seven over a hundred-and-ten' — combines numerators and denominators as if they were whole numbers
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the grid and count: one column is ten squares, so 3/10 covers thirty squares. You can only add once the pieces are the same size. Rebuild the equivalence 3/10 = 30/100 before re-adding.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 7/110 (or 7/100) without converting; on the grid, shades correctly but then ignores the shading and just adds the written numbers

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats 3/10 as three hundredths — shades three single squares for 3/10 and reports 7/100
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lay a tenth-strip beside a single hundredth-square and ask how many small squares fit in the strip; rebuild the column-of-ten before returning to the sum.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Shades three tiny squares (not three columns) for 3/10; treats a tenth and a hundredth as the same-sized piece

errorPatterns.pattern: Converts correctly but miscounts the squares when tallying (loses track counting in tens then ones)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the count ('ten, twenty, thirty… thirty-one, two, three, four'); do not reteach the concept — the idea is held, the count slipped.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Method is sound — three columns plus four squares — but the reported total is off by a small amount (e.g. says 33 or 35)

responseLevels.gap: Adds numerators and/or denominators directly (7/110 or 7/100), or shades three lone squares for 3/10 — no conversion happens and tenths and hundredths are treated as the same size.
responseLevels.full: Converts 3/10 → 30/100 fluently, combines to 34/100, explains that a tenth is ten hundredths, writes 0.34, and transfers to a fresh pair such as 6/10 + 7/100 without needing the grid.
responseLevels.partial: Converts 3/10 to 30/100 when working on the grid and reaches 34/100, but cannot yet do it fluently on paper without the grid, or lists the steps without being able to say why one column is ten hundredths.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put a blank 10×10 hundredths grid in front of the child. Say: 'Show me 3/10 on this grid, then show me 4/100 as well, and tell me how much you have altogether written as hundredths.' Then watch — say nothing about how to do it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands turns the tenths into hundredths physically — three columns become thirty squares — before combining, so the answer is 34/100. A child who does not either shades three lone squares for 3/10 (reporting 7/100) or writes 7/110 by adding tops and bottoms. The grid forces the tenth-as-ten-hundredths relationship into the open, so the error is visible in what they shade, not just what they write.

sources.claim: Creating a common denominator via the equivalent-fraction principle (multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number) is the foundation for adding fractions with unlike denominators, and adding numerators AND denominators is a documented, high-frequency error.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide: Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for Kindergarten Through 8th Grade

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Decimals for Tenths & Hundredths
topic.description: Use decimal notation for fractions with denominators 10 or 100; read and write decimal numbers as fractions (e.g. 0.62 = 62/100, 0.71 = 71/100)
evidence: Rewrite 0.62 as 62/100
Write 3/10 as 0.3 and locate on a number line
Read 0.07 and express as 7/100
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a price tag showing £0.65, can they rewrite it as a fraction — and go the other way, turning 47/100 into a decimal?

pedagogy.summary: This is the procedural fluency of moving both ways between decimal notation and tenths/hundredths fractions: read 0.62 as 62/100, write 3/10 as 0.3, read 0.07 as 7/100, and locate them on a number line. It rests on the place-value meaning that the first place after the point is tenths and the second is hundredths, so the number of decimal places is governed by the denominator (10 → one place, 100 → two places) and a placeholder zero is required when the numerator has fewer digits than the denominator has zeros (7/100 = 0.07). The skill is assessed by WATCHING the child convert both directions, especially on the placeholder cases that a digit-copying rule gets wrong.
bestPractices: Practise BOTH directions from the start (decimal→fraction and fraction→decimal) using a place-value chart so the child reads the denominator off the final place.
Foreground the placeholder: pair 3/10 = 0.3 with 7/100 = 0.07 and 3/100 = 0.03 so the child learns that hundredths always occupy two places and a zero holds an empty tenths place.
Link every conversion to a picture — a hundredths grid and a number-line location — so the symbolic answer is checked against a quantity, catching reversals like 0.62 → 6/2.
Use ragged and single-digit-numerator cases deliberately (0.4, 0.07, 9/100) because these are where the placeholder rule bites and hollow digit-copying fails.
Have the child read the decimal aloud in place-value language ('sixty-two hundredths') before writing the fraction, so the denominator is heard.
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart (tenths | hundredths) beside the fraction
10×10 hundredths grid shaded to match the decimal and the fraction
Number line for locating 0.3, 0.4, 0.62
Contrasting sets {3/10, 3/100} and {0.7, 0.07} to drill the placeholder
Bidirectional conversion cards (decimal on one side, fraction on the other)
commonMisconceptions: Dropping the placeholder zero: writing 9/100 as 0.9, or reading 0.07 as 7/10.
Adding an unneeded zero: writing 3/10 as 0.03 by over-applying 'hundredths = two places'.
Using one denominator for every decimal: writing 0.4 as 4/100 regardless of the number of places.
Reversing digits or reading position wrong: 0.62 → 6/2 or 26/100.
Placing decimals on the number line by whole-number reasoning rather than by tenths/hundredths.

learn.summary: Learners move fluently in BOTH directions between decimal notation and tenths/hundredths fractions: read 0.62 as 62/100, write 3/10 as 0.3, read 0.07 as 7/100, and locate these on a 0–1 number line. The skill rests on place-value meaning — the first place after the point is tenths, the second is hundredths — so the denominator is read from the final place (10 → one place, 100 → two places), and a placeholder zero is needed when the numerator has fewer digits than the denominator has zeros (7/100 = 0.07). Learning and checking should deliberately use placeholder and single-digit-numerator cases, because a digit-copying rule produces correct answers on easy items but fails exactly there.

activities.title: Two-way converter checked against a grid and a number line
feedback: If a learner writes 0.9 for 9/100, point to the grid: ninety squares versus nine. The nine belongs in the hundredths (second) place, so a zero holds the empty tenths place — contrast 9/10 = 0.9 with 9/100 = 0.09.
If a learner writes 0.4 as 4/100, read the final place aloud: 0.4 ends in the tenths place, so it is 4/10 (or equivalently 40/100). Shade 4 columns versus 4 single squares to contrast.

If a learner over-applies 'hundredths means two places' and writes 3/10 as 0.03, contrast 3/10 = 0.3 (one place) with 3/100 = 0.03 (two places): a placeholder is needed only when the denominator has more zeros than the numerator has digits.
If a learner reverses digits (0.62 → 26/100) or loses the place value (0.62 → 6/2), use the place-value chart to name each digit's place before writing the fraction.
activities.rationale: Bidirectional conversion is a doing-skill, so the learner should produce many items with immediate quantity-based feedback rather than only reading a worked rule. Linking symbol, grid and number line lets placeholder errors show as mismatched pictures, turning a rote rule into a self-correcting action. Deliberately including placeholder and ragged cases targets exactly where digit-copying fails. Live grid shading and the number-line marker are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete; a paper hundredths grid and a drawn number line serve the same purpose.
sourceClaims: Errors in decimal notation stem largely from false analogies with whole numbers and incomplete place-value understanding; because faulty digit-based rules can produce correct answers on easy items, instruction and assessment must use cases (single-digit numerators, ragged decimals) that expose the placeholder and place-value meaning.
learnerActions: Enter a decimal (e.g. 0.62) and write the matching fraction; confirm against a 10×10 hundredths grid that shades 62 squares and a number-line marker that lands just past halfway.
Enter a fraction (e.g. 3/10) and write the matching decimal (0.3); confirm by shading 3 of the ten columns and placing the point on the line.
Do the hard placeholder case: for 9/100, if you write 0.9 the grid floods with ninety squares — far more than nine — so the mismatch is obvious; correct it to 0.09 so exactly nine squares glow.
Run rapid two-way rounds (decimal→fraction and fraction→decimal) across a deliberate set of placeholder and ragged cases: 0.07, 9/100, 0.4, 3/100.
Read each decimal aloud in place-value language ('sixty-two hundredths', 'seven hundredths') before writing the fraction, so the denominator is heard.
activities.intendedInsight: The placeholder zero is not a rule to memorise but something you can see: for 9/100 the zero keeps the nine out of the tenths place. The denominator is determined by the final decimal place, and every symbolic answer can be checked against a shaded quantity and a position on the line.

activities.title: Contrast sets that drill the placeholder
feedback: If a learner treats 3/10 and 3/100 as the same, compare the two shaded grids directly — the quantities are visibly different.
If a learner uses one denominator for every decimal, have them name the final place of each decimal aloud before choosing the denominator.
activities.rationale: Deliberately pairing ragged and single-digit-numerator cases targets exactly where digit-copying fails, as the decimal-research-based source recommends. Contrasting cards (decimal one side, fraction the other) support self-checking without requiring any particular device.
sourceClaims: Errors in decimal notation stem largely from false analogies with whole numbers and incomplete place-value understanding; because faulty digit-based rules can produce correct answers on easy items, instruction and assessment must use cases (single-digit numerators, ragged decimals) that expose the placeholder and place-value meaning.
learnerActions: Work matched pairs side by side: {3/10, 3/100} and {0.7, 0.07}, writing each as both a fraction and a decimal.
For each pair, shade a hundredths grid for both members so the size difference is visible (3 columns vs 3 squares; 70 squares vs 7 squares).
State in words why one needs a placeholder zero and the other does not.
Sort a mixed set of cards (decimal on one side, fraction on the other) and self-check by flipping, giving special attention to 0.4, 0.07 and 9/100.
activities.intendedInsight: Tenths and hundredths of the same digit look similar in writing but differ ten-fold in size; the number of decimal places and the presence of a placeholder zero both follow from which place the final digit occupies.

activities.title: Annotated place-value chart as a reference (scaffold)
feedback: After reading, ask the learner to convert a fresh placeholder case unaided (e.g. 0.07 → 7/100) and explain each step in place-value terms.
activities.rationale: A static annotated chart can present the rule and worked examples as a reference, which supports learners who need the method spelled out. It is a scaffold: on its own it does not provide the repeated production-with-feedback that builds conversion fluency, so it should lead back into active conversion.
learnerActions: Study a place-value chart (tenths | hundredths) beside a couple of worked conversions, e.g. 0.62 = 62/100 and 9/100 = 0.09.
Read a short explanation of why the placeholder zero appears in 0.09 but not in 0.3.
Return to the converter or contrast-set tasks and reproduce the method on new values without looking.
activities.intendedInsight: A worked reference makes the place–denominator link and the placeholder rule explicit, but fluency comes from doing many items, not from reading examples.

constraints: Practise both directions (decimal→fraction and fraction→decimal) from the start; a learner may be fluent one way but not the other.
Deliberately include placeholder and single-digit-numerator cases (0.07, 9/100, 0.4, 3/100): easy items can be answered correctly by digit-copying and so do not reveal understanding.
Correct answers: 0.62 = 62/100; 0.07 = 7/100; 0.4 = 4/10 (equivalently 40/100); 3/10 = 0.3; 9/100 = 0.09; 0.03 = 3/100; 0.4 sits at four tenths, just below halfway on a 0–1 line.
Check every conversion against a quantity (shaded grid) and a position (number line) to catch place-value errors such as 0.62 → 6/2 (dropping the place value) or 0.62 → 26/100 (reversing digits).
The annotated chart is a reference scaffold, not a substitute for repeated production with feedback.
Fixed worked examples can still teach the method; they simply cannot be manipulated, so pair them with learner-generated items.

A scored check can be used during teaching to surface errors, but on its own it measures the skill more than it builds it; use its placeholder distractors (e.g. 0.9 for 9/100, 7/10 for 0.07) diagnostically.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source national-curriculum claim is marked verified:false in the original row and supports the topic/statutory requirement rather than any activity's teaching principle; it was therefore not retained as an activity sourceClaim. It remains relevant as age-appropriate curriculum context (Year 4, ages 9–10): pupils should recognise and write decimal notation for fractions with denominators 10 or 100.

The original artefact ratings asserted that 3D 'adds no conceptual value', that a character/dialogue format 'adds nothing', and that assessment-format steps 'do not build' the skill. These are catalog-preference judgements, not established pedagogical laws; they have been softened to scoped statements about affordances or omitted as universal claims.
No arithmetic or place-value error was found in the source conversions; all stated conversions (0.62=62/100, 0.07=7/100, 0.4=4/10, 3/10=0.3, 9/100=0.09, 3/100=0.03) are correct and retained.

probeDeeper: You wrote 0.07 = 7/100. What would 0.7 be instead — and how do the two differ in size?
How did you decide 0.4 is 4/10 and not 4/100? What tells you the denominator?
Where does 0.4 sit relative to a half on this line — and how do you know without measuring?
A friend writes 3/10 as 0.03. Is that right? If not, what is 0.03 as a fraction?

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the placeholder zero — reads 0.07 as 7/10, or writes 9/100 as 0.9 — mapping the digit straight after the point.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the place-value chart / grid: the 9 belongs in the hundredths (second) place, so a zero holds the tenths place; contrast 9/10 = 0.9 with 9/100 = 0.09. Reteach that place fixes the denominator.

errorPatterns.pattern: Forces one denominator on every decimal — writes 0.4 as 4/100 (or 40/1000), ignoring the number of places.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Read the final place aloud: 0.4 ends in the tenths place, so 4/10; shade 4 columns vs 4 squares to contrast. Reteach reading the denominator from the last place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 0.4 → 4/100; treats every decimal as hundredths regardless of length.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds an unneeded zero — over-applies 'hundredths means two places' and writes 3/10 as 0.03.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast 3/10 = 0.3 (one place) with 3/100 = 0.03 (two places) on the chart; the placeholder is needed only when the denominator has more zeros than the numerator has digits. Reteach the place–denominator link.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 3/10 → 0.03; inserts a placeholder where none is needed.

responseLevels.gap: Converts by copying digits regardless of place (0.07 → 7/10, 0.4 → 4/100), reverses digits, or places 0.4 by whole-number reasoning. No reliable link to place value.
responseLevels.full: Converts both directions accurately including placeholder cases (0.07 = 7/100, 9/100 = 0.09), chooses the denominator from the final place (0.4 = 4/10), locates 0.4 correctly on the line, and explains each step in place-value terms; transfers to new values.
responseLevels.partial: Converts tenths and most hundredths correctly but slips on placeholder cases (0.07, 9/100) or on choosing the denominator (0.4), or converts fluently one way but not the other; can execute without explaining the place–denominator link.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Write these decimals as fractions: 0.62, 0.07, 0.4. Now write these as decimals: 3/10, 9/100. Last, mark 0.4 on this number line from 0 to 1. Show me how you work each one out.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the work separates place-value understanding from digit-copying. The 0.07 and 9/100 items are placeholder discriminators — a hollow rule yields 7/10 and 0.9. The 0.4 item checks whether the child forces every decimal to hundredths (4/100) or reads the place. Doing both directions and locating on the line exposes reversals and whole-number placement that a one-way written check would miss.

sources.claim: Errors in decimal notation stem largely from false analogies with whole numbers and incomplete place-value understanding; because faulty digit-based rules can produce correct answers on easy items, instruction and assessment must use cases (single-digit numerators, ragged decimals) that expose the placeholder and place-value meaning.

sources.claim: Pupils should recognise and write decimal notation for fractions with denominators 10 or 100 (Year 4 statutory content).

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Decimals to three places
topic.description: Solve problems involving numbers with up to three decimal places
evidence: Calculate the total of three measurements: 1.234 m + 0.567 m + 2.199 m
A bottle holds 1.5 litres; 0.375 l is poured out — how much remains?
Find two numbers with 3 d.p. that add to make 1
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is filling a tank that holds 5.000 litres and has poured in 2.375 litres, can they work out how much more is needed to fill it?

pedagogy.summary: Solving problems with up to three decimal places extends place value to thousandths and demands careful alignment. Adding and subtracting means lining up the decimal points and equalising lengths (1.5 = 1.500), treating each column as ones, tenths, hundredths and thousandths, and carrying or borrowing across columns exactly as with whole numbers. Tasks like 'find two numbers to 3 d.p. that make 1' exercise complements to a whole (0.375 + 0.625). Estimation guards against place-value slips.
bestPractices: Align the decimal points and pad ragged lengths with zeros (1.500 − 0.375) so every place value lines up
Read numbers by place value all the way to thousandths
Carry and borrow across decimal columns just as with whole numbers
Use complement-to-1 reasoning (subtract from 1.000) for 'add to make 1' tasks and check by adding
Estimate first (1.5 − 0.375 ≈ 1.5 − 0.4 ≈ 1.1) to catch magnitude errors
keyRepresentations: Place-value columns to thousandths, aligned on the point
Number line zoomed to thousandths
Bar / complement model for 'make 1'
Measuring contexts (litres, metres) for the quantities
commonMisconceptions: Right-justifies ragged decimals instead of aligning the point (1.234 + 0.567 + 2.199)
Treats the decimal tail as a separate whole number ('longer is larger')
Forgets to pad and borrow across the point (1.5 − 0.375)
Complement-to-1 errors: completes each column to 10 independently (0.375 + 0.725) or ignores the required 3 d.p. (0.4 + 0.6)

learn.summary: Solving problems with numbers to three decimal places extends place value to thousandths and depends on careful alignment. Adding and subtracting means lining up the decimal points, equalising lengths by padding with zeros (1.5 = 1.500), reading each column as ones, tenths, hundredths and thousandths, and carrying or borrowing across columns exactly as with whole numbers. 'Find two numbers to 3 d.p. that make 1' exercises complements to a whole (0.375 + 0.625 = 1.000). Estimating first guards against place-value slips.

activities.title: Column workbench: aligning and padding to thousandths
feedback: If columns are lined up by their last digits instead of the point, the sum comes out the wrong size (far from 4): re-align so tenths sit under tenths and thousandths under thousandths, padding shorter numbers with zeros.
If 1.5 is left as two digits, there is nothing to subtract the thousandths from: rewrite it as 1.500 first, then borrow across the hundredths and tenths to reach 1.125 l.
If the estimate (about 1.1) and the written answer disagree in size, a place-value slip has happened — recheck the alignment and borrowing.
activities.rationale: Place-value alignment to thousandths and borrowing across the point is the core procedural skill, and ragged-length numbers are where whole-number thinking (right-justifying, 'longer is larger') shows up; making the padding and the column structure visible turns alignment into a deliberate, checkable step. An interactive medium that snaps digits into labelled columns, shows faint ghost zeros when padding 1.500, and animates the borrow rippling left may make this mechanism concrete; these are optional illustrative supports, not required mechanisms. A static aligned-columns reference with tap-to-reveal place values can model a single worked calculation but does not enforce alignment on new problems, so it suits review rather than independent practice.
sourceClaims: Decimal size and calculation depend on place value, and errors arise from whole-number thinking (treating the decimal tail as a separate whole number, 'longer is larger'); ragged-length decimals are essential for revealing these errors, whereas tidy same-length items let faulty rules pass.
learnerActions: Set out the subtraction 1.5 − 0.375 in place-value columns (ones, tenths, hundredths, thousandths) aligned on the decimal point — the measuring context is a 1.5-litre bottle from which 0.375 l is poured out, finding how much is left.
Rewrite 1.5 as 1.500 by writing zeros in the empty hundredths and thousandths columns before subtracting.
Carry out the subtraction, borrowing just as with whole numbers (from the tenths through the hundredths to the thousandths), to reach 1.125 l remaining.
Add the three ragged measurements 1.2 m + 0.567 m + 2.233 m by first aligning on the point and padding every number to the same length (1.2 = 1.200), then summing each column to get 4.000 m.
Estimate first (1.5 − 0.375 ≈ 1.5 − 0.4 ≈ 1.1) and check the answer's size against the estimate.
activities.intendedInsight: 1.5 and 1.500 are the same number, but writing the padding zeros makes the hundredths and thousandths columns available so the digits line up and the borrow can ripple from the tenths through the hundredths to the thousandths.

activities.title: Make 1: complements to a whole at three decimal places
feedback: If a pair like 0.375 + 0.735 is chosen, each column was completed to 10 separately (that pair totals 1.110, not 1): instead subtract the whole number 1.000 − 0.375 to get 0.625, then add to check the total is exactly 1.000.

If the total comes to 0.999 or similar, each column (including the thousandths) was probably completed to 9, giving 0.624 instead of 0.625. Only the thousandths should make 10, with the tenths and hundredths making 9 because of the carries, so that the total is one whole, written 1.000.
If a pair is not written to three decimal places, rewrite it to 3 d.p. and confirm it still totals 1.000.
activities.rationale: Complement-to-1 tasks rehearse decomposing a whole and expose the common error of completing each column to ten. Checking by adding back links the complement to addition and reinforces that the parts must reconstitute exactly one whole. A bar/length model where the two parts must fill one whole may make 'completing the whole' felt as a length; it is an optional illustrative support, not a required medium.
learnerActions: Given 0.375, find the second number to 3 d.p. that makes exactly 1.000, by subtracting from 1.000 (1.000 − 0.375 = 0.625).
Check the pair by adding the two numbers back together and confirming they total exactly 1.000.
Explain why 0.4 + 0.6, though it equals 1, does not meet the 'three decimal places' requirement, and give a valid 3-d.p. pair (such as 0.001 + 0.999).
Optionally model the complement as two lengths placed end to end along a bar representing one whole, where only the correct pair closes the gap with no gap or overlap and a running total shows 1.000.
activities.intendedInsight: A complement to 1 is found by subtracting from the whole written as 1.000, not by completing each column to 10 independently; the two parts together must make exactly one whole.

constraints: Use ragged-length decimals (different numbers of decimal places) in practice, not only tidy same-length items: equal-length items can let faulty right-justify or 'longer is larger' rules pass undetected.

A static aligned-columns picture or tap-to-reveal reference can illustrate one calculation but does not enforce alignment on new problems; reserve it for modelling or review and require learners to lay out and compute fresh problems themselves.

Multiple-choice or fill-in checks can diagnose misalignment and complement errors but assess recognition of a final value; independent construction requires learners to set out the columns, pad, and carry/borrow themselves.
Insist complements be written to the required three decimal places (reject 0.4 + 0.6 for a 3-d.p. task even though it sums to 1).

When writing distractors for 1.5 − 0.375, the correct answer is 1.125; plausible error-based distractors include 1.275 (subtracting the smaller digit from the larger in each column instead of borrowing) and 1.225 (borrowing without reducing the tenths digit from 5 to 4). Include 1.125 once as the correct option, and make sure no distractor equals it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources have not been re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 1.234 + 0.567 + 2.199 = 4.000; 1.500 − 0.375 = 1.125; 1.000 − 0.375 = 0.625; 0.375 + 0.625 = 1.000 and 0.001 + 0.999 = 1.000 — all verified correct. The original row's complement-error example (0.375 + 0.725 = 1.100) is intentionally used only as an error to diagnose, never as a correct answer.

The source claim supports using ragged-length decimals to reveal place-value errors; it does not establish comparative efficacy of any particular medium (interactive columns vs. picture vs. quiz). Medium recommendations are framed as affordances/limits, not necessity.

The legacy claim that depth/3D 'adds nothing' and that in-role dialogue cannot carry the insight were catalog fit judgements, not established facts; softened or omitted rather than asserted as universal laws.

The litre/bottle measuring context for 1.5 − 0.375 and the metre context for the three-measurement sum are retained to preserve the row's concrete measuring representations; the 'number line to thousandths' representation from the pedagogy field was not expanded into an activity.

probeDeeper: Before adding, roughly what should 1.234 + 0.567 + 2.199 be near — more or less than 4? Why?
Why write 1.5 as 1.500 before subtracting 0.375?
Do 0.4 and 0.6 have three decimal places? Give me a pair written to 3 d.p. that makes exactly 1.
How can you check that your two numbers really add to exactly 1?

errorPatterns.pattern: Right-justifies ragged decimals instead of aligning the point — lines up 1.234, 0.567, 2.199 by their last digits
errorPatterns.nextMove: Align on the decimal point and pad shorter numbers with zeros so tenths sit under tenths, thousandths under thousandths.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Columns don't match place value; the sum is the wrong size (not near 4)

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to pad and borrow across the point — tackles 1.5 − 0.375 without rewriting 1.500, botching the borrow
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rewrite 1.5 as 1.500, then subtract with borrowing across the hundredths and tenths just as in whole-number subtraction.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer like 1.175 or 1.235; leaves 1.5 as two digits and cannot subtract thousandths from nothing

errorPatterns.pattern: Complement-to-1 error — completes each column to 10 independently (0.375 + 0.725) or ignores the 3-d.p. requirement (0.4 + 0.6)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Find the complement by subtracting from 1.000 (1.000 − 0.375 = 0.625) and check by adding; stress the whole is 1.000, not 0.999 or ten in each column.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The chosen pair does not total exactly 1.000, or is not to three decimal places

responseLevels.gap: Right-justifies ragged decimals; cannot borrow across the point; gives complements that don't total 1.
responseLevels.full: Aligns on the point and pads ragged lengths, adds and subtracts to 3 d.p. with correct borrowing (4.000; 1.125), finds a valid 3-d.p. complement to 1, and estimates to check; transfers to a new problem.
responseLevels.partial: Adds/subtracts equal-length decimals correctly but misaligns ragged ones or forgets to pad, or finds a 'make 1' pair only when it is tidy (0.5 + 0.5) rather than to 3 d.p.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Show me your method for each. First, add 1.234 m + 0.567 m + 2.199 m. Second, a 1.5-litre bottle has 0.375 litres poured out — how much is left? Third, find two numbers, each with three decimal places, that add up to exactly 1.' Watch how they line the numbers up and handle the borrow.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The ragged sum (three different lengths) exposes right-justify misalignment; 1.5 − 0.375 forces padding to 1.500 and a borrow across the point; 'make 1' to 3 d.p. exposes complement errors (many write 0.375 + 0.725, completing each column to 10). A child who aligns on the point, pads with zeros and borrows correctly gets 4.000, 1.125 and a valid complement; a misaligner or column-completer does not.

sources.claim: Decimal size and calculation depend on place value, and errors arise from whole-number thinking (treating the decimal tail as a separate whole number, 'longer is larger'); ragged-length decimals are essential for revealing these errors, whereas tidy same-length items let faulty rules pass.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Tenths (age 9+)
topic.description: Recognise and use thousandths; relate them to tenths, hundredths, and their decimal equivalents (e.g. 1/1000 = 0.001, 35/1000 = 0.035)
evidence: Explain that 1 tenth = 100 thousandths
Place 0.345 on a number line between 0.34 and 0.35
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees the decimal 0.003, can they write it as a fraction and tell you roughly where it sits on a number line between 0 and 0.01?

pedagogy.summary: Thousandths continue the tenfold nesting one place further: split a hundredth into ten and each piece is a thousandth, so 1/100 ÷ 10 = 1/1000, and the places march ones → tenths → hundredths → thousandths, each a tenth of the one before. The coordinating facts are 10 thousandths = 1 hundredth, 100 thousandths = 1 tenth, and 1000 thousandths = 1 whole. In notation, 25 thousandths is 25/1000 = 0.025, where the leading placeholder zero holds the empty tenths place. The recurring obstacle is again whole-number bias — believing a thousandth is bigger than a hundredth 'because 1000 > 100' — and the placeholder error 25/1000 → 0.25. Build thousandths by repeated ÷10 subdivision and by zooming in on the number line between two hundredths.
bestPractices: Derive thousandths by subdividing a hundredth into ten, making 1/100 ÷ 10 = 1/1000 an action the child performs, so the recursive tenfold structure is felt rather than told.
Coordinate two levels of nesting explicitly: 10 thousandths = 1 hundredth AND 100 thousandths = 1 tenth, so children compose the ×10 steps instead of applying a single one.
Zoom the number line: locate 0.345 by zooming between 0.34 and 0.35 and splitting into ten, so a thousandth is seen as a tenth of the gap between hundredths.
Drill the placeholder in notation: 25/1000 = 0.025 (two leading places filled), contrasting 25/100 = 0.25 and 25/10 = 2.5, so place governs the number of zeros.
Confront whole-number bias directly — compare 0.05 and 0.005, or one hundredth against one thousandth — so 'more parts, smaller each' overturns 'bigger denominator, bigger part'.
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart: ones | tenths | hundredths | thousandths
Number line with zoom between two hundredths, split into ten thousandths
Recursive subdivision model (whole → tenth → hundredth → thousandth, ten-for-one each step)
Comparison pair 0.05 vs 0.005 to break whole-number bias
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias: a thousandth taken as bigger than a hundredth or tenth 'because 1000 > 100'.
Placeholder error: writing 25 thousandths as 0.25 (or 0.0025), not 0.025.
Miscoordinating the nesting: saying 10 thousandths = 1 tenth (one ×10 step) instead of 100 thousandths = 1 tenth.
Treating the digits after the point as a whole number, so 0.025 is read as 'twenty-five' and mis-sized.
Thinking the number line 'runs out' at hundredths, so not subdividing further to place a thousandth.

learn.summary: Thousandths continue the tenfold nesting one place further: split a hundredth into ten and each piece is a thousandth, so 1/100 ÷ 10 = 1/1000, and the places march ones → tenths → hundredths → thousandths, each a tenth of the one before. The coordinating facts are 10 thousandths = 1 hundredth, 100 thousandths = 1 tenth, and 1000 thousandths = 1 whole. In notation, 25 thousandths = 25/1000 = 0.025, where the leading placeholder zero holds the empty tenths place. The recurring obstacles are whole-number bias (believing a thousandth is bigger than a hundredth 'because 1000 > 100') and the placeholder error (writing 25/1000 as 0.25). Build thousandths by repeated ÷10 subdivision and by zooming in on the number line between two hundredths.

activities.title: Zoom the number line to place 0.345
feedback: If a learner says the line stops at hundredths, prompt: 'The gap between 0.34 and 0.35 can itself be cut into ten — what is each new piece called?'
If they place 0.345 at the wrong mark, have them count the ten equal steps aloud and check that 0.345 sits on the fifth mark (5 thousandths past 0.34).
If a learner thinks a thousandth is the smallest piece possible, invite them to split it into ten again and name the ten-thousandth, reinforcing that the ÷10 subdivision can always continue.
Confirm success when they can name each step as one thousandth and justify the position of 0.345 by counting thousandths.
activities.rationale: Locating a thousandth by zooming between two hundredths and subdividing into ten makes the recursive tenfold structure an action the child performs, rather than a rule stated to them. If a live number line is used, dragging a zoom control and watching the gap split into ten labelled steps makes the mechanism concrete; a drawn paper number line zoomed and re-divided on a fresh strip serves the same purpose.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — treating a larger denominator or more digits as a larger quantity — is the central obstacle as children extend place value to thousandths, and place-value reasoning built by subdivision and number-line work (rather than a stated rule) is needed; faulty digit-based rules can pass easy items, so placeholder and comparison cases must be used.
Pupils should recognise and use thousandths and relate them to tenths, hundredths and decimal equivalents (Year 5 statutory content).
learnerActions: Start with a number line showing just 0.34 and 0.35, with nothing marked between them, and predict aloud roughly where 0.345 should go.
Zoom into the gap between 0.34 and 0.35 and divide it into ten equal steps; name what each single step is worth (one thousandth, a tenth of the gap between two hundredths).
Count the steps and place 0.345 exactly on the fifth mark (the midpoint of the gap), then state why: it is 5 thousandths past 0.34.
Repeat the zoom-and-split for another thousandth, e.g. place 0.347, so the subdivision becomes a repeatable action, not a one-off.
Extend the action one level further: split a single thousandth into ten equal parts and name each tinier piece a ten-thousandth, illustrating that the ÷10 subdivision can always be repeated again.
activities.intendedInsight: A thousandth is a tenth of the gap between two hundredths; the number line never 'runs out' — you can always subdivide one more time by ten to locate a finer value (a tenth of a thousandth is a ten-thousandth).

activities.title: Split a hundredth and compare sizes to break whole-number bias
feedback: If the learner predicts the thousandth is bigger 'because 1000 beats 100', do not just correct — have them physically lay one thousandth against one hundredth so the size difference is visible, then restate the rule 'more parts means each is smaller'.
For 0.05 vs 0.005, if they pick 0.005, point to the split: 0.005 is 5 thousandths while 0.05 is 50 thousandths (ten times larger); have them count how many thousandths are in each.
Confirm success when the learner states that a thousandth is smaller than a hundredth and can explain why the larger number 1000 does not make the part larger.
activities.rationale: Directly predicting, then confronting the prediction with a visible length comparison, targets whole-number bias in the moment the child commits to a wrong reason. Showing one thousandth beside one hundredth makes 'more parts, smaller each' concrete; a live splitter that recolours or relabels each new piece, or a paper strip cut into ten, both make the subdivision tangible. A paper strip cut into ten has slight thickness, so treat it as a model of the ideal zero-thickness partition, not identical to it.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — treating a larger denominator or more digits as a larger quantity — is the central obstacle as children extend place value to thousandths, and place-value reasoning built by subdivision and number-line work (rather than a stated rule) is needed; faulty digit-based rules can pass easy items, so placeholder and comparison cases must be used.
learnerActions: Before comparing, predict which is bigger, one hundredth or one thousandth, and say WHY in words.
Take one hundredth and split it into ten equal parts; identify each part as one thousandth.
Lay a single thousandth beside a whole hundredth and describe what you see — the thousandth is tiny next to the hundredth.
Reconcile this with your prediction: even though 1000 is a bigger number than 100, a thousandth is a smaller amount because it comes from cutting into more, smaller parts.
Compare 0.05 and 0.005 directly and state which is bigger and why, when both use the digit 5.
activities.intendedInsight: More, smaller parts means each part is smaller: a thousandth is smaller than a hundredth despite 1000 > 100, overturning 'bigger denominator, bigger part'.

activities.title: Write thousandths and justify the placeholder zero
feedback: If the learner writes 0.25 for 25 thousandths, return to the chart: thousandths is the third place after the point, so 25 must occupy hundredths and thousandths, leaving tenths empty and needing a 0.
If they write 0.0025, check column by column: the 5 should sit in thousandths (third place), not further right.
Confirm success when they both write 0.025 correctly and explain, using the chart, why the zero after the point is needed and why 25/100 and 25/1000 differ.
activities.rationale: Writing thousandths within an explicit place-value chart and contrasting 25/10, 25/100, 25/1000 makes the placeholder error visible and correctable by reasoning about place rather than digit-copying. A running chart that updates as the learner fills each column, or a hand-drawn chart, both make the empty tenths cell explicit.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — treating a larger denominator or more digits as a larger quantity — is the central obstacle as children extend place value to thousandths, and place-value reasoning built by subdivision and number-line work (rather than a stated rule) is needed; faulty digit-based rules can pass easy items, so placeholder and comparison cases must be used.
Pupils should recognise and use thousandths and relate them to tenths, hundredths and decimal equivalents (Year 5 statutory content).
learnerActions: Using a place-value chart with columns ones | tenths | hundredths | thousandths, write 25 thousandths: place the 2 in hundredths and the 5 in thousandths.
Fill the empty tenths column with a 0 and write the decimal 0.025, then explain that the zero holds the empty tenths place.
Contrast the set 25/10 = 2.5, 25/100 = 0.25, 25/1000 = 0.025, and describe how the place of the value decides where the digits land and how many leading places are filled.
Write a second example, e.g. 35 thousandths = 35/1000 = 0.035, and say why there is one placeholder zero straight after the decimal point (in the tenths place).
activities.intendedInsight: The place a value occupies, not just the digits, fixes the written decimal; the placeholder zero in 0.025 holds the empty tenths position so the 2 lands in hundredths and the 5 in thousandths.

activities.title: Compose two tenfold steps: 10 and 100 thousandths
feedback: If the learner says 10 thousandths = 1 tenth, build it in stages: 'How many thousandths in a hundredth? And how many hundredths in a tenth? So how many thousandths in a tenth?'
Have them count on a subdivided line through both levels to see the two steps accumulate to 100.
Confirm success when they answer 100 thousandths per tenth and can name both tenfold steps that compose it.
activities.rationale: Explicitly coordinating two levels of nesting addresses the miscoordination error (saying 10 rather than 100 thousandths per tenth) by having the child compose the steps instead of applying one. Counting through the levels on a subdivided line or stacking the facts on a chart both make the two steps visible.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — treating a larger denominator or more digits as a larger quantity — is the central obstacle as children extend place value to thousandths, and place-value reasoning built by subdivision and number-line work (rather than a stated rule) is needed; faulty digit-based rules can pass easy items, so placeholder and comparison cases must be used.
Pupils should recognise and use thousandths and relate them to tenths, hundredths and decimal equivalents (Year 5 statutory content).
learnerActions: State and show that 10 thousandths make 1 hundredth (one ÷10 subdivision).
Then show that 10 hundredths make 1 tenth, so composing the two steps gives 100 thousandths = 1 tenth.
Continue the chain to 1000 thousandths = 1 whole, naming each tenfold step.
Answer the trap question 'How many thousandths are in one tenth?' and justify 100 (two tenfold steps), explaining why 10 is wrong (it skips a step).
activities.intendedInsight: Getting from thousandths to tenths is two tenfold steps, not one: 10 thousandths = 1 hundredth and 100 thousandths = 1 tenth; the nesting composes rather than applying a single ×10.

activities.title: Check and diagnose with targeted questions
feedback: For the comparison item, if the learner selects 0.005 citing 1000 > 100, route back to the split-and-compare activity to re-establish 'more parts, smaller each'.
For 25/1000, if they omit the placeholder zero, return to the place-value chart activity.
Treat the 'why' answers as diagnostic: a learner who answers correctly but cannot explain the two-step nesting or the placeholder still needs the composing and notation activities.
activities.rationale: These checkable items with distractors (the 1000 > 100 comparison, the missing placeholder) surface whole-number bias and placeholder errors diagnostically. Checks assess outcomes rather than build the nesting insight, so they complement, not replace, the subdivision and zoom activities.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — treating a larger denominator or more digits as a larger quantity — is the central obstacle as children extend place value to thousandths, and place-value reasoning built by subdivision and number-line work (rather than a stated rule) is needed; faulty digit-based rules can pass easy items, so placeholder and comparison cases must be used.
learnerActions: Complete 25/1000 = 0.0__ and justify where the 2 and 5 sit and why the zero is there.
Complete '100 thousandths = __ tenth' and explain the two-step reasoning.
Decide which is bigger, 0.05 or 0.005, and give a reason that does not rely on 'more digits means bigger'.
Place 0.345 between 0.34 and 0.35 by stating how many equal steps are in the gap and which step 0.345 is.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct answers plus a stated reason distinguish genuine grasp of the recursive tenth-of-a-tenth-of-a-tenth structure from a memorised conversion or digit-copying.

constraints: Target age roughly 9–10 (Year 5): recognise and use thousandths and relate them to tenths, hundredths and decimal equivalents.
Build thousandths by subdivision and zooming as actions the child performs, so the recursive tenfold structure is felt, not merely asserted.

A reference chart or diagram with tappable nesting facts and a notation flap can communicate the structure as a reference, but on its own it does not let the child perform the subdivision or the zoom; use it as a reference scaffold alongside, not instead of, hands-on subdivision.

Checkable question formats with distractors assess outcomes and can diagnose errors (whole-number bias, placeholder) but do not by themselves elicit the construction of the nesting; use them to check and route, not as the sole means of teaching the insight.
Always use placeholder cases (25/1000 = 0.025) and comparison cases (0.05 vs 0.005) because faulty digit-based rules can pass easy items.
Address whole-number bias directly by making 'more, smaller parts means each is smaller' visible, rather than by rule assertion.
Treat any physical paper split as a model of the ideal zero-thickness partition: real card has slight thickness and only approximates the mathematical subdivision.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The second listed source (DfE National Curriculum) is marked verified:false in the source row; it is cited only for the Year 5 scope/content statement, not for comparative efficacy.

Self-audit of arithmetic and place value: 25/1000 = 0.025 (2 in hundredths, 5 in thousandths, 0 placeholder in tenths); 25/100 = 0.25; 25/10 = 2.5; 35/1000 = 0.035 — all consistent. The ten-for-one chain 10 thousandths = 1 hundredth, 100 thousandths = 1 tenth, 1000 thousandths = 1 whole is internally consistent. Dividing 0.34–0.35 into ten equal steps puts 0.345 on the fifth mark, i.e. the midpoint and 5 thousandths past 0.34; 0.05 = 50 thousandths and 0.005 = 5 thousandths — consistent.

The original 'conversation' and '3D' fit entries asserted a character/depth 'adds nothing'; these universal-dismissal claims were dropped rather than propagated, since the source ratings do not establish such necessity/impossibility claims. No source establishes that the 2D interactive is superior to any other medium; the medium preference is a pedagogical proposal only.

The source probeDeeper and responseLevels.full extend the ÷10 action to ten-thousandths; this was restored as an action and feedback in the zoom activity so the 'never runs out' claim is enacted, not merely asserted.

Physical paper cut into ten parts is an approximation with thickness; it represents the ideal zero-thickness partition and should be treated as a model of it, not identical to it (noted in the relevant activity, not only here).

assess.poeTask: Before comparing, ask the child to PREDICT which is bigger, one hundredth or one thousandth, and to say WHY. The reason is diagnostic: predicting the thousandth is bigger 'because 1000 beats 100' reveals the whole-number bias. Then split one hundredth into ten and lay a single thousandth beside a hundredth — the thousandth is plainly tiny. Have the child reconcile this with their prediction.
probeDeeper: You wrote 25 thousandths as 0.025. Where does the 2 sit, and where does the 5 sit — and why the zero right after the point?
Which is bigger, 0.05 or 0.005 — and why, when the digits are both 5?
If I split one thousandth into ten equal parts again, what would each tiny piece be called?
Show me where 0.345 goes between 0.34 and 0.35 — how many equal steps are in that gap, and which one is 0.345?
assess.correctAnswer: 10 thousandths in one hundredth; 100 thousandths in one tenth. 25 thousandths = 25/1000 = 0.025; the placeholder zero holds the empty tenths place so the 2 lands in hundredths and the 5 in thousandths (each place a tenth of the one before).

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias: 'a thousandth is bigger than a hundredth because 1000 is bigger than 100'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lay one thousandth against one hundredth so the thousandth is visibly tiny; re-establish 'more, smaller parts means each is smaller'. Reteach the tenfold place structure from tenths/hundredths.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a comparison probe (0.05 vs 0.005, or 'which is bigger, a hundredth or a thousandth') picks the thousandth; treats a larger denominator as a larger part.

errorPatterns.pattern: Placeholder error: writes 25 thousandths as 0.25 (or 0.0025) rather than 0.025.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the place-value chart — thousandths is the third place, so 25 occupies hundredths and thousandths with a zero in tenths; contrast 25/100 = 0.25 with 25/1000 = 0.025. Reteach place-fixes-the-value.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 0.25 for 25/1000; does not fill the tenths place with a zero.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscoordinates the nesting: says there are 10 thousandths in a tenth (one ×10 step) instead of 100 (two steps).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build it in stages — 10 thousandths make a hundredth, and 10 hundredths make a tenth, so 100 thousandths make a tenth; count on the subdivided line. Reteach composing tenfold steps.
errorPatterns.distractor: There are 10 thousandths in one tenth.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers '10' for thousandths in a tenth; applies a single tenfold step instead of composing two.

responseLevels.gap: Believes a thousandth is bigger than a hundredth, writes 25/1000 as 0.25, or gives 10 thousandths per tenth. No coordinated nesting.
responseLevels.full: Coordinates the nesting (10 thousandths = 1 hundredth, 100 = 1 tenth, 1000 = 1 whole), writes 25/1000 = 0.025 with the placeholder and justifies it, holds that a thousandth is smaller than a hundredth despite 1000 > 100, places 0.345 by zooming between hundredths, and extends the ÷10 action to ten-thousandths.
responseLevels.partial: Can write 0.025 and recite that 1000 thousandths make a whole, but cannot explain the two-step nesting (100 thousandths = 1 tenth) or why the placeholder is needed — lists facts without relating them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: How many thousandths are in one hundredth, and how many thousandths are in one tenth? Then write 25 thousandths as a fraction and as a decimal, and tell me why it is written that way.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 'How many thousandths in a tenth' checks whether the child composes two ×10 steps (100) or applies just one (10). Writing 25/1000 exposes the placeholder — a digit-copier writes 0.25. The tier-2 'why' separates a memorised conversion from grasp of the recursive tenth-of-a-tenth-of-a-tenth structure and of a thousandth being smaller than a hundredth despite 1000 > 100.
