topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Comparing Decimals
topic.description: Compare two decimals to hundredths (or up to three decimal places) by reasoning about size using place-value understanding; record with >, =, <
evidence: Compare 0.45 and 0.405 and explain which is greater
Order 3.142, 3.14, 3.2 from smallest to largest
Justify that 0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700 using place-value reasoning
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares 0.45 and 0.54, can they use place value to explain which is bigger — without reaching for a calculator?

pedagogy.summary: Comparing decimals is a place-value skill, not a digit-counting one: the digit in the highest place decides the size, so you compare tenths first, then hundredths, then thousandths — exactly as with whole numbers you compare from the left. The whole difficulty is that decimals invite false analogies with whole numbers. Two opposite faulty rules dominate: 'longer-is-larger' (0.45 > 0.5 'because 45 > 5', treating the tail as a separate whole number) and 'shorter-is-larger' (0.4 > 0.87, either because 0.4 is read like 1/4 versus 1/87, or from the partial truth 'tenths are bigger than hundredths'). Both give correct answers on tidy same-length pairs, so RAGGED decimals (different numbers of places) are essential to expose them. Teach comparison through place-value reasoning and a length model, and establish that annexing zeros (0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700) does not change value.
bestPractices: Compare from the highest place value: line up the points, compare tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths — and reason aloud ('0.38 is 3 tenths and 8 hundredths, which is less than 4 tenths').
Use ragged decimals deliberately (0.4 vs 0.38, 0.5 vs 0.45, 0.9 vs 0.11) because same-length pairs let faulty rules pass undetected.
Establish annexing zeros as value-preserving: 0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700, so you may fill to equal length to compare — but only after the meaning is understood, never as a rote substitute.
Use a length model (Linear Arithmetic Blocks) or a number line where size is shown by length, which is conceptually clearer than area/volume blocks, so 0.38 is visibly shorter than 0.4.

Name the misconception to be resisted (metacognitive approach) and show correct and incorrect comparisons side by side, since the error is partly a failure to inhibit the whole-number rule, not only missing knowledge.
Avoid teaching 'add zeros then compare as whole numbers' as the primary method — rules unsupported by place-value understanding are forgotten and mask the misconception.
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart with decimals aligned on the point
Number line (with zoom) for locating and comparing ragged decimals
Linear Arithmetic Blocks / length model where size = length
10×10 hundredths grids shaded for each decimal to compare area
Side-by-side correct vs incorrect comparison cards for discussion
commonMisconceptions: Longer-is-larger: judging the decimal with more digits as larger (0.45 > 0.5, 0.311 > 0.4), treating the tail as a whole number.
Shorter-is-larger (fraction-thinking): 0.4 > 0.87 because 0.4 is read as 1/4 and 0.87 as 1/87 ('sharing among fewer gives more').
Shorter-is-larger (tenths>hundredths): 0.4 > 0.87 from the over-applied partial truth that a tenth is bigger than a hundredth.
Believing annexing a zero changes value (0.7 ≠ 0.70).
Comparing digit-by-digit from the right, or comparing the fractional parts as isolated whole numbers regardless of place.

learn.summary: Comparing decimals is a place-value skill, not digit-counting. You compare from the highest place: any whole-number part first, then tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths, until the digits differ, reasoning aloud ('0.38 is 3 tenths and 8 hundredths, which is less than 4 tenths'). The core difficulty is false analogy with whole numbers, producing two opposite faulty rules: 'longer-is-larger' (claiming 0.45 > 0.5 'because 45 > 5', treating the tail as a whole number) and 'shorter-is-larger' (claiming 0.4 > 0.87, from reading 0.4 as 1/4 vs 0.87 as 1/87, or from over-applying 'tenths are bigger than hundredths'). Both faulty rules give correct answers on tidy same-length pairs, so RAGGED decimals (different numbers of places) are essential to expose them. Teach through place-value reasoning and a length model, and establish that annexing zeros (0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700) does not change value.

activities.title: Order ragged decimals against a length model
feedback: If the learner ranks 0.312 or 0.38 as largest ('more digits'), draw the bars: 0.38 is plainly shorter than 0.4, and 0.312 is shortest. Say in place value: '0.38 is 3 tenths 8 hundredths, less than 4 tenths.'

If the learner picks the shorter decimal as larger using a sharing/fraction analogy on 0.4 vs 0.87 ('like 1/4 vs 1/87'), separate decimal place value from denominator size: 0.4 is four tenths, 0.87 is eight tenths and seven hundredths, so 0.87 is larger; show both lengths.
If the learner says 'tenths beat hundredths so 0.4 > 0.87', compare from the left: 0.87 already has more tenths than 0.4, so it wins before hundredths matter.

If the learner ranks 0.405 above 0.45 because '405 > 45', line up the points: both have 4 tenths, then 0.45 has 5 hundredths while 0.405 has 0 hundredths, so 0.45 is larger — the extra digits in 0.405 are thousandths, not a bigger whole number.
If the learner says 0.7 and 0.70 differ, show seven tenths equals seventy hundredths and the two lengths are identical.
When the learner reasons highest-place-first and justifies in place-value words, confirm the method and extend to a new thousandths case, for example ordering 3.142, 3.14, 3.2.
activities.rationale: Two opposite, documented misconceptions dominate decimal comparison, and both pass on same-length pairs, so ragged decimals are needed to expose them; a length model and place-value reasoning are recommended over rote 'add zeros and compare as whole numbers'. Predicting-then-checking against visible length is intended to confront the longer-is-larger error at the moment the whole-number rule breaks. The main set already exposes longer-is-larger but can hide shorter-is-larger, so 0.4 vs 0.87 is needed to surface shorter-is-larger, while 0.9 vs 0.11 and 0.45 vs 0.405 give further checks on longer-is-larger.
sourceClaims: Two opposite, well-documented misconceptions dominate decimal comparison — 'longer-is-larger' (more digits taken as larger, treating the tail as a whole number) and 'shorter-is-larger', the latter with two sub-types: confusing decimals with fractions (0.4 read as 1/4 vs 0.87 as 1/87) and over-applying 'tenths are bigger than hundredths'. Faulty strategies can yield correct answers on tidy pairs, so ragged decimals are needed to expose them; a length model (Linear Arithmetic Blocks) and place-value reasoning ('0.38 is 3 tenths and 8 hundredths, less than 4 tenths') are recommended over rote 'add zeros and compare as whole numbers'.
learnerActions: Before using any model, predict the order of ragged decimals from smallest to largest and say why, e.g. for 0.4, 0.38, 0.312, 0.5.
Represent each decimal as a bar or length drawn to a common scale (for example a Linear Arithmetic Block / bar model), then check your predicted order against the lengths.

State the correct order (0.312 < 0.38 < 0.4 < 0.5) and justify it in place-value language: 0.312 and 0.38 both have 3 tenths, so they are smaller than 0.4 (4 tenths) and 0.5 (5 tenths); among the 3-tenths numbers, 0.312 (3 tenths 1 hundredth) is less than 0.38 (3 tenths 8 hundredths).

Also compare the counterexample ragged pairs 0.4 vs 0.87, 0.9 vs 0.11, and 0.45 vs 0.405: predict first, then check each against the length model and in place-value words. These pairs deliberately trip both faulty rules — for example 0.45 vs 0.405 tempts longer-is-larger (405 looks bigger than 45), yet 0.45 (4 tenths 5 hundredths) is larger than 0.405 (4 tenths 0 hundredths 5 thousandths); and on the 0.4/0.38/0.312/0.5 set a shorter-is-larger learner can still land the right order.
Locate the decimals on a number line and, where helpful, zoom between 0.3 and 0.4 to see 0.38 and 0.312 separated in the hundredths.
Compare 0.7 with 0.70 (optionally using an annex-zero toggle or shading) and explain why trailing zeros do not change the value.
activities.intendedInsight: The decimal with more digits is not automatically larger, and the one with fewer digits is not automatically larger either; size is decided by the highest place where the digits differ. A length/number-line model shows that more digits need not mean more length (0.38 is shorter than 0.4, but 0.87 is longer than 0.4). Annexing trailing zeros gives decimals the same number of decimal places without changing their value.

activities.title: Name and resist the whole-number rule (correct vs incorrect cards)
feedback: If the learner cannot name why a wrong card is wrong, re-read both decimals in place-value words and point to where the comparison first decides (the highest differing place).
Praise explicit self-monitoring ('I nearly counted the digits — but I compared tenths first').
If the learner only identifies the right answer without naming the faulty rule, prompt: which rule would make someone pick the wrong card here?
activities.rationale: The greater-digits misconception reflects an overgeneralisation of whole-number knowledge and is partly a failure to inhibit the whole-number rule, so metacognitive approaches that name the misconception and present correct/incorrect examples side by side are recommended.
sourceClaims: The 'greater number of digits means greater magnitude' misconception is among the most common in decimal comparison and reflects an overgeneralisation of whole-number knowledge; it is partly a failure to inhibit the whole-number rule, so metacognitive approaches that name the misconception and present correct/incorrect examples side by side are recommended. Longer-is-larger declines with age while shorter-is-larger persists into adulthood.
learnerActions: Look at side-by-side comparison cards, one clearly labelled correct and one clearly labelled wrong, e.g. '0.45 > 0.5' (labelled wrong) beside '0.45 < 0.5' (labelled correct).
Say out loud which faulty rule produced the wrong card ('longer-is-larger: it counted 45 against 5') and explain why it fails here.
Write or state the place-value reason the correct card holds (0.5 is 5 tenths; 0.45 is 4 tenths 5 hundredths; 5 tenths is more).
Before answering each new pair, flag the rule you must NOT use, then compare correctly.
activities.intendedInsight: The error is partly a failure to inhibit the whole-number rule, not only missing knowledge; naming the misconception and inspecting clearly-labelled correct/incorrect examples side by side helps a learner catch and override it.

activities.title: Show equivalence and area with hundredths grids
feedback: If the learner thinks 0.38 covers more than 0.4 because '38 > 4', count tenths columns: 0.4 fills four full columns (40 squares), 0.38 fills three columns and part of a fourth (38 squares).
If the learner denies 0.7 = 0.70, overlay or count: 7 tenths = 70 hundredths cover the same squares.
On the aligned chart, if the learner compares from the right, redirect to the highest place first.
activities.rationale: Grids and an aligned place-value chart are useful references for area comparison and for making annexing-zeros equivalence concrete; however such references need to be paired with practice across many ragged cases with feedback rather than used alone.
learnerActions: Shade 0.4 and 0.38 each on a 10×10 hundredths grid and compare the shaded areas.
Shade 0.7 on one grid and 0.70 on another, and explain why seven tenths fills the same area as seventy hundredths.
Use an aligned place-value chart (points lined up) to read each decimal digit by digit, starting from tenths, and state which decimal is larger and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Decimals can be compared by area as well as by length, and both representations show that annexing a zero (0.7 = 0.70) preserves value while more digits need not mean more size. (Note: the source synthesis treats length as the clearest magnitude model for this topic; the grid is a complementary reference.)

constraints: Use ragged decimals deliberately (e.g. 0.4 vs 0.38, 0.5 vs 0.45, 0.9 vs 0.11, 0.4 vs 0.87, 0.45 vs 0.405); same-length pairs let both faulty rules pass undetected and should not be the only practice.
On the 0.4/0.38/0.312/0.5 ordering set a shorter-is-larger learner can still reach the right order, so include at least one pair (such as 0.4 vs 0.87) that directly exposes shorter-is-larger.
Teach 'annexing zeros is value-preserving' (0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700) only after the meaning is understood, never as a rote substitute for place-value reasoning.
Avoid teaching 'add zeros then compare as whole numbers' as the primary method; rules unsupported by place-value understanding are forgotten and can mask the misconception.

A length model or number line (where size is shown by length) is the recommended visual here; the source synthesis prefers length over volume/3D models for this topic. This is a stated preference for showing decimal magnitude, not a universal claim that other media cannot teach.

A static aligned chart or single shaded grid is a reference/scaffold: it may support reading or checking a comparison but does not by itself provide the repeated ragged-case practice with feedback that builds the comparison skill.

Multiple-choice/ordering/true-false questions with distractors built from longer-is-larger and shorter-is-larger can diagnose which faulty rule a child uses, but recognising the right option does not by itself build place-value insight; pair any quizzing with construction and justification.
Scope: Year 5 expectation is to read, write, order and compare numbers with up to three decimal places; extend from hundredths to thousandths deliberately.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the worked examples: 0.312 < 0.38 < 0.4 < 0.5 is correct; 0.312 and 0.38 share 3 tenths, and 0.312 (3 tenths 1 hundredth) < 0.38 (3 tenths 8 hundredths); 0.4 and 0.5 have 4 and 5 tenths. 0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700 is correct (seven tenths = seventy hundredths). 0.87 > 0.4, 0.9 > 0.11, and 0.45 > 0.405 are correct. Ordering 3.142, 3.14, 3.2 gives 3.14 < 3.142 < 3.2. Grid counts: 0.4 = 4 columns = 40 squares; 0.38 = 38 squares. No arithmetic errors found.

Coherence fix applied: feedback referring to 0.4 vs 0.87, 0.9 vs 0.11 and 0.45 vs 0.405 now has matching learnerActions in Activity 1, because the main ordering set 0.4/0.38/0.312/0.5 can be ordered correctly by a shorter-is-larger learner and therefore does not reveal that misconception on its own.

Source verification is mixed in the original row: the SMART/Victoria synthesis claim is marked verified; the Durkin & Rittle-Johnson / Roell et al. / Steinle & Stacey synthesis claim and the DfE National Curriculum claim are marked unverified. The Durkin-synthesis claim is reused as a sourceClaim because it directly supports the metacognitive-naming principle, but its verification status was not upgraded here.

The original artefact wording asserting that a conversation or 3D model offers 'no spatial gain' and that a static picture 'cannot' teach has been softened to scoped affordances/limits; comparative necessity is a catalog preference, not established efficacy.
The length-over-volume preference is carried from the source synthesis as a recommendation for this topic, not as proof that volume/3D representations cannot teach decimal comparison.

probeDeeper: You placed 0.38 relative to 0.4 — which has more tenths? Does having more digits always mean bigger?
A friend says 0.9 is smaller than 0.11 because 11 is more than 9. What would you tell them?
Is 0.5 bigger or smaller than 0.45? What about 0.5 and 0.500?
How could you use this number line to check your whole order is right?
assess.correctAnswer: 0.312 < 0.38 < 0.4 < 0.5. Reasoning by place value: 0.312 and 0.38 have 3 tenths (smaller), and 0.312 (3 tenths 1 hundredth) is less than 0.38 (3 tenths 8 hundredths); 0.4 and 0.5 have 4 and 5 tenths. 0.7 = 0.70 — seven tenths equals seventy hundredths; the trailing zero does not change the value.

errorPatterns.pattern: Longer-is-larger: 'more digits means bigger — 0.38 is more than 0.4 because 38 is bigger than 4', treating the digits after the point as a whole number.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the length model — 0.38 is shorter than 0.4 — and reason in place value: '0.38 is 3 tenths 8 hundredths, less than 4 tenths'. Use ragged decimals; name and inhibit the whole-number rule. Reteach comparison of same-length decimals first.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ranks 0.312 and/or 0.38 as the largest; orders by digit count rather than by tenths.

errorPatterns.pattern: Shorter-is-larger (fraction-thinking): 'the shorter one is bigger — 0.4 beats 0.87 because sharing among 4 gives more than among 87', reading 0.4 as 1/4 and 0.87 as 1/87.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate decimal place value from denominator-size reasoning: 0.4 is four tenths, 0.87 is eight tenths and seven hundredths, so 0.87 is bigger; show both on the length model. Reteach decimal comparison from place value.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks the shorter decimal as larger and justifies with a sharing/denominator analogy.

errorPatterns.pattern: Shorter-is-larger (tenths>hundredths): 'tenths are bigger than hundredths, so 0.4 is bigger than 0.87' — over-applying a partial truth.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare place by place from the left: 0.87 has more tenths than 0.4, so it wins before hundredths matter; grids/length model make it visible. Reteach highest-place-first comparison.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct on pure tenth-vs-hundredth cases but wrong when the hundredths total exceeds the tenths gap (0.4 vs 0.87); may also mis-order fractions by denominator.

errorPatterns.pattern: Annexing a zero changes the value — '0.7 and 0.70 are different, 0.70 is bigger (or smaller)'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show 7 tenths = 70 hundredths on a grid and equal lengths on the line; trailing zeros fill to equal length without changing size. Reteach place-value equivalence.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the tier-2 question, denies 0.7 = 0.70.

responseLevels.gap: Orders by number of digits (longer- or shorter-is-larger) or compares the tails as whole numbers; denies 0.7 = 0.70. Ragged decimals are mis-ordered.
responseLevels.full: Orders ragged decimals correctly by comparing the highest place value first, justifies in place-value language ('0.38 is 3 tenths 8 hundredths, less than 4 tenths'), knows 0.7 = 0.70, and transfers the method to thousandths and to counterexample pairs like 0.9 vs 0.11.
responseLevels.partial: Compares same-length decimals correctly but slips on ragged decimals, or reaches the right order by annexing zeros without explaining place value — executes a rule without the highest-place-first reasoning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put these in order from smallest to largest and show me how you decided: 0.4, 0.38, 0.312, 0.5. Then tell me — is 0.7 the same size as 0.70, and how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: These are RAGGED decimals, so faulty rules cannot hide. A longer-is-larger child ranks 0.312 or 0.38 as largest ('more digits'). A shorter-is-larger child ranks 0.4/0.5 as largest for the wrong reason and mis-orders 0.312 vs 0.38, or claims 0.4 > 0.5-style errors on other pairs; watching the justification reveals whether it is the fraction-analogy or the tenths>hundredths route. The 0.7 vs 0.70 tier catches the belief that annexing a zero changes value. Same-length pairs would let every faulty rule pass — these do not.

Faulty strategies can yield correct answers on tidy pairs, so ragged decimals are needed to expose them; a length model (Linear Arithmetic Blocks) and place-value reasoning ('0.38 is 3 tenths and 8 hundredths, less than 4 tenths') are recommended over rote 'add zeros and compare as whole numbers'.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Decimals and fractions
topic.description: Solve simple measure and money problems involving fractions and decimals to two decimal places
evidence: Calculate 1/4 of £3.20
A rope is 2.5 m long; how much is left after cutting 0.75 m?
Find 3/10 of 1 kg and express the answer in grams and as a decimal of a kg
topic.assessmentPrompt: If a bottle holds 1.5 litres and {{name}} drinks 0.75 litres, can they work out how much is left — and write it as both a decimal and a fraction?

pedagogy.summary: Money and measure problems weave fractions and decimals together in context: finding a fraction of an amount (¼ of £3.20 = 80p), subtracting decimal measures (2.5 − 0.75 = 1.75 m), and moving between fractions, decimals and units (3/10 of 1 kg = 300 g = 0.3 kg). Success rests on reading a decimal by its place value rather than as two whole numbers, keeping units consistent, and choosing whether a fraction-of or a decimal calculation is easiest.
bestPractices: Read money by place value: £3.20 is 3 pounds and 2 tenths of a pound = 20p, NOT '3 pounds 2 pence'
Equalise decimal lengths and align the point before subtracting (2.50 − 0.75)
Connect a fraction of an amount to division: ¼ of £3.20 = £3.20 ÷ 4 = 80p
Convert between units deliberately and both ways (0.3 kg = 300 g; 300 g = 0.3 kg)
Estimate first to sense-check the size of the answer
keyRepresentations: Bar model partitioned for a fraction of an amount
Place-value columns aligned on the decimal point
Number line / ruler for the rope-length problem
kg↔g (or £↔p) double number line for unit conversion
Coins and notes for money
commonMisconceptions: Reads money as two whole numbers: '£3.20 = 3 pounds 2 pence', '£3.5 = 3 pounds 5 pence'
Misaligns decimals of unequal length when subtracting (2.5 − 0.75)
Miscomputes a fraction of an amount (¼ of £3.20 ≠ 80p)
Unit slips: 0.3 kg read as 30 g or 3000 g, or gives grams but not the decimal of a kg

learn.summary: Children solve money and measure problems that weave fractions and decimals together: finding a fraction of an amount (¼ of £3.20 = 80p), subtracting decimal measures of unequal length (2.5 − 0.75 = 1.75 m), and moving between fractions, decimals and units (3/10 of 1 kg = 300 g = 0.3 kg). Success rests on reading each decimal digit by its place value rather than as two separate whole numbers, keeping units consistent, aligning on the decimal point before subtracting, and connecting 'a fraction of' to division.

activities.title: Split the £3.20 bar: a quarter as division
feedback: If a part reads 8p or 12.8p, check: do the four equal parts add back to £3.20? 80p × 4 = £3.20, so each quarter is 80p.
The 12.8p trap treats £3.20 as the bare number 3.2 and multiplies (3.2 × 4 = 12.8) instead of dividing; 'a quarter OF' makes the amount smaller, so you divide.
If 'a quarter' was treated as 25 of something, connect ¼ to one of four equal parts of this specific amount.
activities.rationale: A partitioned bar model makes the fraction-of-an-amount concrete and links it directly to division, targeting the common error of computing ¼ of £3.20 by an unclear operation. A live splittable bar lets the child act and see each equal part, but a drawn-and-divided paper bar serves the same purpose.
learnerActions: Take a bar representing £3.20 and split it into four equal parts.
Read what one part is worth and label it (80p / £0.80).
Write the matching calculation: ¼ of £3.20 = £3.20 ÷ 4 = 80p.
Check by adding or multiplying back: 80p × 4 = £3.20.
State in your own words why 'a quarter of' means dividing by 4.
activities.intendedInsight: Finding a fraction of an amount is a division: a quarter of £3.20 is £3.20 shared into 4 equal parts, which is 80p.

activities.title: Cut the rope: align the point before subtracting
feedback: If your answer is not 1.75 m, or does not match your ruler estimate, check whether 2.5 and 0.75 were lined up by their last digits instead of by the decimal point, and whether the exchange (borrowing) was done correctly.
Rewriting 2.5 as 2.50 does not change its value — it just makes the hundredths column visible for 0.75.
Compare your answer to the ruler: cutting a bit less than 1 m off 2.5 m should leave a bit more than 1.5 m and less than 2 m, so 1.75 m is sensible.
activities.rationale: The unequal lengths of 2.5 and 0.75 directly expose the misalignment error (right-justifying ragged decimals). A ruler or number line gives an independent size-check. Showing the aligned column subtraction makes the place-value structure explicit.
sourceClaims: Decimal errors in money and measurement contexts stem from whole-number thinking — reading the digits after the point as a separate whole number (the 'longer-is-larger' / whole-number-bias family) — rather than reasoning about each digit's place value; secure work requires place-value reasoning, not memorised digit rules.

KS2 money/measure problems require reading £3.20 as 3 pounds 20 pence (the tenths digit = 20p) and aligning decimal points when calculating; unit conversion (1 kg = 1000 g) links fractions, decimals and measures.
learnerActions: Start with a 2.5 m rope marked on a ruler or number line.
Cut off 0.75 m and predict the remaining length before calculating.
Rewrite 2.5 as 2.50 so both numbers have the same number of decimal places.
Stack 2.50 above 0.75 with the decimal points lined up vertically, then subtract with borrowing.
Read the remaining length (1.75 m) and check it against your prediction on the ruler.
activities.intendedInsight: Decimals with different numbers of decimal places must be aligned on the decimal point before subtracting, because columns must match in place value; writing 2.5 as 2.50 is a helpful way to make the empty hundredths column visible.

activities.title: One mass, two notations: 3/10 of 1 kg
feedback: If 0.3 kg is converted to 30 g or 3000 g, recount the powers of ten: 3/10 of 1000 g is 300 g.
If only the grams (or only the decimal) were given, remember the question asks for both forms of the same mass.
A slider or double number line that lights up 300 g and 0.3 kg together shows they mark the same point.
activities.rationale: Converting both ways and expressing a single mass in two notations targets the unit-slip error and the half-answered question. The double number line keeps 1 kg = 1000 g visible as the anchor.
sourceClaims: KS2 money/measure problems require reading £3.20 as 3 pounds 20 pence (the tenths digit = 20p) and aligning decimal points when calculating; unit conversion (1 kg = 1000 g) links fractions, decimals and measures.
learnerActions: Anchor the fact 1 kg = 1000 g, e.g. on a double number line (kg on one side, g on the other).
Express the same mass as a decimal of a kilogram: 300 g = 0.3 kg.
Convert back the other way too: 0.3 kg = 300 g.
Explain why 300 g and 0.3 kg are two notations for the same amount.
activities.intendedInsight: A quantity can be written as a fraction, as grams, or as a decimal of a kilogram, and converting fluently in both directions depends on anchoring 1 kg = 1000 g.

activities.title: Read the money by place value
feedback: If £3.20 is read as '3 pounds 2 pence', place coins: 2 tenths of a pound is two 10p coins = 20p.
If 2.5 m is read as '2 m and 5 cm', note that 5 tenths of a metre is 50 cm, since 1 m = 100 cm.
On the trap case, £3.5 is £3.50, because the 5 sits in the tenths place.
activities.rationale: This activity confronts the whole-number-bias misconception head-on by making the tenths digit concrete with coins and a ruler. The trap case is a diagnostic discrimination that is immediately resolved in favour of the place-value reading. Coins and a ruler are optional supports that make the tenth tangible; the reasoning is about place value, not the manipulative itself.
sourceClaims: Decimal errors in money and measurement contexts stem from whole-number thinking — reading the digits after the point as a separate whole number (the 'longer-is-larger' / whole-number-bias family) — rather than reasoning about each digit's place value; secure work requires place-value reasoning, not memorised digit rules.

KS2 money/measure problems require reading £3.20 as 3 pounds 20 pence (the tenths digit = 20p) and aligning decimal points when calculating; unit conversion (1 kg = 1000 g) links fractions, decimals and measures.
learnerActions: Look at £3.20 and say what each digit is worth: 3 pounds, 2 tenths of a pound, and 0 hundredths of a pound.
State what the 2 is worth in pence (20p, not 2p) and justify it.
Discuss the trap case: does £3.5 mean 3 pounds 5 pence or 3 pounds 50 pence? Explain which is correct and why.
Model an amount with coins and notes to confirm the tenths of a pound are 10p coins.
Repeat for a length: in 2.5 m, the 5 is 5 tenths of a metre = 50 cm, not 5 cm.
activities.intendedInsight: The digit after the decimal point is tenths of the unit, so the 2 in £3.20 is 20p and the 5 in £3.5 is 50p — not a separate whole number of the smaller unit.

activities.title: Quick checks on money, measure and conversion
feedback: 80p is correct because £3.20 ÷ 4 = 80p; the 12.8p trap comes from treating £3.20 as the bare number 3.2 and multiplying (3.2 × 4 = 12.8) instead of dividing, and the 8p trap from dividing (3.2 ÷ 4 = 0.8) and misreading 0.8 of a pound as 8p rather than 80p.
For 2.50 − 0.75, align the points and exchange 1 one for 10 tenths: the answer is 1.75. A different result usually means the numbers were not lined up by the decimal point or the exchange went wrong.
0.3 kg = 300 g because 1 kg = 1000 g; 30 g or 3000 g uses the wrong power of ten.
activities.rationale: A short recognition/fill check consolidates the procedures and surfaces named error patterns. Recognition and fill-in-the-blank confirm answers but do not by themselves show independent construction of the method, so pairing them with a written step keeps the reasoning visible.
learnerActions: Answer: what is ¼ of £3.20? (Correct: 80p / £0.80. The traps 8p and 12.8p are wrong.)
Fill the blank: 2.50 − 0.75 = ___ m. (Correct: 1.75 m.)
Match 0.3 kg to its equivalent in grams (300 g).
For each, briefly write the step you used so the method is visible, not just the answer.
activities.intendedInsight: These calculations are cleanly checkable, and the wrong options correspond to specific errors (money-as-two-numbers, misalignment, unit slips) worth recognising and avoiding.

constraints: A static labelled shopping or measuring scene with tap-to-reveal can consolidate known facts and act as a reference, but it does not let the child perform the calculation, so it is a scaffold rather than the main activity.

Multiple-choice and fill-in-the-blank items confirm correct answers and catch specific errors, but recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of the method; ask the child to show steps.

Coins, notes, rulers, bar models and double number lines are optional supports that make tenths and conversions tangible; the target reasoning is place value and division, which can also be shown on paper.
Always require the child to show method (how they align the subtraction, how they divide for the fraction), not just the final number, because the method reveals the misconception.
Encourage estimating first to sense-check the size of each answer.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched this session. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One listed source (DfE national curriculum) is marked verified:false / not fetched this session in the original row; its claim is retained only where it directly supports a principle (reading £3.20 as 20p, point alignment, unit conversion), and its evidentiary strength is unconfirmed.

Independent self-audit of arithmetic: ¼ of £3.20 = £3.20 ÷ 4 = 80p (80p × 4 = £3.20 ✓); the 12.8p trap = 3.2 × 4 (bare-number multiply) and the 8p trap = 3.2 ÷ 4 = 0.8 misread as 8p; 2.50 − 0.75 = 1.75 m ✓; 3/10 of 1 kg = 300 g = 0.3 kg ✓; £3.5 = £3.50 (tenths place) ✓. The 8p/12.8p attributions are consistent across activities 1 and 5.

The DfE source claim was removed from the fraction-of-an-amount activity, where it supported only the money topic and not the division principle; it remains where it directly supports reading £3.20 as 20p, point alignment, or unit conversion.

The £3.20-as-20p and £3.5-as-£3.50 prompts deliberately present the misconception as a discrimination to be explained, mirroring the original assessment's probing; each is immediately resolved in favour of the place-value reading in the feedback, so the wrong reading is never left standing as valid.

The original artefact-fit notes claimed depth 'adds nothing' for 3D and that in-role dialogue cannot deliver the insight; these are catalog preferences, not established facts, and have been dropped rather than asserted as universal laws.
The original suggestion to let the child mis-key '£3.20 = 302p' so a coin view corrects it is retained in spirit as an optional error-surfacing interaction, not as a required mechanism.

probeDeeper: In £3.20, what is the 2 worth — 2 pence or 20 pence? How do you know?
Why did you (or should you) write 2.5 as 2.50 before taking away 0.75?
How could you check that 80p really is a quarter of £3.20?
3/10 of 1 kg is 300 g — how do you write that as a decimal part of a kilogram, and why?

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads a money or measure decimal as two whole numbers — '£3.20 is 3 pounds 2 pence', or 2.5 m is '2 m and 5 cm'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild place value: the 2 in £3.20 is 2 tenths of a pound = 20p; 0.5 m is 5 tenths of a metre = 50 cm. Use coins/ruler to make the tenth concrete.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the digit after the point as ones of the smaller unit regardless of place; ¼ of £3.20 comes out as pennies of '3.2', or 2.5 m handled as 2 m 5 cm

errorPatterns.pattern: Misaligns decimals of unequal length when subtracting — lines up 2.5 and 0.75 by their last digits instead of the point
errorPatterns.nextMove: Equalise lengths (2.50) and align on the decimal point, then subtract with borrowing exactly as for whole numbers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Does not rewrite 2.5 as 2.50; subtracts columns that don't match place value; answer like 1.85 or 2.25

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscomputes the fraction of an amount — ¼ of £3.20 by an unclear operation, not £3.20 ÷ 4
errorPatterns.nextMove: Connect 'a quarter of' to dividing by 4 on the bar model; check 80p × 4 = £3.20.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: ¼ of £3.20 ≠ 80p; multiplies by 4, or takes 'a quarter' as 25 of something

errorPatterns.pattern: Unit-conversion slip — 0.3 kg given as 30 g or 3000 g, or grams found but not expressed as a decimal of a kg
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor 1 kg = 1000 g on a double number line; 3/10 of 1000 g = 300 g, and 300 g of 1000 is 0.3 kg.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Wrong power of ten in the kg→g conversion, or only half the question answered

responseLevels.gap: Reads money/measure decimals as two whole numbers and misaligns ragged subtractions; cannot reliably find a fraction of an amount or convert units.
responseLevels.full: Computes all three correctly with place-value reasoning — 80p as £3.20÷4, 1.75 m by aligned subtraction, 300 g = 0.3 kg both ways — estimates to check, and transfers to a new money/measure problem.
responseLevels.partial: Handles one or two parts correctly (e.g. ¼ of £3.20) but slips on the ragged subtraction or the unit conversion, or answers only part of the kilogram question.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Work these out and show your steps. First, what is 1/4 of £3.20? Second, a rope is 2.5 metres long and you cut off 0.75 metres — how much is left? Third, find 3/10 of 1 kilogram, and give the answer both in grams and as a decimal of a kilogram.' Watch the method — especially how they line up 2.5 and 0.75.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The rope (2.5 − 0.75, unequal lengths) exposes decimal misalignment; the money reveals whether the child reads the 2 in £3.20 as 2 tenths of a pound (20p) or as 2 pence; the kilogram question checks unit fluency in both directions. A child who reads decimals as two whole numbers or right-justifies the subtraction gets the rope or the money wrong; a child reasoning by place value gets 80p, 1.75 m and 300 g / 0.3 kg.

sources.claim: Decimal errors in money and measurement contexts stem from whole-number thinking — reading the digits after the point as a separate whole number (the 'longer-is-larger' / whole-number-bias family) — rather than reasoning about each digit's place value; secure work requires place-value reasoning, not memorised digit rules.
sources.source: SMART / Steinle & Stacey, 'Comparing Decimal Numbers' (Specific Mathematics Assessments that Reveal Thinking, University of Melbourne)

sources.claim: KS2 money/measure problems require reading £3.20 as 3 pounds 20 pence (the tenths digit = 20p) and aligning decimal points when calculating; unit conversion (1 kg = 1000 g) links fractions, decimals and measures.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Decimals and fractions (age 10+)
topic.description: Associate a fraction with division and calculate decimal fraction equivalents for simple fractions (e.g. 3/8 = 0.375); recall and use equivalences between simple fractions, decimals, and percentages in different contexts
evidence: Convert 3/8 to 0.375 by dividing 3 ÷ 8
State that 1/5 = 0.2 = 20% from memory
Use fraction–decimal–percentage equivalences to compare 30%, 1/3, and 0.35 and put them in order
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees 3/8 written on a worksheet, can they convert it to a decimal — and also say roughly what percentage that is?

pedagogy.summary: By age 10-11 children must fuse three ideas they have met separately: that a fraction IS a division (a/b = a ÷ b), that dividing gives a decimal, and that fractions, decimals and percentages are three interchangeable names for one quantity. The pedagogical work is not teaching a new procedure but building fluent, flexible movement between the three forms so a child can pick whichever form makes a comparison easiest — e.g. converting 30%, 1/3 and 0.35 to a common form to order them. The load-bearing insight is that the fraction bar means 'divide the top by the bottom', which lets 3/8 be evaluated as 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375.
bestPractices: Establish the fraction-as-division meaning explicitly: 3/8 means 3 shared into 8, and 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375 — connect the bar notation to a division the child can carry out.
Teach a small set of recall equivalents as landmarks (1/2, 1/4, 3/4, 1/5, 1/10, 1/3≈0.33) so children convert by memory for common cases and by division for the rest.
Make ordering across forms the core task: give mixed sets (30%, 1/3, 0.35) and require conversion to ONE common form before comparing — this is where the equivalence pays off.
Use the fact that percentages and decimals are hundredths and tenths to move fluidly (0.35 = 35% = 35/100), reserving division for fractions that aren't already tenths/hundredths.
Confront non-terminating cases honestly: 1/3 = 0.333... is NOT 0.3; round only when told to, and show why the division never stops.
keyRepresentations: Long/short division laid out for 3 ÷ 8 (with the decimal point and trailing zeros) to show a fraction becoming a decimal
A triple-labelled bar or hundred-grid showing the same shaded quantity named as fraction, decimal and percentage at once
A number line from 0 to 1 with fractions, decimals and percentages all plotted, so order is visible spatially
A double number line / equivalence table of the landmark fractions and their decimal & percentage partners
commonMisconceptions: Reverses the division: reads 3/8 as 8 ÷ 3 (divides the larger by the smaller out of habit), giving 2.67 instead of 0.375.
Compares mixed forms by surface digits — thinks 1/3 is largest of {30%, 1/3, 0.35} because '3 is a big number' or because the numbers look bigger, without converting to a common form.
Treats 1/3 as exactly 0.3 (or 0.33) and terminating, not recognising the recurring decimal.
Believes every fraction gives a neat terminating decimal, so is thrown when a division doesn't stop.

learn.summary: For ages 10-11, the goal is fluent, flexible movement between fractions, decimals and percentages as three names for one quantity. The load-bearing insight is that the fraction bar means 'divide the top by the bottom', so 3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375. Learners should pick whichever form makes a comparison easiest, converting a mixed set to one common form before ordering (e.g. 30%, 1/3, 0.35 → 0.30, 0.333..., 0.35, so the order is 30% < 1/3 < 0.35). Note that 1/3 landing between 30% and 0.35 is counter-intuitive and is where the surface-digit misconception is confronted.

activities.title: Watch a fraction become a decimal: 3 ÷ 8
feedback: If you got 2.67, you divided 8 by 3 instead of 3 by 8. Re-read 3/8 as '3 shared among 8', which must be less than one whole — so it is 3 ÷ 8.
Model it concretely: 3 pizzas shared among 8 people gives each person less than half a pizza, so the answer must be below 1.
If you wrote 1/3 = 0.3, keep dividing 1 ÷ 3: the 3s never stop, so 1/3 is a little bigger than 0.3 and bigger than 30%.
If a division doesn't stop, that's expected for fractions like 1/3 — not every fraction gives a neat terminating decimal.
activities.rationale: Connecting bar notation to a division the learner actually carries out builds the fraction-as-division meaning, and watching a recurring case confronts the belief that every fraction terminates. Predicting before dividing surfaces the reversed-division habit at a teachable moment.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils 'associate a fraction with division and calculate decimal fraction equivalents [for example, 0.375] for a simple fraction [for example, 3/8]'; for simple fractions with recurring decimal equivalents pupils learn about rounding to three decimal places (statutory wording + notes).
Fraction-decimal-percentage equivalence and ordering across forms is a key Year 6 structural connection; the fraction bar (vinculum) is understood as a division.

Children commonly reverse fraction-as-division, computing a/b as b/a (dividing the larger by the smaller), rooted in the primitive 'divisor must be smaller than dividend / division makes smaller' model.
learnerActions: Before dividing, predict: will 3/8 be more than 1 or less than 1, and roughly what? Say why (3 shared among 8 people is less than one whole).
Carry out the division 3.000 ÷ 8 step by step, keeping the decimal point and trailing zeros, to reach 0.375.
Compare the result against your prediction. If you predicted more than 1, check whether you divided 3 by 8 or 8 by 3.
Try a case that never stops: carry out 1 ÷ 3 far enough to see 0.333... keep repeating, and note it does NOT equal 0.3.
Round only when told to (e.g. 1/3 ≈ 0.333 to three decimal places), and explain why the division never terminates.
activities.intendedInsight: The fraction bar means 'divide the numerator by the denominator'; 3/8 is 3 ÷ 8, and some divisions (like 1 ÷ 3) produce recurring, non-terminating decimals.

activities.title: Order a mixed set by converting to a common form
feedback: If you ranked 1/3 largest 'because 3 is a big number', convert first: 1/3 = 0.333..., which lands between 0.30 and 0.35.
Comparing by how big the written digits look is unreliable; the number line places each value by its converted size, so the order falls out of position.
To turn 30% into a comparable form, use that per cent means 'out of 100': 30% = 0.30 = 30/100.
If you treated 1/3 as exactly 0.3, place 1/3 and 0.3 as separate points — 1/3 is slightly to the right (0.333... > 0.30), so 1/3 > 30%.
activities.rationale: Ordering across forms is where cross-form equivalence pays off; requiring conversion to a common form before comparing directly targets the documented surface-digit error, and the counter-intuitive placement of 1/3 makes the need to convert felt.
sourceClaims: Comparing and ordering fractions, decimals and percentages requires converting to a common representation; comparing by surface digits (which look bigger) is a persistent, documented error.
Fraction-decimal-percentage equivalence and ordering across forms is a key Year 6 structural connection; the fraction bar (vinculum) is understood as a division.
learnerActions: Take the set 30%, 1/3 and 0.35. First predict the order smallest→largest by eye, and say why.
Convert all three to ONE common form (decimals: 0.30, 0.333..., 0.35), using that percentages are hundredths and division for 1/3.
Plot each converted value on a 0-1 number line and read off the order from position, not appearance.
Compare your conversion-based order (30% < 1/3 < 0.35) with your by-eye prediction and note where they differed — especially whether you expected 1/3 to be biggest.
Transfer the method to a new set, e.g. 30%, 2/5, 0.35: convert each (0.30, 0.40, 0.35) and say where 2/5 goes, and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Different forms cannot be reliably compared by surface digits; converting every item to one common form (then plotting on a line) makes the true order visible — and 1/3 sits between 30% and 0.35.

activities.title: Build a landmark equivalence set
feedback: If you wrote 1/3 = 0.33 exactly, flag it as approximate: the decimal recurs (0.333...), so 1/3 is a touch above 0.33 and above 30%.
Use the hundredths/tenths link to move fluidly: 0.35 = 35% = 35/100 without any new division.
A triple-labelled bar is for consolidating recall; pair it with the division and ordering tasks to practise flexible conversion, not just memory.
activities.rationale: A small set of recalled equivalents reduces load for common conversions so effort can go to the ordering work, and a shared representation reinforces that one quantity has three interchangeable names; noting which landmarks recur keeps rounding honest.
sourceClaims: Fraction-decimal-percentage equivalence and ordering across forms is a key Year 6 structural connection; the fraction bar (vinculum) is understood as a division.

Year 6 pupils 'associate a fraction with division and calculate decimal fraction equivalents [for example, 0.375] for a simple fraction [for example, 3/8]'; for simple fractions with recurring decimal equivalents pupils learn about rounding to three decimal places (statutory wording + notes).
learnerActions: For each landmark, show all three names on one shared bar or hundred-grid so the same shaded quantity is seen as fraction, decimal and percentage at once.

Match a form to its partners from memory (e.g. given 1/5, recall 0.2 and 20%); for fractions that are not landmarks, rewrite them as tenths or hundredths where easy (e.g. 3/20 = 15/100), and otherwise use division.
Note which landmarks are exact and which (like 1/3) are recurring, so you don't record 1/3 as a terminating 0.33.
activities.intendedInsight: Memorised landmark equivalents let you convert common cases instantly, reserving division for less familiar fractions, while a shared visual shows the three forms name one quantity.

constraints: A tap-to-reveal triple-labelled bar of landmark equivalents consolidates recall but does not let the learner choose and carry out a division or order an arbitrary mixed set, so it builds memory rather than the flexible conversion at the heart of this topic — pair it with active division and ordering work.

Recognition and matching checks (e.g. pairing 1/5↔0.2↔20%, or ordering a given set) can confirm the target skill but do not by themselves require the learner to independently construct a conversion; include tasks where the learner carries out 3 ÷ 8 and explains their ordering.
1/3 does not equal 0.3 or exactly 0.33: it is the recurring 0.333..., so it is slightly larger than 30%. Round only when instructed, and treat 33.3% as a rounded value too.
Read 3/8 as 3 ÷ 8 (numerator ÷ denominator), not 8 ÷ 3; the reversed division giving 2.67 is a misconception to correct, never a valid answer.

Interactive panels (a digit-by-digit division display, a draggable 0-1 ordering line, a convert-to-common-form toggle) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; they are helpful illustrations, not required equipment, and the same tasks can be done on paper.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375 (confirmed). The reversed 8 ÷ 3 ≈ 2.666... ≈ 2.67 (confirmed as the misconception distractor, kept only in feedback/diagnosis, never as a valid answer). 1 ÷ 3 = 0.333... recurring (confirmed). Order 0.30 < 0.333... < 0.35, i.e. 30% < 1/3 < 0.35 (confirmed). Transfer set 2/5 = 0.40, so 30% < 0.35 < 2/5 (confirmed).

The source claim about reversing fraction-as-division (Fischbein et al.; Tirosh & Graeber) is marked verified:false in the source row; treat the cited mechanism as informative background, not established fact, in activity 1.
The original stated 1/3 ≈ 0.33 as a landmark; retained but flagged as approximate/recurring (0.333... ≈ 33.3%) to avoid teaching it as terminating or as an exact percentage.

Activity 3's sourceClaims: the NCETM structural-connection claim is the direct support for the three-interchangeable-names/recall principle; the statutory claim is retained only because action 4 covers the recurring/rounding sub-action, and gives partial (sub-action) support, not full principle support. No new source verification was performed.

assess.poeTask: Before dividing: 'I'm going to work out 3/8 as a decimal. First predict — will it be more than 1 or less than 1, and roughly what? Say why.' A child holding fraction-as-division predicts less than 1 (3 shared among 8) near a third-ish; a child reversing the division predicts more than 1 (8÷3). Then carry out 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375 and compare against the prediction — the mismatch is the teachable moment for the reversed-division child.
probeDeeper: You said 3/8 = 0.375 — is that bigger or smaller than 1? How do you know from the fraction itself?
How did you turn 30% into something you could compare with 1/3?
What if I'd asked you to order 30%, 2/5 and 0.35 instead — where would 2/5 go, and why?
Someone says 1/3 must be the biggest because 3 is the biggest number in the list. What would you say to them?
assess.correctAnswer: 3/8 = 0.375, found by dividing 3 ÷ 8. Order: 30% < 1/3 < 0.35 (i.e. 0.30 < 0.333... < 0.35), compared by converting all three to the same form — decimals: 0.30, 0.333..., 0.35.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the fraction-as-division: 'I divide the big number by the small one, so 3/8 is 8 ÷ 3 = 2.67' — divides larger by smaller out of whole-number habit.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the meaning of the bar: 3/8 is 3 things shared among 8, which must be less than one, so it is 3 ÷ 8. Model with 3 pizzas shared by 8 people before re-doing the division.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 3/8 = 2.6 or 2.67, or says 'it's more than 1', and the shown method divides 8 by 3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares mixed forms by surface digits: 'the biggest is 1/3 because 3, and 0.35 is smallest because it's tiny decimals' — ranks by how big the visible digits look rather than converting to a common form.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on converting all three to one form first; use a 0-1 number line and plot each after converting, so the child sees the ordering fall out of position, not appearance.
errorPatterns.distractor: 1/3 < 0.35 < 30% (ordered by how small the written numbers look)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders without converting, e.g. places 1/3 largest or 0.35 smallest; explanation cites the size of the digits, not a common form.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats 1/3 as exactly 0.3 and terminating: 'one third is 0.3, so it's less than 0.35 and equal to 30%' — collapses the recurring decimal to one tenth.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Carry out 1 ÷ 3 far enough to see 0.333... never stop; place 1/3 and 0.3 as distinct points on the line and show 1/3 is a little bigger than 0.3, hence bigger than 30%.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 1/3 = 0.3 and consequently rates 1/3 = 30%, or cannot decide between 1/3 and 30%.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot convert 3/8 (or reverses to 8÷3), and orders the mixed set by appearance of digits with no conversion; cannot say how the three forms relate.
responseLevels.full: Divides 3÷8 = 0.375 the right way round, converts all of 30%, 1/3, 0.35 to a common form, orders them 30% < 1/3 < 0.35, and explains that comparison requires a shared form — transferring the method to a new item (e.g. 2/5) without prompting.
responseLevels.partial: Converts 3/8 correctly and knows the landmark equivalents, and can name each form, but when ordering the mixed set either doesn't convert to a common form or converts only some, so the ordering is unreliable and the comparison isn't explained.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Convert 3/8 to a decimal and show how you got it. Then take 30%, 1/3 and 0.35, put them in order from smallest to largest, and tell me how you compared them.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who genuinely holds fraction-as-division and cross-form equivalence divides 3÷8 the right way round AND converts the mixed set to a common form before ordering. A child operating on surface features reveals it two ways that a correct reasoner never would: dividing 8÷3 (bigger-by-smaller habit) and ranking 1/3 as largest 'because 3'. The reason-tier ('how you compared them') is what separates a lucky ordering from real equivalence reasoning — 1/3 sitting between 30% and 0.35 is counter-intuitive, so getting it right for a stated reason is hard to fake.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Decimals and fractions (age 11+)
topic.description: Work interchangeably with terminating decimals and their corresponding fractions (such as 3.5 and 7/2 or 0.375 and 3/8); convert fluently between the two forms
evidence: Convert any terminating decimal to a fraction in simplest form
Convert any fraction with a denominator whose prime factors are only 2 and 5 to a terminating decimal
Explain why some fractions produce terminating decimals and others do not
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees 0.375 on a calculator display, can they convert it to a fraction in its simplest form — without using the calculator?

pedagogy.summary: A terminating decimal IS a fraction with a power-of-ten denominator: 0.375 = 375/1000, which simplifies to 3/8. Converting a fraction to a decimal is division (3 ÷ 8 = 0.375) or, equivalently, scaling the denominator up to 10, 100, 1000… Whether a fraction terminates is decided entirely by the prime factors of its denominator in lowest terms: only 2 and 5 (the prime factors of ten) give a terminating decimal; any other prime factor (3, 7, 11…) produces a recurring decimal. Fractions, decimals and percentages are three notations for one value.
bestPractices: Read a decimal by its LAST place value to get the denominator (0.375 = 375 thousandths), then simplify to lowest terms
Teach fraction→decimal two ways — as division (numerator ÷ denominator) AND as scaling the denominator to a power of ten (3/8 = 375/1000 via ×125)
Make the '2s and 5s only' test explicit by contrasting terminators (1/8, 1/20, 1/40) with recurrers (1/3, 1/6, 1/7) and factorising each denominator
Treat FDP as three views of one number on a triple number line so conversion is re-notation, not new arithmetic
Show a recurring decimal actually recurring (1/3 = 0.333…) so children do not truncate it and call it exact
keyRepresentations: Place-value columns (tenths, hundredths, thousandths)
Prime-factor trees of denominators
Short division for fraction→decimal
FDP triple number line / equivalence cards
Hundredths and thousandths grids
commonMisconceptions: Reads 0.375 as 375/100 (denominator doesn't match the last place value)
Inverts the division, computing 8 ÷ 3 instead of 3 ÷ 8
Believes every fraction terminates, or truncates a recurring decimal (1/3 = 0.3) and treats it as exact
Decides whether a decimal terminates from the numerator or 'how neat it looks' rather than the denominator's prime factors

learn.summary: Terminating decimals and fractions are two notations for one value, with percentages a third. A terminating decimal is read by its LAST place value to get a power-of-ten denominator (0.375 = 375/1000), then simplified (= 3/8). Converting a fraction to a decimal is division (3 ÷ 8 = 0.375) or, equivalently, scaling the denominator up to a power of ten (3/8 = 375/1000 via ×125). The deep idea: a fraction in lowest terms terminates exactly when its denominator's only prime factors are 2 and/or 5 (the primes of ten); any other prime factor (3, 7, 11…) makes it recur. Learners should both convert fluently in both directions AND predict termination from the denominator's prime factorisation, not by dividing and guessing.

activities.title: Scale to a power of ten — does it land?
feedback: If a learner says 1/6 stops: factorise 6 = 2×3. The factor 3 is not 2 or 5, so no power of ten is a multiple of 6 and the decimal recurs (0.1666…). Show it recurring rather than truncating to 0.17.

If they truncate a recurring decimal and call it exact (1/3 = 0.3): run the division further so the 3s keep coming; 0.333… is not equal to 0.3. (Year 6 learners meet rounding recurring decimals to three decimal places — rounding is an approximation, not the exact value.)

If they decide termination from the numerator or 'how neat it looks': remind them the numerator is irrelevant once the fraction is simplified — only the lowest-terms denominator's prime factors decide.
activities.rationale: Contrasting a fraction that scales onto a power of ten against one that never does, with prime-factor readouts shown together, is intended to make the 2-and-5 rule discoverable rather than merely asserted; sorting fractions and factorising each denominator is a documented route to the rule.
sourceClaims: A fraction IN LOWEST TERMS gives a terminating decimal if and only if its denominator's only prime factors are 2 and/or 5; the reason is base-10 (10 = 2x5), so the denominator terminates exactly when it divides a power of ten. Sorting fractions into terminating/recurring columns and writing each denominator as its prime factorisation makes the rule discoverable; the numerator is irrelevant and the fraction must be simplified first.

Year 6 pupils 'associate a fraction with division and calculate decimal fraction equivalents [0.375] for a simple fraction [3/8]'; for simple fractions with recurring decimal equivalents they learn about rounding to three decimal places - so recurring decimals are met and must not be treated as terminating.
learnerActions: Take 1/8 and try to turn it into tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths: find the multiplier (×125) that makes the denominator 1000, giving 125/1000 = 0.125; confirm it 'lands' exactly.
Now try 1/3 the same way: aim for 10, 100, 1000… and find that no power of ten works; carry out the division 1 ÷ 3 and watch the 3s continue (0.333…), a recurring decimal that never stops.
Write each denominator as a product of primes side by side: 8 = 2×2×2; 6 = 2×3; 3 = 3. Mark which denominators are built only from 2s and 5s.
State the rule you discover in your own words, then test it on 1/20, 1/40 (should terminate) and 1/6, 1/7 (should recur), factorising each denominator first.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction in lowest terms terminates exactly when its denominator is built only from the primes 2 and/or 5 — because those are the primes of ten, so the denominator can be scaled to a power of ten. Any other prime factor forces a recurring decimal.

activities.title: Read a decimal by its last place value
feedback: If a learner writes 0.375 = 375/100: the last digit (5) sits in the thousandths place, so the denominator is 1000, not 100. Re-read several decimals aloud by their final place value before writing the fraction.

If they invert the division and compute 8 ÷ 3 for 3/8 (getting 2.66…): re-establish that a/b means a ÷ b — numerator divided by denominator — grounded in sharing 3 wholes among 8 people, which gives less than one each (0.375).
activities.rationale: Anchoring the denominator to the last place value is intended to address the most common conversion error (reading onto the wrong power of ten), and practising division-as-conversion in the reverse direction aims to reinforce fraction-as-division, a documented sticking point.
sourceClaims: Converting a fraction to a decimal is the division numerator / denominator (fraction-as-division); understanding fractions as division underpins decimal equivalence and is a documented sticking point.

Year 6 pupils 'associate a fraction with division and calculate decimal fraction equivalents [0.375] for a simple fraction [3/8]'; for simple fractions with recurring decimal equivalents they learn about rounding to three decimal places - so recurring decimals are met and must not be treated as terminating.
learnerActions: Name the place value of the LAST digit of 0.375 (thousandths), so the starting denominator is 1000: write 0.375 = 375/1000.
Simplify stepwise to lowest terms: 375/1000 = 3/8 (divide both by 125). Check the simplified fraction against the original decimal.
Repeat with other decimals (0.2 = 2/10 = 1/5; 0.25 = 25/100 = 1/4; 0.35 = 35/100 = 7/20), each time naming the last place value first.
Reverse the direction: convert 3/8 to a decimal two ways — divide 3 ÷ 8, and scale 3/8 to 375/1000 — and confirm both give 0.375.
activities.intendedInsight: A terminating decimal IS a fraction with a power-of-ten denominator; reading the last place value gives that denominator, and simplifying gives lowest terms. Fraction→decimal is division (numerator ÷ denominator), equivalently scaling to a power of ten.

activities.title: Sort, match and fill the gaps (consolidation)
feedback: If a learner sorts by dividing and rounding: that only shows what happens to begin with, not whether it stops forever. Ask them to factorise the denominator in lowest terms and apply the 2-and-5 test instead.
If a chain step is wrong, point back to the place-value reading (last digit → denominator) and the simplification factor (×125 or ÷125).
activities.rationale: Matching, categorising and fill-in-and-explain tasks give repeated, checkable practice across both directions and foreground the structural (prime-factor) test over empirical division; the fill-in step asks the learner to produce values and explain each one, so this activity consolidates and partly requires articulation of the discovered rule, not its first teaching.
sourceClaims: A fraction IN LOWEST TERMS gives a terminating decimal if and only if its denominator's only prime factors are 2 and/or 5; the reason is base-10 (10 = 2x5), so the denominator terminates exactly when it divides a power of ten. Sorting fractions into terminating/recurring columns and writing each denominator as its prime factorisation makes the rule discoverable; the numerator is irrelevant and the fraction must be simplified first.
learnerActions: Match terminating decimals to their simplest fractions: 0.375 ↔ 3/8, 0.2 ↔ 1/5, 0.25 ↔ 1/4.
Sort a set of fractions into two columns, 'terminates' and 'recurs', by inspecting each denominator's prime factors (not by dividing): e.g. 7/40 and 1/20 terminate; 5/12 and 1/6 recur.
Fill in the chain 0.375 = __/1000 = __/8, then explain each step (last place value → denominator, then the ÷125 simplification).

Transfer to unfamiliar fractions: predict whether 9/25, 4/15 and 6/15 terminate, justify from the prime factors of each denominator in lowest terms (6/15 = 2/5), then check by converting (9/25 = 0.36; 4/15 = 0.2666…; 6/15 = 0.4).
activities.intendedInsight: Bidirectional conversion to simplest form becomes fluent, and the terminate/recur judgement is made from the denominator's prime factors rather than by trial division.

activities.title: Predict and justify: will it stop? (optional discussion)
feedback: Accept only reasons that cite the denominator's prime factors; 'it looks neat' or 'I tried dividing' is not a structural justification.
If the learner can convert but cannot say why 1/8 stops and 1/6 does not, return to factorising the two denominators side by side.
activities.rationale: A short predict-and-justify exchange is proposed to supplement procedural practice by targeting the 'why do some fractions never stop?' reasoning; it supplements rather than replaces conversion practice, since the objective is procedural fluency. Its effect on reasoning is untested here.
learnerActions: Before converting, predict aloud whether a given fraction (e.g. 1/6, 7/40, 5/12) terminates or recurs, and say WHY from the denominator.
Justify the prediction by naming the prime factors of the denominator and relating them to the primes of ten (2 and 5).
Have a partner or adult pose the question 'How could you know without doing the whole division?' and respond with a reasoned argument, then check by converting.
activities.intendedInsight: Verbalising the prediction and its reason is intended to reveal whether the learner reasons from structure (prime factors) or merely from procedures; articulating the reason aims to strengthen the conceptual link, though that effect is not established here.

constraints: Recurring decimals must be shown genuinely recurring (1/3 = 0.333…); do not truncate (0.3 or 0.33) and call it exact. Rounding a recurring decimal to a set number of places is an approximation introduced for Year 6, not the exact value.
The 2-and-5 rule applies only to the denominator IN LOWEST TERMS; simplify first and ignore the numerator when judging termination.

Matching is recognition-and-recall practice, a sort checks classification of denominators, and a fill-in chain asks the learner to produce values; on their own these task types do not require the learner to carry out a full conversion in both directions and articulate the reason, so pair them with at least one activity where the learner constructs and explains a full conversion and a termination prediction (as the fill-in-and-explain and predict-and-justify steps do).

A tap-to-reveal equivalence card (fraction → decimal → percentage with denominator prime factors) is a useful reference aid but cannot let a learner test the terminate/recur boundary themselves; use it alongside, not instead of, the scaling/conversion work.
Fraction-as-division must be the direction numerator ÷ denominator (3 ÷ 8), not denominator ÷ numerator.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and no claim of empirical testing is made.

Legacy design described two linked on-screen panels (scale-to-power-of-ten with a prime-factor readout, and place-value decimal-to-fraction simplifier) with a 'lights up/it fits' response. These interaction examples are preserved as optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; they are not mandatory. A fixed printed chart can still teach the conversions even though it cannot be manipulated.

The legacy source framed interactive scaling as the way the rule 'clicks' and rated dialogue/3D as weaker. Those comparative fit judgements are catalog preferences, not established efficacy; the alternatives are kept here as activities with stated purposes and limits rather than as a ranking.

Editorial change: efficacy-asserting wording in the activity rationales and in activity[3]'s intendedInsight ('removes the error', 'reinforces', 'strengthening the conceptual link') was softened to intended/aims wording, since the sources identify the misconceptions/sticking points but do not establish that these specific activities fix them.

Self-audit of arithmetic and logic: 0.375 = 375/1000 = 3/8 (÷125) is correct; 3/8 = 0.375 is correct; 1/8 = 0.125 via ×125 to 125/1000 is correct; 8 = 2³, 6 = 2×3, 3 = 3 are correct; 1/6 = 0.1666… recurs (3 is not 2 or 5) is correct; 7/40 terminates (40 = 2³×5) and 5/12 recurs (12 = 2²×3) are correct; 0.2=1/5, 0.25=1/4, 0.35=7/20 are correct; 8 ÷ 3 = 2.66… correctly identifies the inverted-division error. No arithmetic errors found in learner-facing content.

probeDeeper: What place value is the last digit of 0.375 in? So what denominator do you start with before simplifying?
For 3/8, which number do you divide by which — and why that way round?
Will 1/6 stop or go on forever? What is it about the 6 that tells you, without dividing all the way?
1/8 stops but 1/3 does not. What is different about the denominators when you break each into prime factors?
assess.correctAnswer: 0.375 = 375/1000 = 3/8 (dividing by 125); 3/8 = 0.375 (3 ÷ 8, or ×125 to make 375/1000). 1/6 does NOT stop — 6 = 2×3, and the factor 3 is not 2 or 5, so it recurs (0.1666…).

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the decimal onto the wrong power of ten: 0.375 = 375/100
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the last digit's place (thousandths), so the denominator is 1000; then simplify. Re-read several decimals by their final place value.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denominator does not match the last digit's place value; the simplified fraction is wrong or won't simplify to 3/8

errorPatterns.pattern: Inverts the division for fraction→decimal: computes 8 ÷ 3 for 3/8
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-establish fraction-as-division: a/b means a ÷ b (numerator into denominator), grounded in sharing 3 wholes among 8.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Divides the larger number by the smaller, or gets 2.66… for 3/8

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges whether a fraction terminates from the numerator or how 'neat' it looks, or believes every fraction terminates — so claims 1/6 stops, or truncates it to 0.17 and calls it exact
errorPatterns.nextMove: Factorise the denominators side by side (8 = 2³ terminates; 6 = 2×3 recurs) and connect 2 and 5 to the primes of ten; show 1/6 genuinely recurring.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 1/6 stops; decides by trying to divide and rounding rather than by the denominator's prime factors; cannot explain WHY 1/8 stops but 1/6 does not

responseLevels.gap: Mis-reads the decimal's denominator or inverts the division; believes all fractions terminate; cannot connect terminating to the denominator.
responseLevels.full: Converts both directions fluently to simplest form AND predicts termination from the denominator's prime factorisation (only 2 and 5), explaining why (it can be scaled to a power of ten); transfers to a new fraction such as 7/40 (terminates) or 5/12 (recurs).
responseLevels.partial: Converts 0.375 ↔ 3/8 correctly by procedure, but decides termination empirically by dividing and rounding rather than from the denominator's prime factors, or states the 2-and-5 rule only after prompting.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Convert 0.375 to a fraction in its simplest form, and convert 3/8 to a decimal. Then tell me — will 1/6 give a decimal that stops, or one that goes on forever? How could you know without doing the whole division?' Watch how they work and listen to the reason for 1/6.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Converting 0.375 both ways is routine and does not separate understanding from memorised steps. The 1/6 question is the hinge: a child who grasps the structure inspects the denominator's prime factors (only 2 and 5 terminate) and answers WITHOUT dividing; a child who has only procedures tries to divide and rounds, guesses, or asserts that all fractions stop. Reasoning correctly and reasoning wrongly give visibly different responses here.

sources.claim: A fraction IN LOWEST TERMS gives a terminating decimal if and only if its denominator's only prime factors are 2 and/or 5; the reason is base-10 (10 = 2x5), so the denominator terminates exactly when it divides a power of ten. Sorting fractions into terminating/recurring columns and writing each denominator as its prime factorisation makes the rule discoverable; the numerator is irrelevant and the fraction must be simplified first.
sources.source: NRICH (Univ. of Cambridge / Millennium Mathematics Project), 'Terminating or Not' (ages 11-14)

sources.source: DfE, National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study, Year 6
