topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Fractions, Decimals & Percentages
topic.description: Look for and use mathematical structure: exploit the relationship between fractions, decimals, and percentages; use factor pairs to simplify multiplication; apply angle facts to find unknowns; use properties of regular polygons systematically
evidence: Use the structure 25 × 16 = 25 × 4 × 4 = 100 × 4 = 400 by exploiting factor pairs
Recognise that 0.75 = 3/4 = 75% and use whichever form is most efficient for the problem
Use the fact that angles on a straight line sum to 180° as a structural tool to find missing angles
topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} notices that fractions, decimals, and percentages are just different ways of writing the same thing, do they use that understanding to switch between them fluidly when it makes a calculation easier?

pedagogy.summary: At 9-10, using structure is about choosing the most efficient form or route by exploiting relationships: rewriting 25×16 as 25×4×4 = 100×4 = 400 via factor pairs, treating 0.75, 3/4 and 75% as one quantity in three dresses and picking whichever makes the problem easy, and deploying angle facts (angles on a line sum to 180°) as deductive tools instead of measuring. The pedagogy is to make the strategic saving visible — compare the clever route against the grind — and to build fluency moving between fraction/decimal/percentage forms so the child reaches for the handiest one.
bestPractices: Show 25×16 both ways — the column algorithm and the 25×4×4 = 100×4 regrouping — so the factor-pair route is felt as a shortcut, not a trick
Use a triple number line / double-sided cards linking 0.75 = 3/4 = 75% so the forms are interchangeable and the child selects by convenience
Present missing-angle problems where measuring is awkward so the child must deduce from 180°/360°/vertically-opposite facts
Ask 'which form / which route makes this easiest, and why?' so structure use is a deliberate choice
keyRepresentations: Factor trees and factor-pair regrouping (16 = 4×4; 25×4 = 100)
Triple representation of FDP (bar, number line, and 0.75 / 3⁄₄ / 75% cards)
Angle diagrams with a straight line / point as the structural constraint
Area/array models linking factors to products
commonMisconceptions: Runs the standard column algorithm for 25×16 without looking for factor pairs that make it a mental step
Converts laboriously every time instead of recognising 0.75, 3/4 and 75% as the same number
Measures a missing angle with a protractor rather than deducing it from an angle fact
Picks the fraction/decimal/percentage form by habit rather than by which is efficient for the task

learn.summary: For ages 9-10, 'using structure' means deliberately choosing an efficient route or form by exploiting relationships rather than grinding: rewriting 25×16 as 25×4×4 = 100×4 = 400 via factor pairs; treating 0.75, 3/4 and 75% as one quantity and picking whichever form makes a task a one-step job; and deducing missing angles from facts (angles on a straight line sum to 180°, around a point 360°, vertically opposite angles equal) instead of measuring. The core teaching move is to make the strategic saving visible — run the clever route alongside the grind — and to build fluent movement between fraction/decimal/percentage forms so the child reaches for the handiest one and can say why.

activities.title: Factor-pair regrouping run beside the column method
feedback: If the child runs column multiplication without regrouping, explore the factor pairs of 16 (4×4, 2×8) and the fact 25×4 = 100; lay it out on an array so the friendly 100 appears visibly.
If the child cannot name why 25 and 16 are a convenient pair, prompt: 'What times 25 gives 100? Can 16 be split to hand you that factor?'

For 23×16, affirm that there is no clean pairing to a hundred here: 23 is prime, so its only factor pair is 1×23, and neither 23 nor 16 is a factor of 100. 23 can still be split by adding (20 + 3) for a different method, but no factor pair builds 100 — this explains why 25×16 is a special case, not a universal trick.
activities.rationale: Showing the shortcut and the long method side by side lets the saving be felt rather than asserted, and testing a non-example checks the child understands the condition that enables the structure, supporting deliberate choice of efficient methods.
sourceClaims: Proficient students look for and make use of structure, e.g. rewriting expressions and seeing composed objects, to solve efficiently rather than by brute computation
Pupils should recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships and choose efficient methods; teaching should compare representations and strategies for efficiency
learnerActions: Work out 25×16 without the column algorithm, splitting 16 into 4×4, then pairing one 4 with 25 to make 100, so the product collapses to 100×4 = 400 in two moves
Carry out the column method for 25×16 as well, and compare how many steps each route took
State the 'hinge' that made the shortcut work (25×4 = 100) and explain why spotting it saved effort
Try the same thinking on 50×16 and 25×24: regroup each to a friendly round number (50×2×8 = 100×8 = 800; 25×4×6 = 100×6 = 600) and show the route
Test a non-example, 23×16: try to find a neat factor pair to a hundred and explain why 25×16 is 'luckier'
activities.intendedInsight: A hard-looking multiplication can dissolve when you spot a factor pair that builds a friendly round number (here 25×4 = 100); recognising WHAT makes a shortcut available is the skill, not just reaching the answer.

activities.title: One quantity in three forms: choose the handiest
feedback: If the child converts 75% to 0.75 and multiplies laboriously, show the 3/4 route (£80 ÷ 4 = £20, ×3 = £60) and ask which took fewer steps.
If the child always uses the same form, pose numbers where each form wins in turn so the 'it depends on the numbers' idea surfaces.
Praise reasoning that names why a form fits — e.g. '3/4 suits £80 because 80 divides by 4 cleanly.'
activities.rationale: Lining the three forms up as one point and asking for a justified choice targets flexible, efficient selection rather than rote conversion, matching the aim of choosing efficient methods and comparing representations.
sourceClaims: Pupils should recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships and choose efficient methods; teaching should compare representations and strategies for efficiency
learnerActions: Look at a single amount shown at once as 3/4, 0.75 and 75% (on a bar or number line marking the same point) and confirm they are one number
Find 75% of £80 and decide whether to use 75%, 0.75 or 3/4; show that 3/4 gives ÷4 then ×3 = £60 in one line
For 30% of £90, decide between 0.3, 3/10 or 30% and justify the choice (3/10 of £90 = £27)
Then try 12.5% of £80 and notice whether the handiest form changes (e.g. 1/8 of 80 = £10), explaining why the best form depends on the numbers
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction, decimal and percentage can name the same quantity, so a flexible solver selects whichever form makes the particular numbers easiest instead of converting by habit.

activities.title: Deduce missing angles instead of measuring
feedback: If the child reaches for a protractor, present a diagram drawn not-to-scale or with an angle off the page so measuring fails and the fact must be used.
Prompt 'What do these angles add up to, or which pair must be equal?' to surface the structural constraint before working it out.
If a regular polygon is involved, draw attention to the repeated equal angles so one deduction covers several.
activities.rationale: Posing problems where measurement is impractical forces reliance on the angle fact as a structural tool, building deductive reasoning over measurement.
sourceClaims: Proficient students look for and make use of structure, e.g. rewriting expressions and seeing composed objects, to solve efficiently rather than by brute computation
learnerActions: Given a diagram where measuring is awkward or impossible, find the missing angle by using a fact (angles on a straight line sum to 180°, around a point 360°, or vertically opposite angles equal)
Name which fact you leaned on and show the working (e.g. 180° − known angle, or 'these two are vertically opposite so they are equal')
Explain how you know the answer is right without a protractor

Extend to a regular polygon: use its equal angles/sides with a known fact (e.g. one given angle, or the equal angles at the centre adding up to 360°) to find unknown angles systematically rather than measuring each one
activities.intendedInsight: Angle facts are deductive tools: depending on the fact you either subtract the given parts from a known total (180° on a line, 360° around a point) or set vertically opposite angles equal — both give an exact answer, unlike the approximation of measuring.

activities.title: Explain the choice: a tap-to-reveal and short explanation
feedback: Accept any correct route, but press for the reason: a strong response names the hinge (25×4 = 100) or the fitting form (3/4 for a ÷4-friendly number).
If the explanation is missing, replay the two routes side by side and ask which took fewer steps and why.
A reference card and angle-fact diagram can consolidate recall, but follow with a problem that requires choosing a route so the child demonstrates selection, not just recognition.
activities.rationale: A reveal/match format and a short explanation question consolidate equivalences and surface the reasoning behind the chosen route; because both 400 and £60 are reachable by grinding, articulating the reason is what distinguishes structural from procedural work.
learnerActions: Match or reveal FDP equivalents (0.75 = 3/4 = 75%) and annotate a worked angle diagram to consolidate the facts
After solving, answer 'which route/form did you choose and why was it quickest?' in your own words
Compare your chosen route against a slower alternative and state what made the difference
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to state WHY a route is efficient — not just getting the answer — is the sign of structural thinking; the answer alone can be reached by grinding.

constraints: Reference cards, FDP match tasks and static angle-fact posters consolidate recall but do not let the child test alternative routes or feel the efficiency difference; pair them with problems that require choosing a method and explaining the choice.

Scored matching or 'which route is quickest?' items can check the structural choice but can mask whether efficiency was actually reasoned; always ask the child to say why, so recognition is not mistaken for independent construction.

The 25×4 = 100 factor-pair shortcut is specific: it works because 25 is a factor of 100 and 16 splits to supply the needed 4. State this condition and include non-examples (e.g. 23×16) so the move is not over-generalised as a universal trick.
The best FDP form is numbers-dependent (3/4 suits £80, 1/8 suits 12.5% of £80); do not teach a single 'always use' form.

Factor regrouping, FDP equivalence and these angle facts live in number lines, arrays and 2D diagrams; a 3D model is not needed here, though this reflects the topic's flat content rather than a general rule about 3D.

Open discussion alone gives the child no numbers, bars or diagrams to regroup or manipulate; these activities need those representations present, which does not imply dialogue cannot support the reasoning.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy source framed open conversation and 3D as 'poor' and claimed a quiz 'hides' reasoning; these are reframed as scoped limits (the tasks need concrete numbers; this topic's content is flat; scores can mask reasoning so pair with an explanation probe) rather than universal laws about media.

The 23×16 non-example is retained as a check on the shortcut's condition: 23 is prime and neither it nor 16 is a factor of 100, so no clean pairing to a hundred exists — this is the intended teaching point.

Activity 3's intended insight covers both deduction types so vertically opposite angles (found by equality) are not misdescribed as 'total minus parts', keeping the stated insight consistent with every method the child uses.

Independent re-audit: arithmetic, units, the FDP equivalences, angle facts and the factor-pair condition were re-checked and are internally consistent; no categorical medium-superiority claims remain and efficacy wording stays qualified.

probeDeeper: Ask 'would the factor-pair trick help for 25×24 or 50×16 too? how would you regroup those?' to test whether the structure generalises
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'for 23×16 is there a neat factor pair to a hundred? why is 25×16 luckier?' to check the child understands WHAT makes the shortcut available
Ask 'to find 30% of £90 would you use 0.3, 3/10 or 30%? does your choice change if it's 12.5% of £80?' to probe deliberate form selection
Ask 'how do you know the missing angle without measuring? what fact are you leaning on?' to surface the structural constraint
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for exploiting factor pairs (25×16 = 25×4×4 = 100×4 = 400 because 25×4 makes 100) and for choosing 3/4 of £80 as easiest (÷4 then ×3 = £60) with a reason about which form suits the number. The reasoning about WHY the route is efficient is the target.

errorPatterns.pattern: Does not spot the factor pair and runs the standard algorithm for 25×16, because 16 is not seen as 4×4 or 25 as a quarter of 100
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explore factor pairs of 16 and the fact 25×4=100; regroup on an array so the friendly 100 appears
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child sets out column multiplication rather than regrouping; cannot say what makes 25 and 16 a convenient pair

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats 0.75, 3/4 and 75% as separate things to convert each time rather than one number, so no efficient form is chosen
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line up the three forms on one bar/number line as the same point; practise picking the form that fits the given number
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child laboriously converts 75% to a decimal and multiplies, unaware 3/4 gives a one-line answer for £80

errorPatterns.pattern: Reaches for a protractor to find a missing angle instead of deducing it from angles on a line summing to 180°
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pose diagrams where measuring is awkward or impossible so the angle fact must be used as a tool; subtract from the known total
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Given a missing-angle diagram, the child measures rather than subtracting from 180°/360°

responseLevels.gap: Column-multiplies 25×16, converts every FDP form from scratch, and measures missing angles; no structural shortcut sought
responseLevels.full: Spontaneously spots the factor pair and names the hinge (25×4=100), selects the handiest FDP form with a reason, and deduces angles from facts — transferring 'what structure makes this easy?' to new numbers and diagrams
responseLevels.partial: Can use a factor pair, switch FDP form, or apply an angle fact when prompted, but does not choose the efficient route independently or explain why it is efficient

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work out 25 × 16 in the cleverest way you can — no column method — and tell me how you spotted the shortcut. Then: to find 75% of £80, would you rather work with 75%, 0.75 or 3/4, and why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Both 400 and £60 are reachable by grinding; what discriminates is whether the child SPOTS the factor pair / chooses the handy form and can articulate why. A structural thinker names 25×4=100 as the hinge and picks 3/4 for a ÷4-friendly number; a non-structural one column-multiplies and converts 75% laboriously.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Mixed numbers and improper fractions
topic.description: Recognise mixed numbers and improper fractions; convert from one form to the other (e.g. 2/5 + 4/5 = 6/5 = 1 1/5)
evidence: Convert 11/4 to 2 3/4
Convert 3 2/5 to 17/5
Write 6/5 + 4/5 = 10/5 = 2 as both improper fraction and whole number
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees the fraction 9/4, can they convert it to a mixed number — and then turn 2 and 3/5 back into an improper fraction?

pedagogy.summary: A mixed number (2¾) and an improper fraction (11/4) name the SAME quantity in two forms; converting between them rests on 'how many wholes fit', because b/b = 1 whole. So 11/4 = 8/4 + 3/4 = 2 wholes and 3/4 = 2¾; reversing, 3⅖ = 3 wholes = 15 fifths, plus 2 fifths = 17/5. It is grounded in iterating unit fractions past the whole (counting quarters past 4/4) and in recognising that b copies of 1/b rebuild one whole.
bestPractices: Build from unit-fraction iteration on a number line or bar — count quarters past 4/4 = 1 whole — so the child SEES wholes forming inside an improper fraction
Make 'b bths = 1 whole' explicit, so 11/4 groups into wholes and 3 wholes = 15 fifths is understood, not memorised
Teach mixed→improper as 'each whole is b bths' (3 wholes × 5 = 15 fifths, add the 2) rather than a bare '× then add' trick; keep the denominator unchanged
Always verify by converting back (17/5 → 3⅖) so the two forms are seen as equal
Treat improper fractions as legitimate numbers, not mistakes to be 'fixed'
keyRepresentations: Number line with unit-fraction jumps continuing past 1 whole
Fraction bars/tiles where b pieces fuse into one whole tile
Area circles showing 11/4 as two full circles plus three quarters
Improper fraction and mixed number marked at the SAME point
commonMisconceptions: Mixed→improper adds the whole to the numerator: 3⅖ → (3+2)/5 = 5/5
Multiplies but forgets to add the numerator (15/5), or concatenates the digits (32/5)
Improper→mixed miscounts the wholes (e.g. 11/4 → 3¾)
Believes an improper fraction is 'not allowed' and must always be written as a mixed number
Changes the denominator during conversion

learn.summary: A mixed number (2¾) and an improper fraction (11/4) name the same quantity in two forms. Converting between them rests on 'how many wholes fit', because b copies of 1/b rebuild one whole (b/b = 1). So 11/4 = 8/4 + 3/4 = 2 wholes and 3/4 = 2¾; reversing, 3⅖ = 3 wholes = 15 fifths, plus 2 fifths = 17/5. Ground the work in iterating unit fractions past the whole (counting quarters past 4/4) rather than a bare rule, and treat improper fractions as legitimate numbers.

activities.title: Stamp quarters past the whole and watch wholes form
feedback: If a learner writes 3⅖ = 5/5, rebuild the 3 wholes as fifths on the bar: one whole is 5 fifths (not 1), so 3 wholes = 15 fifths, then add the 2 → 17/5.
If a learner writes 15/5, praise the ×b step (three wholes make fifteen fifths) and prompt the missing step: 'now add the two more fifths'.
If a learner writes 32/5, point out that gluing the 3 and 2 together ignores what the digits count; ask how many fifths are in 3 wholes.
If a learner reads 11/4 as 3¾ or subtracts 11 − 4, group the eleven quarters into fours on the bar: two complete groups of four (2 wholes) with three quarters left.

As an alternative representation, show 11/4 as area circles: two fully shaded circles plus three quarters of a third circle give the same 2¾ — another way to see the wholes already sitting inside the improper fraction.
Always close by converting back (17/5 → 3⅖, or 2¾ → 11/4) to confirm the two forms are equal.
activities.rationale: Building from unit-fraction iteration lets the child SEE wholes forming inside an improper fraction, so conversion is understood as regrouping rather than a half-remembered digit trick. Making 'b bths = 1 whole' explicit is intended to target the add-to-numerator error by showing a whole becoming b pieces rather than one.
sourceClaims: Improper fractions are legitimate numbers locatable on the number line (values greater than one); a fraction a/b (a>1) is b copies of the unit fraction 1/b, so b of them rebuild one whole — the basis for mixed↔improper conversion.
learnerActions: On a number line marked in quarters, add one quarter at a time, counting aloud: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4.
At the 4th quarter, group the four quarters into one whole unit; do the same again at the 8th quarter.
Keep going to the 11th quarter and read off what you have: two whole units with three quarters sitting past them, so 11/4 = 2¾.
Now work the other way for 3⅖: break each of the 3 wholes into fifths (one whole = 5 fifths, so 3 wholes = 15 fifths), then add the 2 extra fifths to get 17/5.
Keep the denominator unchanged throughout, and say the running total in both forms as you go.
activities.intendedInsight: The improper form and the mixed form mark the SAME point: every b copies of 1/b fuse into one whole, and each whole breaks back into b pieces. This is why you multiply 3 × 5 (each whole is 5 fifths) and then add the 2, not add the whole to the numerator.

activities.title: Convert both directions and verify by reversing
feedback: Answers: 11/4 = 2¾ (8/4 = 2 wholes, 3/4 left over); 3⅖ = 17/5 (3 wholes = 15 fifths, plus 2 fifths), denominator unchanged.
If a learner insists 7/4 must become 1¾ to be 'allowed', confirm 7/4 and 1¾ are the same size and that a top-heavy fraction is a legitimate number sitting past 1.
If a learner changes the denominator during conversion, stop and ask what size the pieces are — the piece size (the denominator) does not change, only how they are grouped.
Probe with: 'How many quarters make one whole? So how many quarters are in 2 wholes?' and 'For 3⅖, why work out 3 × 5 before adding the 2 — what does the 15 count?'
activities.rationale: Bidirectional conversion with a built-in reverse-check makes the equality of the two forms explicit (grounded in b copies of 1/b rebuilding a whole) and surfaces the distinct add-to-numerator (5/5), forgot-to-add (15/5), and concatenate (32/5) errors as visibly different wrong answers to diagnose.
sourceClaims: Improper fractions are legitimate numbers locatable on the number line (values greater than one); a fraction a/b (a>1) is b copies of the unit fraction 1/b, so b of them rebuild one whole — the basis for mixed↔improper conversion.
learnerActions: Convert 11/4 to a mixed number and 3⅖ to an improper fraction, showing your working for each.
For the improper→mixed task, state how many wholes you found and how many pieces are left over.
For the mixed→improper task, say out loud what the first product counts (e.g. '15 counts the fifths in 3 wholes') before adding the leftover pieces.
Check each answer by converting it back to the other form and confirming you return to where you started.
Also write 6/5 + 4/5 = 10/5 as both an improper fraction and a whole number (2).
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent two-way conversion with a reverse-check confirms the forms are equal and that improper fractions such as 7/4 or 17/5 are valid answers, not mistakes to be 'fixed'.

activities.title: Reveal the wholes hidden inside an improper fraction (support)
feedback: If the learner marks the wrong number of groups, re-count: four quarters per whole, so eleven quarters give two full groups with three left.

This labelled picture is a reference aid; follow it up by actually performing the grouping and the reverse (breaking wholes back into pieces) so the conversion is practised as a reversible action, not only recognised.
activities.rationale: A labelled static bar helps a learner who needs to first SEE the wholes inside 11/4 before enacting the regrouping; it is a stepping stone toward independent conversion. The source supports the underlying content (whole groups sit inside an improper fraction); the scaffold itself is an unvalidated design choice.
sourceClaims: Improper fractions are legitimate numbers locatable on the number line (values greater than one); a fraction a/b (a>1) is b copies of the unit fraction 1/b, so b of them rebuild one whole — the basis for mixed↔improper conversion.
learnerActions: Look at a bar showing 11/4 drawn as individual quarters.
Circle or mark off the complete groups of four quarters, naming each group as one whole.
Read what is left after grouping and write the mixed number: 2 wholes + 3 quarters = 2¾.
activities.intendedInsight: An improper fraction already contains whole groups; finding them is a matter of grouping b pieces at a time, with the leftover pieces naming the fraction part.

constraints: Keep the denominator unchanged during conversion — only the grouping of equal-sized pieces changes.
Teach mixed→improper as 'each whole is b bths' (3 wholes × 5 = 15 fifths, then add 2), not as a bare '× then add' trick, so the first product is understood as counting pieces.
Treat improper fractions as legitimate numbers, not errors that must always be rewritten as mixed numbers.

The labelled static-bar activity is a scaffold: it can show and name the wholes inside an improper fraction but does not require the learner to enact the reversible grouping, so pair it with hands-on or line-based conversion.

Multiple-choice or fill-in tasks using the distractors 5/5, 15/5 and 32/5 can surface misconceptions, but watching the learner's working (grouping pieces vs. manipulating digits) is what discriminates understanding from a half-remembered rule; a recognition-only response does not by itself show independent construction.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified, and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Depth/3D and open-dialogue formats were noted in the source as weak fits for this quantitative, procedural topic; this was retained as a design observation only and not asserted as a universal pedagogical law.

Worked arithmetic was independently checked: 11/4 = 8/4 + 3/4 = 2¾; 3⅖ = 15 fifths + 2 fifths = 17/5; 6/5 + 4/5 = 10/5 = 2. The distractors 5/5, 15/5, 32/5 are deliberately WRONG answers for diagnosis and must never be presented as correct.
The audible 'click'/'snap' fusing effect from the original recommendation is an optional interaction detail; it is offered as an example of making the grouping concrete, not as a required mechanism.

The area-circle model (two full circles plus three quarters for 11/4) is reinstated from the original key representations as an alternative to the number line/bar; efficacy of any one representation over another is not independently measured here.

The IES/WWC source directly supports the mathematical basis of conversion (b copies of 1/b rebuild one whole; improper fractions as legitimate numbers), not the comparative effectiveness of the specific scaffolds proposed; scaffold choices remain unvalidated.

probeDeeper: How many quarters make one whole? So how many quarters are in 2 whole ones?
For 3⅖, why do we work out 3 × 5 before adding the 2 — what does the 15 count?
Is 7/4 a proper answer, or must it be written as a mixed number? Are 7/4 and 1¾ the same size?
Check your 17/5 by turning it back into a mixed number — what do you get?
assess.correctAnswer: 11/4 = 2¾ (8/4 = 2 wholes, 3/4 left over); 3⅖ = 17/5 (3 wholes = 15 fifths, plus 2 fifths = 17/5), denominator unchanged.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mixed→improper adds the whole number to the numerator: 3⅖ → (3 + 2)/5 = 5/5
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild 3 wholes as fifths on the bar: one whole is 5 fifths, not 1, so 3 wholes = 15 fifths. Then add the 2.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 5/5 (or 5 over 5) for 3⅖; adds 3 + 2

errorPatterns.pattern: Multiplies the whole by the denominator but forgets to add the numerator (15/5), or concatenates the digits (32/5)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the two steps ('three wholes make fifteen fifths… now add the two more fifths'); the method is nearly there — do not reteach the concept.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 15/5 (dropped the +2) or 32/5 (glued 3 and 2); the × b step is present but the +a step is missing or mis-executed

errorPatterns.pattern: Improper→mixed miscounts the wholes: 11/4 → 3¾, or subtracts (11 − 4) to get the numerator
errorPatterns.nextMove: Group the eleven quarters into fours on the bar: two complete groups (2 wholes) with three quarters left.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports the wrong number of wholes, or manipulates 11 and 4 by subtracting rather than grouping into fours

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes an improper fraction is 'not allowed' — calls 11/4 a mistake or insists everything must be written as a mixed number
errorPatterns.nextMove: Iterate unit fractions past the whole on a number line to show 11/4 is a real, legitimate number that simply sits past 1.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a top-heavy fraction is wrong, or refuses to accept 17/5 as a valid answer

responseLevels.gap: Adds the whole to the numerator or miscounts the wholes; treats improper fractions as invalid; changes the denominator.
responseLevels.full: Converts both directions fluently, explains each step from b/b = 1 whole, verifies by converting back, and accepts improper fractions as legitimate numbers; transfers to a new pair.
responseLevels.partial: Converts one direction reliably but stumbles on the other, or reaches the answer by a rule without being able to explain the × b step as 'each whole is b bths'.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Convert 11/4 into a mixed number, and convert 3⅖ into an improper fraction. Show me how you work each one out.' Watch the method for each — do not tell them a rule.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the working shows whether the child groups b bths into wholes (understanding) or manipulates digits by a half-remembered rule. 3⅖ is the hinge for mixed→improper: adding the whole to the numerator gives 5/5, multiplying but forgetting to add gives 15/5, concatenating gives 32/5 — three visibly different wrong answers — while a secure child gets 17/5 and can say why (3 wholes = 15 fifths). The 11/4 direction checks whether they count the wholes correctly.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Mixed & Improper Fractions
topic.description: Use the four operations with formal written methods applied to integers, decimals, proper and improper fractions, and mixed numbers, all both positive and negative
evidence: Add, subtract, multiply, and divide with positive and negative integers
Apply formal written methods to calculations with decimals of any size
Perform all four operations with proper fractions, improper fractions, and mixed numbers
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to work out −1/2 + 3/4 − 1 and 1/4 as part of a longer problem, can they do it using written methods — showing each step clearly?

pedagogy.summary: This KS3 synthesis topic asks pupils to apply formal written methods for all four operations across integers (including negatives), decimals, and proper/improper fractions and mixed numbers. The central difficulty is not any single algorithm but KEEPING THEM APART: IES documents that students — and even many teachers — confuse the procedures, e.g. importing the common-denominator step of addition into multiplication, or leaving the denominator unchanged in multiplication because they meet more addition problems. Add to this negative-number sign handling and the need to convert mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying or dividing. Teach by contrasting the four operations on the SAME operands so pupils see WHEN a common denominator is needed and when it is not, always estimating for reasonableness.
bestPractices: Contrast all four operations on the same pair (e.g. 3/4 and 2/3) so pupils see addition/subtraction need a common denominator while multiplication/division do not
Require an estimate before every calculation to catch mis-applied algorithms and sign errors
Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying or dividing; keep the meaning (measurement/partition) attached to division
Handle negative signs explicitly on a number line and with stated rules, separating 'combining signed quantities' from 'multiplying/dividing signs'
Confront algorithm confusion directly (IES): show a correctly and an incorrectly chosen method side by side and discuss why each is right or wrong
keyRepresentations: A comparison table of +, −, ×, ÷ applied to the same two fractions, exposing which needs a common denominator
Number line for signed-integer addition/subtraction
Improper-fraction rewrites for × and ÷ of mixed numbers
Estimation with benchmarks / whole-number bounds
commonMisconceptions: Applies the wrong algorithm for the operation — finds a common denominator to multiply, or multiplies across to add
Leaves the denominator unchanged in multiplication, or seeks a common denominator in multiplication/division
Sign errors with negatives (e.g. −5 + 3 treated as −(5+3), or confusing −×− with −+−)
Multiplies or divides mixed numbers without first converting to improper fractions (distributes incompletely)

learn.summary: KS3 pupils apply formal written methods for all four operations across integers (including negatives), decimals, and proper/improper fractions and mixed numbers. The central difficulty is not any single algorithm but keeping them apart: students (and even some teachers) confuse the procedures — importing addition's common-denominator step into multiplication, or leaving a denominator unchanged in multiplication. Add negative-sign handling and the standard step of converting mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying or dividing, since working on the mixed form directly is only correct if every part is fully distributed. Teach by contrasting the four operations on the SAME operands so pupils see when a common denominator is needed and when it is not, always estimating for reasonableness.

activities.title: Same two fractions, four operations
feedback: If a learner finds a common denominator to multiply (3/4 × 2/3 recut to 9/12 × 8/12 first), point out that this step is unnecessary. It only gives a wrong answer if the shared denominator is kept (72/12 instead of 72/144 = 1/2). Contrast it directly with the standard method on the same pair and name the principle: multiplication scales, so you multiply numerators and multiply denominators (4×3 = 12).
If a learner multiplies across to add (3/4 + 2/3 → 6/12), re-establish that addition combines same-size parts, which first requires recutting to a common denominator.
If the estimate and exact answer disagree (e.g. an answer less than 1 for 3/4 + 2/3), treat the mismatch as a signal to recheck which method was used.
activities.rationale: Running the same operands through contrasting operations makes method-selection visible and structural rather than memorised; a side-by-side comparison exposes the documented algorithm confusion.
sourceClaims: Students and even many teachers confuse the algorithms for adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing fractions, and over-generalise a rule that fits one operation to another (e.g. leaving the denominator unchanged in multiplication, or seeking a common denominator where multiplication does not need one); the panel recommends confronting these confusions directly.
learnerActions: Fix two operands, e.g. 3/4 and 2/3, and work all four operations on this same pair, writing out each method.
For addition and subtraction, recut both to a common denominator (9/12 and 8/12) before combining: 3/4 + 2/3 = 9/12 + 8/12 = 17/12 = 1 5/12.
For multiplication, multiply across without a common denominator: 3/4 × 2/3 = 6/12 = 1/2 — notice a common denominator is NOT needed here.
State out loud or in writing when a common denominator is required and when it is not, and say why (addition combines same-size parts; multiplication scales).
Before each calculation, estimate: should 3/4 + 2/3 be more or less than 1? Check your exact answer agrees.
activities.intendedInsight: Whether a common denominator is needed is a structural feature of the OPERATION, not a ritual applied to every fraction calculation: addition/subtraction combine same-size parts (need a common denominator) while multiplication/division scale (do not, in the standard methods).

activities.title: Spot the wrong method
feedback: When a learner catches a common-denominator step inside a multiplication, confirm it and have them restate why multiplication does not need one.
When a learner catches an add-across in an addition, confirm it and have them restate why same-size parts must be made first.
If a learner cannot spot the error, return to the same-operands comparison and let them rebuild the correct method before re-attempting.
activities.rationale: Directly confronting the misconception — showing a correctly and an incorrectly chosen method side by side — is the recommended response to algorithm confusion.
sourceClaims: Students and even many teachers confuse the algorithms for adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing fractions, and over-generalise a rule that fits one operation to another (e.g. leaving the denominator unchanged in multiplication, or seeking a common denominator where multiplication does not need one); the panel recommends confronting these confusions directly.
learnerActions: Examine worked examples where an algorithm has been mis-applied: a multiplication where the common denominator was kept (e.g. 9/12 × 8/12 written as 72/12), or an addition done straight across.
Catch the error, name which operation's method was wrongly imported, and redo the calculation correctly.
Match each incorrect worked example to the specific error it contains.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to diagnose a wrongly chosen method gives evidence that the pupil distinguishes the procedures, though it should be confirmed by the pupil producing correct methods; it confronts the exact confusion documented as tripping up students and teachers alike.

activities.title: Signed integers on a number line
feedback: If a learner gives −8 for −5 + 3, they have treated it as −(5+3); walk the move of 3 to the right from −5 to land at −2.
If a learner gives 8, the sign has been dropped; re-model the starting point at −5 and the direction of the move to land at −2.
Reinforce by distinguishing −×− (sign rule for multiplication) from −+− (combining on the line).
activities.rationale: A number line makes the direction and magnitude of combining signed quantities concrete and separates it from sign-rule arithmetic for multiplication and division.
learnerActions: Model −5 + 3 as a move of 3 to the right starting from −5, landing at −2.
Answer: is −5 + 3 bigger or smaller than −5, which direction do you move, and why?
Separate 'combining signed quantities' (addition/subtraction) from 'multiplying/dividing signs', stating the rule for each.
Estimate and check: does combining a negative with a positive of smaller magnitude (e.g. −5 + 3) stay negative?
activities.intendedInsight: Adding a positive to a negative moves right along the number line, toward zero and past it if the positive has the larger magnitude (e.g. −5 + 8 = 3); the sign is not simply inherited and magnitudes are not simply summed. Combining signed quantities is a different process from multiplying/dividing signs.

activities.title: Convert mixed numbers before × and ÷
feedback: If a learner multiplies/divides only the whole-number part, show how the fractional part is dropped and return to the improper-fraction rewrite.

If a learner keeps only one denominator when multiplying the improper forms (e.g. 5/2 × 2/3 → 10/2 instead of 10/6), return to the area meaning: both denominators partition the unit, so both are multiplied (2×3 = 6).
activities.rationale: Converting to improper fractions first and anchoring division in its measurement/partition meaning prevents incomplete distribution and keeps the computation meaningful.
learnerActions: Rewrite a mixed number as an improper fraction before multiplying or dividing, e.g. 2 1/2 = 5/2.
Divide: 2 1/2 ÷ 1/2 by working from the improper form 5/2 ÷ 1/2.
Keep the meaning of division attached — for example reading a division as 'how many halves fit?' — and check the answer makes sense.
Estimate first so an incomplete distribution (multiplying only the whole part) is caught.
activities.intendedInsight: Converting mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying or dividing is the standard, reliable method; working on the mixed form directly often leads to incomplete distribution (e.g. operating on only the whole part) unless every part is distributed.

constraints: Scored multiple-choice or sorting tasks (e.g. 'which method does this need?', sorting calculations into needs/does-not-need a common denominator, matching a wrong worked example to its error) may efficiently check which method a pupil selects and surface algorithm confusion, but recognition of a method is not the same as producing one: such tasks do not themselves require a pupil to construct and justify a full written method, so pair them with pupils writing out and explaining their own working.

A static comparison chart of the four operations on one pair (tap-to-reveal each worked method, lift-the-flap 'why does × not need a common denominator?') supports the contrast but cannot let a pupil test method-selection on new operands; use it as a reference scaffold, not the main task.
Always require an estimate before each calculation to catch mis-applied algorithms and sign errors.
Watch and discuss the written method, not just the final answer, since the imported procedure is where the confusion shows.

A tutor-style 'which method and why?' dialogue can press past 'because that's the rule' and surface a pupil's reasoning, but the computation and the signed/mixed manipulations need a visual or symbolic working surface alongside it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 3/4 + 2/3 = 9/12 + 8/12 = 17/12 = 1 5/12 ✓; 3/4 × 2/3 = 6/12 = 1/2 ✓; −5 + 3 = −2 ✓; 2 1/2 = 5/2 ✓; 5/2 ÷ 1/2 = 5 ✓; 5/2 × 2/3 = 10/6 ✓. The listed misconception endpoints (−8, 8, 10/2, keeping one denominator) are labelled as errors, not as valid answers.

Multiplication (and standard division) 'not needing' a common denominator is correct as a standard-method statement; an equivalent-fractions or common-denominator-division route can incidentally share a denominator but is never required. Kept scoped to the required method.

The KS3 curriculum source claim establishes the overall synthesis requirement (all four operations across integers, decimals, proper/improper fractions and mixed numbers, positive and negative) but is not attached to any activity's sourceClaims, because no individual activity rationale depends on that requirement specifically rather than on the method-contrast principle.

sourceClaims on the signed-integer and mixed-number activities are [] because the two available sources address fraction algorithm confusion and the KS3 curriculum requirement, not number-line sign handling or conversion efficacy specifically.

The decimals strand of the objective is named in the summary but has no dedicated activity; a formal-written-method decimals task would complete coverage and could reuse the estimate-first and show-your-method constraints.

probeDeeper: Why does the addition need a common denominator but the multiplication doesn't?
Is −5 + 3 bigger or smaller than −5 — which way do you move on the number line, and why?
Turn 2 1/2 into an improper fraction — how would you then divide it by 1/2?
Estimate 3/4 + 2/3 — should it be more or less than 1, and does your exact answer agree?

errorPatterns.pattern: Imports the wrong algorithm: finds a common denominator to MULTIPLY (3/4 × 2/3 → recuts to twelfths first), or multiplies across to ADD (3/4 + 2/3 → 6/12)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the two on the same operands and name the principle — addition combines same-size parts (needs a common denominator), multiplication scales (does not); re-establish the ± common-denominator method
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The method for (b) shows a common-denominator step, or (a) shows a straight-across multiplication; the two operations are handled by the same ritual

errorPatterns.pattern: Leaves a denominator unchanged in multiplication: 3/4 × 2/3 → 6/4 (or 6/3), multiplying numerators but keeping one denominator
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the area meaning of fraction multiplication — both denominators partition the unit — so both are multiplied; recompute on a tiled square
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Product keeps an original denominator rather than 4×3 = 12

errorPatterns.pattern: Sign error combining signed integers: −5 + 3 treated as −(5+3) = −8, or the sign dropped to give 8
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model −5 + 3 as a move of 3 to the right from −5 on a number line, landing at −2; separate combining signed quantities from multiplying signs
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer −8 or 8; the 3 is added to the magnitude or the sign is mishandled

responseLevels.gap: Confuses the algorithms (common denominator in ×, or add-across in +) and/or makes sign errors; no reliable method-selection.
responseLevels.full: Selects and applies the correct method for each operation fluently across fractions, mixed numbers and signed integers, converts to improper fractions for ×/÷, handles signs on a number line, estimates for reasonableness, and transfers to unfamiliar mixed cases.
responseLevels.partial: Each operation is correct in isolation but the child hesitates or slips when operations are interleaved, does not convert mixed numbers to improper before ×/÷, and offers no estimate to check.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out, showing your method for each: (a) 3/4 + 2/3; (b) 3/4 × 2/3; (c) −5 + 3.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Pairing addition and multiplication of the SAME fractions is the trap for algorithm confusion: a child who genuinely distinguishes the methods finds a common denominator for (a) and multiplies straight across for (b); a confused child either seeks a common denominator in (b) or multiplies across in (a). The signed item (c) separates 'combining signed quantities' from magnitude arithmetic — −2 versus −8 or 8. Watching the written method, not just the answers, shows exactly which procedure was imported where.
